questions.strategy: Chvostek sign is the answer students remember, which makes it the distractor. It confirms the problem; stridor is the emergency.

steps.detail: The parathyroid glands can be damaged during thyroid surgery.
Only one option is about breathing.
Chvostek sign and cramps confirm the problem; stridor is the danger.

elimination.verdict: Noisy high-pitched breathing. The airway comes first.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old taking hydrochlorothiazide has a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L. Which finding is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Reports mild nausea and a poor appetite
options.rationale: A real finding in hyponatremia, and it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous.

options.text: New confusion and difficulty staying awake since this morning
options.rationale: Cerebral change. Water is moving into brain cells inside a rigid skull, and confusion and lethargy are the steps before seizures and coma.

options.text: Urine output of 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. Nothing to act on.

options.text: Dry oral mucous membranes
options.rationale: Points to volume status, which matters for choosing treatment. It does not threaten her the way the brain change does.

questions.takeaway: In sodium imbalance, the brain is the organ at risk. A change in level of consciousness is the finding you act on first.
questions.strategy: Every option could appear in a patient with low sodium. Ask which one belongs to the organ that cannot swell safely.

steps.detail: Sodium moves water into and out of brain cells.
40 mL per hour is fine.
Nausea and dry mucosa are uncomfortable. New confusion is progressing.

elimination.verdict: New confusion and lethargy. Protect the brain first.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old patient taking furosemide was admitted with a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. The admission ECG showed flat T waves with prominent U waves. Bowel sounds were hypoactive. The patient has received IV potassium chloride by infusion pump at 10 mEq/hr. Which finding shows the nurse that the potassium replacement is achieving the expected outcome?

options.text: Tall peaked T waves with a widened QRS on the monitor
options.rationale: These are signs of high potassium. They mean the replacement has overshot and the nurse must stop the infusion and report.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds with abdominal cramping
options.rationale: An irritable gut is a finding of high potassium. It suggests overcorrection and needs follow up.

options.text: Upright T waves with no U waves visible on the monitor
options.rationale: Flat T waves and U waves are the low potassium ECG. Their disappearance shows that the potassium is back toward 3.5 to 5.0.

options.text: Bowel sounds remain hypoactive and the patient reports constipation
options.rationale: These are the same slowed findings the patient had on admission. They show the low potassium has not resolved yet.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium slows things: flat T waves, U waves and a sluggish gut. High potassium irritates things: peaked T waves and diarrhea. When you evaluate replacement, look for the low findings to fade without the high findings appearing.
questions.strategy: Sort each option into low potassium, normal or high potassium. A finding that stays low means not yet. A finding that turns high means too much. Only a return to normal means the plan worked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Peaked T waves are high potassium. Upright T waves without U waves are normal.
Hyperactive cramping is high. Hypoactive sounds are still low.
Only the ECG that has returned to normal shows the goal was met.

elimination.verdict: C. The other options show the problem persisting or the replacement overshooting.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer has a serum calcium of 13.1 mg/dL. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate implementing first to lower the calcium?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Normal saline helps the kidneys excrete calcium and corrects the dehydration that often comes with it.

options.text: IV furosemide started right away
options.rationale: A loop diuretic increases calcium excretion. It is given once fluid volume is restored, because diuresing a dry patient worsens the dehydration.

options.text: A bisphosphonate as prescribed
options.rationale: It keeps calcium in the bone instead of the blood. It is part of the plan but does not come before hydration.

options.text: Hold oral calcium supplements
options.rationale: Stop every source of calcium. Holding a supplement does not remove the calcium already in the blood.

questions.takeaway: For hypercalcemia: flush with normal saline first, then add a loop diuretic once volume is restored. Stop the sources, keep calcium in the bone and put the patient on a monitor.
questions.strategy: All four options belong in the plan. The question is order. Furosemide is the correct drug at the wrong time if the patient is still dry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what each option does to calcium
steps.detail: All four help lower it or keep it from rising.
Hydration comes before diuresis.
Holding a supplement and a bisphosphonate do not clear the calcium already in the blood.

elimination.verdict: A. Normal saline comes first.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use is admitted with a magnesium of 1.1 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse expect?

options.text: Absent deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: That is high magnesium.

options.text: Respiratory depression
options.rationale: High magnesium depresses breathing. Low magnesium does not.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes nerves excitable, the same as low calcium. Brisk reflexes are the deck's key sign of low magnesium.

options.text: Flushing and a feeling of warmth
options.rationale: Flushing comes from the vasodilation of high magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium looks like low calcium: Chvostek sign, brisk reflexes, tetany, prolonged QT. It also travels with low potassium and low calcium, so replace magnesium to fix them.
questions.strategy: Three options belong to high magnesium. Decide the direction first, then pick the finding that matches.

steps.detail: 1.1 is low. Low magnesium means excitable.
Absent reflexes, slowed breathing and flushing all belong to high magnesium.
Hyperactive reflexes are the odd one out and the answer.

elimination.verdict: C. Low magnesium gives brisk reflexes.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L, heart rate 48, tall peaked T waves on the monitor
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes and bradycardia means the heart is already affected. The next rhythm may be ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.3 mEq/L, reports leg cramps, taking oral potassium with breakfast
options.rationale: Low, treated, and the symptom is expected. Stable.

options.text: Serum sodium 133 mEq/L, alert, eating breakfast
options.rationale: Just below range with no symptoms.

options.text: Serum potassium 5.3 mEq/L, normal sinus rhythm, no complaints
options.rationale: Mildly high with a normal rhythm. Recheck it and review medications, but the heart is not affected yet.

questions.takeaway: In hyperkalemia, ECG changes mean the heart is already involved. A high potassium with peaked T waves and bradycardia beats every other abnormal lab on the floor.
questions.strategy: Two patients have high potassium. The ECG tells you which one is unstable.

steps.detail: Only option A has rhythm changes.

steps.action: Compare the two high potassium patients
steps.detail: 5.3 with a normal rhythm is stable. 6.4 with peaked T waves is not.
Cramps with a low potassium that is being replaced are expected.

elimination.verdict: Potassium 6.4 with peaked T waves and bradycardia.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for two patients. The first has a serum osmolarity of 312 mOsm/L, which is above the normal range of 270 to 300 mOsm/L. The provider orders 0.45% sodium chloride. The nurse expects it to move water into the shrunken cells. The second patient has new swelling of the brain. The provider orders the same fluid for this patient. The nurse questions the second order. Which rationale supports the nurse's decision?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride contains too much sodium
options.rationale: It contains half the sodium of plasma.

options.text: Hypotonic fluid expands plasma volume too quickly
options.rationale: Most of it leaves the vessels. The danger is where the water goes, not how fast the plasma grows.

options.text: A hypotonic fluid moves water into brain cells and can worsen the swelling
options.rationale: The brain sits in a rigid skull with little room to swell. Adding free water to swollen cells raises intracranial pressure.

options.text: Only colloids can be given to patients with neurologic problems
options.rationale: An absolute that is not true. Isotonic crystalloids are commonly used.

questions.takeaway: Water follows solute. Hypotonic fluid swells cells, hypertonic fluid shrinks them. Colloids hold water in the vessels by oncotic pressure.
questions.strategy: For each fluid, ask where the water will end up. Then ask whether that place needs water or is already swollen. The same movement that helps the first patient harms the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic. It has half the sodium of plasma, so A is false.
Hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels and moves into cells. B worries about the wrong compartment.
"Only colloids" is not true for neurologic patients.
Free water into swollen brain cells raises intracranial pressure.

elimination.verdict: C. Hypotonic fluid worsens brain swelling.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old is on postoperative day 1 after a hip repair. She has received lactated Ringer's at 125 mL per hour plus two 500 mL boluses for low urine output overnight. Weight is 64.3 kg, up from 62.1 kg before surgery. Vital signs at 0400 were BP 132/78, HR 84, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air. At 0800 they are BP 158/90, HR 96 and bounding, RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air. Neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees. Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Urine output was 30 mL per hour for the last 2 hours. Hematocrit is 31%, down from 36% before surgery. Serum sodium is 133 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give another 500 mL bolus because urine output is only 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: This is the order that caused the problem. 30 mL/hr is at the usual minimum. Her rising BP, bounding pulse, neck vein distention and crackles show overload. More fluid pushes her toward pulmonary edema.

options.text: Slow the infusion to the lowest prescribed rate and notify the provider
options.rationale: She has fluid volume excess. She is receiving more fluid than her heart and kidneys can handle. You stop adding to the problem first, then get a prescription such as a loop diuretic.

options.text: Recheck lung sounds, respiratory rate and SpO2 in 1 hour to confirm the trend
options.rationale: Monitoring the lungs is correct because worsening crackles and falling saturation show pulmonary edema progressing. The trend is already confirmed over 4 hours. Waiting another hour while the fluid runs lets her get worse.

options.text: Weigh her daily on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing
options.rationale: The deck calls rapid weight gain the best indicator of fluid overload. One liter of fluid weighs about 1 kg. Daily weight tracks her response over days. It does nothing for her lungs this morning.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult receiving IV fluid, rising weight, bounding pulse, distended neck veins and new crackles mean overload. Stop adding fluid first. Then sit her up and watch the lungs.
questions.strategy: Two findings (low urine output and a falling hematocrit) look like bleeding. Read the whole trend. Rising BP with bounding pulse and neck vein distention cannot be hypovolemia. Her hematocrit is low because the blood is diluted.

steps.action: Name the problem from the trend
steps.detail: BP, HR and RR all rose over 4 hours while SpO2 fell. Weight is up 2.2 kg. This is fluid volume excess.
A diluted hematocrit falls in overload too. Bleeding would flatten the neck veins and weaken the pulse.
The bolus makes pulmonary edema worse.
Rechecking in an hour and a daily weight are monitoring. The data already calls for action. Stopping the source comes first.

elimination.verdict: B.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews data for four patients on a medical unit. Which patient's findings reflect a response caused primarily by aldosterone?

options.text: A 70-year-old has gone 14 hours without water. Serum osmolarity is 308 mOsm/L. Urine output is 20 mL/hr and dark amber.
options.rationale: High osmolarity triggers ADH from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys keep water alone, so the urine becomes small and concentrated.

options.text: A 64-year-old with heart failure has a weight gain of 3 kg with distended neck veins. The body responds by excreting sodium and water.
options.rationale: High volume stretches the heart, which releases natriuretic peptides. They get rid of sodium and water, which is the opposite of aldosterone.

options.text: A 55-year-old has a serum sodium of 131 mEq/L. The kidneys respond by reabsorbing sodium and water. The serum potassium falls to 3.3 mEq/L.
options.rationale: Low sodium triggers aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. The kidney keeps sodium with water and excretes potassium, which explains the falling potassium.

options.text: A 68-year-old with SIADH has concentrated urine with weight gain. The serum sodium is 126 mEq/L.
options.rationale: Too much ADH keeps too much water. The water dilutes the sodium even though no sodium was lost.

questions.takeaway: ADH keeps water. Aldosterone keeps sodium with water while it excretes potassium. Natriuretic peptides from the heart get rid of sodium and water.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each patient. What triggered the response? What is the kidney keeping? Water alone means ADH. Sodium with water means aldosterone. Losing both means natriuretic peptides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: High osmolarity points to ADH. Low sodium points to aldosterone. High volume points to the heart.
A and D keep water alone. B keeps nothing. C keeps sodium with water.
Only aldosterone trades sodium for potassium.

elimination.verdict: C. Low sodium triggers aldosterone, which keeps sodium while it loses potassium.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews this admission note: 84-year-old admitted from home with new confusion that her daughter noticed yesterday. Takes hydrochlorothiazide and lisinopril daily and a laxative most nights. States she is not thirsty. Skin on the back of the hand stays tented for several seconds. Skin over the sternum stays tented. BP 142/80 lying and 114/66 standing, with dizziness on standing. Urine output 380 mL in the last 24 hours, dark amber. Hematocrit 48%, up from 41% at a clinic visit last month. Lungs clear; no peripheral edema. Which assessment finding is a reliable sign of fluid volume deficit in this patient rather than an age-related change?

options.text: Skin on the back of the hand stays tented for several seconds
options.rationale: Aging skin loses elasticity, so the hand is unreliable. This finding may be present even with normal hydration.

options.text: States she is not thirsty
options.rationale: A blunted thirst reflex is an age-related cause of deficit named in class. It explains why she did not replace her losses. It is a cause, not a sign. It is not reassurance.

options.text: Lungs clear; no peripheral edema
options.rationale: Normal findings. They argue against overload but do not show a deficit.

options.text: Skin over the sternum stays tented
options.rationale: The sternum is the correct site in older adults. Tenting here points to a real deficit.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, check turgor at the sternum. Read the hematocrit trend. Treat new confusion as a possible fluid problem. A lack of thirst is not reassurance.
questions.strategy: Hand turgor is the trap: aging skin makes it unreliable. Denying thirst is a blunted reflex that helps explain the deficit. It does not prove one. Ask which finding still means something in an 84-year-old.

steps.detail: Reliable sign, rather than an age-related change.
Hand and sternum are a pair. In older adults only the sternum counts.
Blunted thirst is itself an age-related change. It explains the deficit but does not confirm it.
Clear lungs and no edema rule out overload. They do not show a deficit.

elimination.verdict: D, sternal tenting.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with chronic kidney disease had a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L at 1200 with peaked T waves. At 1300 the nurse gave IV calcium gluconate, regular insulin 10 units IV with 25 g of dextrose. The nurse also gave a dose of sodium polystyrene sulfonate. At 1400 the patient is sweating and says his hands feel shaky. Potassium is 5.9 mEq/L. Capillary glucose is 54 mg/dL. Heart rate is 76 and the T waves are less peaked. He has had two loose stools. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Potassium of 5.9 mEq/L
options.rationale: Still above 5.0, but it fell 0.9 mEq/L within an hour of treatment. The treatment is working, so this is a trend to keep watching rather than a new problem.

options.text: Glucose of 54 mg/dL with sweating and shakiness
options.rationale: Correct. Insulin moves potassium into cells. It moves glucose in too. Dextrose was given to prevent exactly this, yet he is now hypoglycemic with symptoms. Low glucose can progress to seizures and loss of consciousness within minutes, so it needs treatment now.

options.text: Two loose stools since the binder was given
options.rationale: Expected. The binder pulls potassium into the gut. The stool is how it leaves the body. This means the drug is doing its job.

options.text: T waves that are still slightly peaked
options.rationale: The ECG is moving toward normal as the potassium falls. Calcium also protects the heart muscle while the level comes down. Improvement is not a reason to act.

questions.takeaway: After insulin and dextrose for hyperkalemia, watch the glucose as closely as the potassium. The deck names rebound hypoglycemia as a treatment risk.
questions.strategy: Three options describe hyperkalemia getting better. One describes a new problem caused by the treatment. The new problem wins.

steps.action: Read each value as a trend
steps.detail: Potassium is falling and the ECG is improving. Both show the treatment working.
Loose stools are the expected effect of the binder.
A glucose of 54 with symptoms is a complication of insulin that can quickly harm the brain.

elimination.verdict: Glucose 54 with symptoms. Treat the hypoglycemia the insulin caused.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old from a care facility was admitted at 0600 with a serum sodium of 164 mEq/L after several days of fever and poor intake. D5W was started at 150 mL per hour. At 1400 the sodium is 151 mEq/L. Urine output has been 45 mL per hour. The patient was more alert at noon but now reports a headache and has vomited once. The patient is also harder to rouse than an hour ago. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Increase the D5W rate because the sodium is still above 145 mEq/L
options.rationale: The number is still high, but lowering it faster is exactly what is causing harm. This moves in the wrong direction.

options.text: Stop or slow the D5W and notify the provider of the rapid fall in sodium and the neurologic change
options.rationale: Correct. The sodium dropped 13 mEq/L in 8 hours. When sodium falls quickly, water rushes into brain cells that had adapted to the high level. The brain swells inside the rigid skull. Headache, vomiting and a falling level of consciousness are the signs. The deck says to lower sodium gradually for this reason.

options.text: Give the ordered acetaminophen and antiemetic and recheck in an hour
options.rationale: These treat the symptoms but leave the cause running. Waiting an hour lets more free water reach the brain.

options.text: Encourage the patient to drink water to replace free water by mouth
options.rationale: The deck does recommend oral water for older adults with hypernatremia. Here it adds more free water to a brain that is already swelling. A patient who is vomiting and hard to rouse cannot safely swallow.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia is corrected slowly. New headache, vomiting or a drop in consciousness during treatment points to cerebral edema from correcting too fast.
questions.strategy: The patient was improving and then got worse while the sodium was still high. Ask what changed. The answer is the speed of the fall.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 164 to 151 in 8 hours is a fast drop.

steps.action: Link the trend to the findings
steps.detail: Headache, vomiting and new drowsiness are signs of brain swelling.
Raising the rate and pushing oral water both speed the shift.
Medications for headache and nausea leave the cause in place.

elimination.verdict: Slow the hypotonic fluid and report it. The fall was too fast.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient with heart failure was admitted with fluid overload. Admission findings were weight 88.4 kg, BP 164/94, a bounding pulse of 104, distended neck veins and crackles in both lung bases. The patient receives IV furosemide twice daily with a fluid and sodium restriction. On day 3, which finding best indicates that the diuretic therapy is achieving the expected outcome?

options.text: Weight of 86.1 kg on the same scale with lung sounds now clear
options.rationale: A loss of 2.3 kg means about 2.3 liters of fluid have left the body. Clear lungs show that the priority goal of preventing pulmonary edema is being met.

options.text: Intake of 2,600 mL with an output of 1,800 mL over the last 24 hours
options.rationale: Intake exceeds measured output by 800 mL. The balance is still positive, so this finding does not show that fluid is leaving.

options.text: Pulse full and bounding at 102 beats a minute
options.rationale: A bounding pulse is a sign of fluid overload. It shows the excess volume is still present.

options.text: Serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L
options.rationale: Furosemide causes potassium loss. This is an adverse effect that needs follow up rather than evidence that the fluid overload is resolving.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate diuretic therapy for fluid overload with daily weight, lung sounds, neck veins and intake and output. A low potassium on a loop diuretic is a side effect to report, not a sign of success.
questions.strategy: The question asks whether the fluid problem is resolving. Choose the option where the overload findings have improved. Cut the option that describes a side effect, even though it is true.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Remove extra fluid and prevent pulmonary edema.

steps.action: Check each finding against the goal
steps.detail: A positive balance and a bounding pulse mean overload remains.
A low potassium is real but it measures harm from the drug, not the outcome.

elimination.verdict: A. Weight loss with clear lungs shows the fluid is leaving.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old patient with chronic kidney disease has a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves on the monitor. The nurse administered IV calcium, then regular insulin IV with dextrose, then patiromer as prescribed. One hour later, which finding shows the nurse that the treatment has lowered the serum potassium as intended?

options.text: Repeat serum potassium of 5.0 mEq/L with smaller T waves on the monitor
options.rationale: Insulin shifts potassium from the blood into the cells. The patiromer removes it through the gut. A value back at the top of the 3.5 to 5.0 range with a flatter T wave shows the plan worked.

options.text: The heart rhythm stabilized within minutes of the IV calcium
options.rationale: IV calcium protects the heart muscle. It does not lower the potassium, so a stable rhythm alone does not show the level has fallen.

options.text: Blood glucose of 54 mg/dL with diaphoresis
options.rationale: This is hypoglycemia from the insulin. It is a complication that needs immediate follow up.

options.text: Continued tingling with new weakness in both legs
options.rationale: Early tingling that moves on to weakness from the feet upward is a sign of worsening hyperkalemia. The problem is progressing.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium protects the heart without lowering potassium. Insulin with dextrose shifts potassium into cells. Binders remove it. Evaluate the result with a repeat potassium level and the ECG. Watch for hypoglycemia and rebound hypokalemia.
questions.strategy: The stem asks which finding shows the potassium has fallen. Only a lab value with a matching ECG change measures that. The calcium option is the trap because it looks like success.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A lower serum potassium.
Calcium stabilizes the heart. It does not change the level.
Low glucose and ascending weakness need follow up.

elimination.verdict: A. The repeat level with smaller T waves is direct evidence the potassium fell.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is 3 days post stroke. Her Snellen result is 20/30 with her glasses. She repeats a whispered word correctly with each ear. At lunch she calls her water cup a hat. When the call bell chimes she says the doorbell is ringing. At which stage of sensory experience does the nurse place her deficit?

options.text: Reception
options.rationale: Reception is stimulation of the sensory receptors. Her acuity and whisper results show that light and sound are reaching the receptors.

options.text: Perception
options.rationale: Perception is the brain interpreting the stimulus. It depends on the cortex, which the stroke affected. Intact receptors with a wrong interpretation place the deficit here.

options.text: Reaction
options.rationale: Reaction is the response to the stimulus. She is responding. She is responding to a misread signal.

options.text: Sensory deprivation
options.rationale: Deprivation is too little meaningful stimulation. Nothing in the data shows an isolated or restricted setting. The stimuli are present and misinterpreted.

questions.takeaway: Reception, perception, reaction. Normal acuity and hearing tests clear reception. Misreading what arrives after a stroke points to perception.
questions.strategy: The stem gives you normal test results on purpose. Use them to rule out the first stage before you look at the behavior.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vision at 20/30 and a correct whisper test.
The stimulus is reaching the receptors.
She misinterprets what arrives. That is perception.

elimination.verdict: Perception. The stroke damaged interpretation, not sensing.

questions.stem: A patient in intensive care on day three is agitated, cannot follow a sentence, and keeps pulling at the telemetry leads. There is no delirium screening tool result and the neurologic exam is unchanged. Which nursing action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain an order for soft wrist restraints
options.rationale: The trap, and it looks like safety. Restraints treat the behavior and leave the cause running, and every alternative comes first.

options.text: Cluster care and provide an uninterrupted quiet period
options.rationale: The picture is sensory overload: three days of alarms, lights, multiple caregivers and no protected sleep. Reducing input is the intervention that addresses the cause.

options.text: Request a psychiatric consultation for the agitation
options.rationale: Escalates a problem the nurse can address, and it leaves the environment unchanged in the meantime.

options.text: Increase orientation by explaining each piece of equipment in detail
options.rationale: Orientation helps deprivation. This patient is receiving too much input already, so more talking adds to the load.

questions.takeaway: A client pulling at lines because of sensory overload does not need restraints, needs the overload reduced. Least restrictive intervention first, and cluster care is that intervention.
questions.strategy: Two options add something and one removes freedom. Only one option reduces what is actually driving the behavior.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three days of unrelieved stimulation.
Never before alternatives, and it does not address the cause.
Right for deprivation, wrong for overload.
Escalates before acting.

elimination.verdict: Cluster care and protect sleep. Any item pairing restraints with a less restrictive option is testing least restrictive first.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is described by staff as "becoming demented." He has been withdrawn, answers questions incorrectly and has stopped joining meals. Which action by the nurse is the priority?

options.text: Check his ear canals, glasses and medication list for a reversible cause
options.rationale: Uncorrected hearing or vision loss produces withdrawal and misunderstanding that look exactly like cognitive decline. Drugs are the first hypothesis for a new symptom in an older adult, not the last.

options.text: Request a referral for cognitive testing
options.rationale: Formal testing has a place once reversible causes are ruled out. Ordering it first accepts the label before it has been tested.

options.text: Encourage him to join the other residents at meals
options.rationale: An unstimulating environment does produce withdrawal. Encouragement treats the behavior without looking for its cause.

options.text: Document the behavior change and reassess in one week
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. A week of untreated reversible deficit is a week of avoidable disability.

questions.takeaway: Uncorrected sensory deficit imitates dementia and is reversible. Check the glasses, the hearing aid, the ear canal and the medication list before anyone writes the word confusion.
questions.strategy: Three options accept the description of dementia. One tests it.

steps.detail: Documentation follows the intervention. It does not replace it.
It is the right step at the wrong time.
It treats a behavior before its cause is known.
Ears, eyes and drugs are all reversible.

elimination.verdict: A. New is never normal aging.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a hospital room for a patient who is newly blind. Which action best promotes safety?

options.text: Rearrange the furniture so the path to the bathroom is shortest
options.rationale: Well intentioned and dangerous. A blind patient navigates by a memorized layout, and moving furniture removes the map.

options.text: Orient the patient to the room and then leave everything where it is
options.rationale: Predictability is the safety intervention. Once the layout is learned, it has to stay constant, and anything moved gets announced.

options.text: Keep the room dimly lit to reduce glare and confusion
options.rationale: Light level is irrelevant to a patient with no usable vision and creates a hazard for everyone else in the room.

options.text: Use the call light to summon the patient rather than entering unannounced
options.rationale: The call light summons the nurse, not the patient. What matters is that staff identify themselves on entering and say when they leave.

questions.takeaway: For a visual deficit, safety is built out of consistency: a predictable layout, announced entries and exits, and nothing moved without telling the patient.
questions.strategy: Three options change something about the environment. The correct one is the only one that keeps it still.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a blind patient navigates by
steps.detail: Memory of a fixed layout.
It erases the map.
Irrelevant to no usable vision.
It runs the wrong direction.

elimination.verdict: Orient once, then keep the room constant.

questions.stem: A patient who reads lips is admitted to a unit where staff wear masks. Which adaptation best preserves effective communication?

options.text: Speak more loudly through the mask so the words carry
options.rationale: Volume is not the problem. A mask removes the visual half of the message, and raising the pitch makes a high-frequency loss worse.

options.text: Use a clear-window mask or written communication, and confirm with teach-back
options.rationale: Restores the visual channel or replaces it, and teach-back is how you verify the message actually arrived rather than assuming a nod means understanding.

options.text: Ask a family member to relay all instructions by phone
options.rationale: Offloads the nurse's legal duty onto a third party and introduces a second chance for the message to be lost.

options.text: Shorten conversations to reduce the patient's frustration
options.rationale: Reduces the burden on the nurse and the information reaching the patient. Frustration is not the safety risk; missed information is.

questions.takeaway: Effective communication is a legal and ethical requirement. When the visual channel is removed, you restore it or replace it, and you verify with teach-back.
questions.strategy: One option is louder, one is shorter, one delegates. None of those puts the information back.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The lips and the expression.
Shouting raises pitch into the lost range.
Both reduce the information the patient receives.

elimination.verdict: Restore the visual channel and confirm with teach-back. Nodding is not comprehension.

questions.scenario: A nurse rounds on four patients in different areas of the hospital.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the environment places them at risk for sensory deprivation or sensory overload.

rows.text: In protective isolation in a windowless room with no clock, television or visitors
rows.rationale: Isolation, no natural light, no time cues and nothing meaningful coming in. Every element of deprivation at once.

rows.text: Day three in intensive care with continuous alarms, hourly assessments and no protected sleep
rows.rationale: More input than the patient can sort, with no recovery period. This is the picture that produces agitation and pulling at lines.

rows.text: An older adult whose glasses and hearing aid were left at home on admission
rows.rationale: The stimulus is present and cannot reach the patient. An uncorrected deficit produces withdrawal and misunderstanding that imitate dementia.

rows.text: In the emergency department during a busy shift with bright lights and multiple caregivers asking questions
rows.rationale: Noise, light and several people competing for attention. Too much arriving at once to process.

questions.takeaway: Deprivation is too little meaningful input, or input the person cannot interpret. Overload is more than they can process. Both produce confusion, and both are reversible.
questions.strategy: The missing glasses row is the one students miss, because the environment is busy. Ask what is reaching the patient, not what is happening in the room.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Quiet and empty is deprivation.

steps.action: Ask how much can be processed
steps.detail: Alarms and interruptions with no rest is overload.
A busy room the patient cannot see or hear is still deprivation.

elimination.verdict: Two deprivation, two overload, and the deficit row is the trap.

questions.stem: A patient with expressive aphasia after a stroke becomes visibly frustrated trying to answer a question. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: Finish the sentence for the patient to reduce the effort
options.rationale: Feels kind and takes the communication away. It also risks putting words in the patient's mouth that are not what they meant.

options.text: Allow time, ask questions that can be answered yes or no, and offer a communication board
options.rationale: Expressive aphasia means comprehension is intact and output is impaired. Time, closed questions and an alternative output channel all work with that.

options.text: Speak more slowly and loudly so the patient can understand
options.rationale: Treats it as a comprehension or hearing problem. In expressive aphasia the patient understands you perfectly, and volume implies otherwise.

options.text: Ask the family to interpret what the patient is trying to say
options.rationale: Bypasses the patient. Useful as a supplement, and not a substitute for communicating with the patient directly.

questions.takeaway: Expressive aphasia is an output problem with intact comprehension. Give time, use yes and no questions, and supply an alternative channel.
questions.strategy: Two options treat it as a hearing or comprehension problem. Two of them take the communication away from the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Expressive: understanding intact, speech impaired.
That addresses comprehension, which is not affected.

steps.action: Cut finishing sentences and family interpreting
steps.detail: Both remove the patient from the exchange.

elimination.verdict: Time, closed questions and a communication board.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a community group about preventing sensory loss. Which statement by a participant indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I should wear hearing and eye protection whenever I am exposed at work."
options.rationale: Correct. Noise-induced loss is the major preventable cause of sensory hearing loss. Protection before the exposure is the only thing that changes it.

options.text: "Every 20 minutes of close work, I should look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds."
options.rationale: Correct. The 20-20-20 rule. The distance is the active ingredient, because it is what relaxes the ciliary muscle.

options.text: "Any hearing change after I turn 70 is just normal aging."
options.rationale: Sudden or one-sided change is never aging. Presbycusis is the most common age-related loss, yet impacted cerumen is the most common correctable cause. A new change is assessed rather than attributed.

options.text: "Ultraviolet-blocking sunglasses lower my risk of cataract."
options.rationale: Correct. Chronic sun exposure is a named cataract risk. Blocking it is a cheap preventive measure.

questions.takeaway: Prevention is protection before exposure plus screening at intervals. Never accept a new change as age-related.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. The distractors are all correct teaching. The answer is a belief that sounds reassuring.

steps.detail: Look for the statement that is false.
Protection, 20-20-20 and sunglasses are all correct.
"Any" hearing change covers sudden and one-sided loss, which is never aging.

elimination.verdict: C. A new hearing change is assessed, not attributed to age.

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a patient with moderate hearing loss and macular degeneration who lives alone. Which finding does the nurse address as the highest safety priority?

options.text: The patient has stopped attending a weekly social group
options.rationale: Social withdrawal is a real consequence of sensory loss and a quality of life concern. It is not what kills someone tonight.

options.text: The smoke alarm is a standard audible model with no visual alert
options.rationale: A patient who cannot hear the alarm has no warning of a fire. A flashing alert system is a safety intervention, not an accessory.

options.text: Medication bottles are labeled in standard-size print
options.rationale: A genuine problem with a straightforward fix, and it does not carry the same immediate lethality.

options.text: The patient reports the television is turned up very loud
options.rationale: A finding that confirms the hearing loss rather than a hazard in itself.

questions.takeaway: Hearing loss is a safety problem before it is a communication problem. A client who cannot hear the alarm is in danger in a way that has nothing to do with conversation.
questions.strategy: Every option is a real finding. Rank them by what happens if nothing is done.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option involves a fire.

steps.action: Cut the withdrawal and the television
steps.detail: Both are consequences, not hazards.
Important, fixable, and not immediately dangerous.

elimination.verdict: The smoke alarm. Visual alerting devices belong in discharge teaching.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man has been in contact isolation for 5 days. He has had no visitors. Last night he told the nurse he saw bugs crawling on the wall. The nurse teaches his daughter about sensory deprivation. The plan includes a clock, family photos, his hearing aids and scheduled video calls. Which statement by the daughter shows the teaching needs follow up?

options.text: "Being alone in this room with nothing familiar can make him confused."
options.rationale: Accurate. Isolation is a common setting for sensory deprivation. Confusion is one of its cognitive effects.

options.text: "I will bring his hearing aids so he can follow what people say to him."
options.rationale: Accurate. A correctable sensory deficit adds to deprivation. Working assistive devices are part of the plan.

options.text: "His photos and a clock give him something meaningful to focus on."
options.rationale: Accurate. Meaningful stimuli such as photos and clocks are critical for preventing deprivation.

options.text: "Seeing bugs means his dementia has started, so we should plan for memory care."
options.rationale: This statement needs follow up. Perceptual changes and confusion are documented effects of sensory deprivation, which is reversible. Assuming dementia skips the cause the plan is meant to correct.

questions.takeaway: New confusion or misperception in an isolated patient has a reversible cause until proven otherwise. Sensory deprivation is one of those causes. A new or sudden change is never assumed to be age related or permanent.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: you are looking for the statement that is wrong. Test each one as true or false against the plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is false.
Isolation confuses, hearing aids help, meaningful stimuli prevent deprivation.
It labels a reversible finding as dementia.

elimination.verdict: D. It closes off the reversible cause.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old is admitted for a hip replacement. During the admission assessment the nurse gathers several findings. Total bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL. Which finding requires the most immediate follow-up?

options.text: Sclerae have a faint yellow tint
options.rationale: Class specifically warns you not to use the sclera to judge jaundice in older adults. Her bilirubin is normal, which confirms it is an expected change.

options.text: Right ear has felt full and muffled for two days
options.rationale: Drier cerumen does impact more easily with age. A new two-day change still needs an otoscopic exam. It is often correctable, so it should not be written off. It is not an emergency, so it is not the most immediate.

options.text: Has had more trouble hearing her granddaughters than her sons over the past several years
options.rationale: High-frequency sounds are lost first with aging. Higher-pitched voices fade before lower ones. The change was also gradual, so it is expected.

options.text: Noticed a dark curtain over the outer part of her left eye's vision when she woke this morning
options.rationale: A sudden, painless curtain is the classic sign of retinal detachment. It is an emergency no matter how old she is.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual and predictable. Anything sudden or new gets followed up even when a known aging process could explain it. A sudden loss of vision outranks a new but correctable ear problem.
questions.strategy: Look at the time course in each option before the body part. Years means aging. This morning or two days means follow up. The yellow sclera is the trap, because in a younger adult it would mean jaundice.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gradual hearing change over years fits aging. Changes since this morning or over two days do not.
Do not read the sclera for jaundice in older adults. The normal bilirubin backs this up.
The ear needs follow-up but is often a treatable impaction. A sudden curtain over the vision is an emergency.

elimination.verdict: The dark curtain over her left eye's vision.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old who lives alone has been in contact isolation for a MRSA wound infection for 9 days. His hearing aids have been in the bedside drawer since admission because the batteries died. The blinds stay closed and there is no clock in the room. Today he says it is Tuesday when it is Saturday. He cries easily, cannot follow the dressing change teaching and misjudges the distance to his chair. Temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 78, oxygen saturation 96 percent, glucose 104 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L. There are no new medications and his neurologic exam is unchanged from admission. Which intervention should the nurse implement first?

options.text: Reorient him to the day and date
options.rationale: A correct intervention, at the wrong time. Reorientation he cannot hear will not work.

options.text: Place a clock and calendar in view and set up scheduled video calls with family
options.rationale: Clocks, photos, music and social contact are the meaningful stimuli named in class. This belongs in his plan for the rest of the isolation period. It still depends on him being able to hear, so it is not first.

options.text: Replace the hearing aid batteries and put the aids in
options.rationale: Every other intervention depends on him hearing you. Restoring his assistive device fixes a sensory deficit that is feeding the deprivation. He shows all three effect groups from class: disorientation and poor learning are cognitive, crying easily is affective and misjudging distance is perceptual.

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative to help him sleep
options.rationale: Sedation adds a medication that impairs perception. It treats the behavior while leaving the cause in place.

questions.takeaway: Isolation plus a missing assistive device is a recipe for sensory deprivation. Restore what lets the patient receive stimuli first. Then add stimuli that mean something to him.
questions.strategy: Rule out the physical causes with the data given. Then ask what the environment took away from him. Two options are good care. The first one is the fix every other intervention depends on.

steps.detail: Normal vitals, glucose, sodium and neuro exam make sepsis and a new neurologic event unlikely.
Cognitive, affective and perceptual changes in an understimulating room point to sensory deprivation.

steps.action: Drop the option that hides the cause
steps.detail: A sedative treats the behavior and further dulls perception.
Reorientation and a clock with family calls both need him to hear. The hearing aids come first.

elimination.verdict: Replace the hearing aid batteries and put the aids in.

questions.nursesNote: Clinic visit: 67-year-old with type 2 diabetes who swims daily. Diagnosed with right external otitis 10 days ago and prescribed antibiotic and steroid ear drops. Reports the ear pain is worse than when treatment started and now keeps him awake at night. Pain increases when the nurse moves the pinna. Canal is swollen and he describes a plugged feeling. Hearing is slightly muffled on the right. Temperature 38.4 C. Fingerstick glucose 286 mg/dL; A1c 9.4%. Right corner of the mouth droops when he smiles, new since yesterday. Blood pressure 134/82.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are not expected in uncomplicated external otitis and require prompt follow-up.

segments.text: Reports the ear pain is worse than when treatment started and now keeps him awake at night
segments.rationale: External otitis should improve on drops. Worsening pain after 10 days of treatment means the infection is not being controlled.

segments.text: Pain increases when the nurse moves the pinna
segments.rationale: Pain with pinna or tragus movement is the classic sign of external otitis. It is part of the known diagnosis.

segments.text: Canal is swollen and he describes a plugged feeling
segments.rationale: Expected with external otitis.

segments.text: Hearing is slightly muffled on the right
segments.rationale: Temporary hearing loss from canal swelling is expected.

segments.text: Temperature 38.4 C
segments.rationale: Simple swimmer's ear rarely causes fever. Fever suggests the infection is spreading beyond the canal skin.

segments.text: Fingerstick glucose 286 mg/dL; A1c 9.4%
segments.rationale: Diabetes is the risk factor class names for necrotizing otitis. His poor control (glucose 286, A1c 9.4%) raises that risk and weakens his defense against infection.

segments.text: Right corner of the mouth droops when he smiles, new since yesterday
segments.rationale: The facial nerve runs close to the ear. New facial weakness suggests the infection has reached deeper structures. This is the most urgent finding in the note.

segments.text: Blood pressure 134/82
segments.rationale: Within an acceptable range.

questions.takeaway: External otitis in a patient with diabetes that gets worse on treatment, or brings fever or facial weakness, may be necrotizing otitis. It can be fatal, so escalate it the same day.
questions.strategy: Three findings are the textbook picture of swimmer's ear. They are there to tempt you. Look for what does not belong to a canal skin infection: worsening, systemic signs and a nerve deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pinna pain, a swollen canal and muffled hearing are the expected diagnosis.
Pain should fall on treatment. His is rising.
Glucose 286 with an A1c of 9.4.
Fever and new facial droop point past the canal.

elimination.verdict: s1, s5, s6 and s7.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old who sleeps in her contact lenses comes to urgent care with two days of worsening right eye pain, tearing and sensitivity to light. Vision in the right eye is blurred at 20/60. The left eye is 20/20. The right cornea looks hazy and takes up green stain with fluorescein. Pupils are equal and reactive. She has no nausea. Temperature is 37.4 C. Which condition is the patient most likely experiencing?

options.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Also painful with a hazy (edematous) cornea, but it comes on suddenly with sudden vision loss and a red eye. Raised pressure does not take up fluorescein stain. Her pupils are equal and reactive. Green uptake marks a surface defect.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: Painless flashes, floaters and a curtain. Her problem is painful and on the surface.

options.text: Corneal abrasion with infection
options.rationale: Contact lens overwear, pain, light sensitivity, a hazy cornea and green fluorescein uptake. Class calls an infected cornea an emergency because it has no separate blood supply.

options.text: Cataract
options.rationale: Painless and gradual over years.

questions.takeaway: A painful, hazy cornea that stains green in a contact lens wearer is an infection emergency. Frequent antibiotic drops and no lenses until it heals. Track acuity and pain.
questions.strategy: Angle closure is the tempting distractor because both are painful with a hazy cornea. The green fluorescein uptake and the contact lens history tip it to the cornea.

steps.detail: Retinal detachment and cataract are painless. Remove them.

steps.action: Break the tie with the stain
steps.detail: Green fluorescein uptake marks a surface defect. Raised pressure does not stain.
Sleeping in contact lenses points to the cornea.

elimination.verdict: C. Corneal infection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with severe myopia had scleral buckling surgery with a gas bubble for a left retinal detachment this morning. He is being discharged. Which instruction does the nurse include?

options.text: Lie flat on your back as much as possible so the eye can rest
options.rationale: Sounds restful and could float the bubble away from the tear. The position depends on where the tear is. It is not a standard supine rest.

options.text: Bending at the waist to tie your shoes is fine after the second day
options.rationale: Bending forward raises intraocular pressure. There is no two-day exception.

options.text: Keep your head in the exact position the surgeon prescribed
options.rationale: The gas bubble has to press against the tear to hold the retina in place. Only the surgeon's position does that for his tear.

options.text: Eye pain with nausea is common for the first two days, so take acetaminophen and rest
options.rationale: This is the most dangerous distractor. Sudden pain, or pain with nausea, is on the report immediately list. It can signal hemorrhage or a pressure rise.

questions.takeaway: After retinal repair: surgeon's positioning, no pressure spikes, no close work for a week. Pain with nausea or new visual symptoms get reported now.
questions.strategy: Two distractors sound kind. Lying flat sounds like rest and treating pain at home sounds reassuring. Ask whether each option protects the repair or hides a complication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supine rest is not the surgeon's instruction for this bubble.
Bending at the waist raises intraocular pressure on any day.
Pain with nausea gets reported immediately.
The prescribed position holds the bubble against the tear.

elimination.verdict: C. Keep the surgeon's prescribed head position.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old with severe myopia is admitted after noticing flashes of light, a shower of floaters and a dark curtain over the upper half of his right visual field this morning. The eye is not painful. Intraocular pressure is 16 mm Hg. Scleral buckling surgery is scheduled for tomorrow morning. He says he is bored and asks for something to read. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Encourage him to walk the hallway every 2 hours to prevent complications of bed rest
options.rationale: Walking helps most hospitalized patients. Before retinal surgery, activity and head movement can extend the detachment.

options.text: Restrict his head movement and activity and place a patch over the affected eye
options.rationale: Correct. The deck lists activity and head movement restriction plus an eye patch before surgery. Each eye movement tugs on the loose retina. Patching reduces eye movement and helps keep the detachment from spreading before the repair.

options.text: Provide large-print reading material to prevent sensory deprivation
options.rationale: Boredom is real and sensory deprivation is a valid concern. Reading causes constant, rapid eye movement, which is the opposite of what the retina needs. Offer audio options instead.

options.text: Notify the surgeon now because the vision loss is painless
options.rationale: Painless loss with flashes and floaters is the classic picture of retinal detachment. It is expected and already known. The surgery is already scheduled, so this adds nothing new.

questions.takeaway: Before retinal detachment surgery, limit activity and head movement. Patch the eye to reduce eye movement. Reading is close work that keeps the eyes moving.
questions.strategy: Two options are good general nursing care. Ask which one fits a retina that is pulling away. Movement is the enemy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flashes, floaters, a curtain and no pain in a myopic patient point to retinal detachment.
Painless vision loss is the classic sign, not a change to report.

steps.action: Test each remaining option against eye movement
steps.detail: Walking and reading both increase movement. Patching and restriction reduce it.

elimination.verdict: Restrict activity and patch the eye. Keep the retina still until surgery.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old comes to the emergency department 30 minutes after an insect flew into his left ear while he was camping. He hears loud buzzing and has sharp pain. He had ear infections as a child but none in years. Otoscope examination shows a live insect moving in the canal. The tympanic membrane looks intact. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate first?

options.text: Irrigate the canal with warm water to flush the insect out
options.rationale: The deck says never to irrigate a live insect. Water can drive a moving insect deeper. It may scratch or sting the eardrum.

options.text: Instill oil into the canal to suffocate the insect before it is removed
options.rationale: Correct. Oil kills the insect so it stops moving. A still insect can be removed without further trauma to the canal or eardrum. The buzzing and pain stop.

options.text: Instill carbamide peroxide drops to soften the canal contents
options.rationale: Ceruminolytics soften wax. They do not stop a live insect and delay the step that matters.

options.text: Remove the insect with a cotton swab while the patient holds still
options.rationale: A swab pushes objects deeper and can injure the canal skin. The deck lists swab trauma as a cause of external otitis.

questions.takeaway: A live insect in the ear is killed with oil first and removed after. Irrigation is never used for a live insect.
questions.strategy: The childhood infection history is a distractor. The eardrum is intact now. The deciding fact is that the insect is alive.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A live insect behaves differently from wax or a bead.
Old ear infections do not change today's plan when the eardrum is intact.

steps.action: Reject methods that move the insect
steps.detail: Water and a swab both push or agitate it.
Oil stops movement so removal is safe.

elimination.verdict: Oil first. A still insect is a safe insect to remove.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is 2 days post op in the ICU. Monitors alarm often. Staff enter her room many times each night. She has racing thoughts, pulls at her dressing and needs constant reorientation. The nurse combines care activities, schedules rest periods and institutes quiet time at night. Which finding on the third day best shows the interventions were effective?

options.text: She sleeps in 3-hour stretches overnight and leaves her dressing alone
options.rationale: Rest and the end of the tube and dressing behavior show her brain can again filter stimuli. That is the goal of controlling stimuli in sensory overload.

options.text: She says she feels calmer but is picking at her IV tubing
options.rationale: Playing with tubes is a behavioral sign of ongoing overload. Her report of calm does not outweigh the behavior.

options.text: She still needs reorientation about every 15 minutes
options.rationale: Constant reorientation is a listed effect of overload. It shows the problem continues.

options.text: Staff document that her monitor alarm volume was lowered
options.rationale: This documents that an intervention was done. It is not a patient outcome.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate overload by the patient's behavior. Rest, calm attention and leaving tubes and dressings alone show the environment is no longer overwhelming her.
questions.strategy: An outcome is a change in the patient. Remove the option that describes staff actions. Then pick the option where every finding has improved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A lowered alarm is an intervention, not an outcome.
Picking at tubing is still overload.
Frequent reorientation is still overload.

elimination.verdict: A. Every finding in it has moved in the right direction.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is discharged after phacoemulsification with a lens implant in his right eye. The nurse teaches postoperative care. Which statement by the patient shows he needs further teaching?

options.text: "I will wear dark glasses when I am outside or in bright light."
options.rationale: Correct. Dark glasses are part of the postoperative instructions.

options.text: "If I get sudden eye pain or lose vision, I will call the surgeon right away."
options.rationale: Correct. Sudden pain or vision loss must be reported immediately.

options.text: "I will carry my 25-pound bag of dog food in from the car tomorrow."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. Lifting more than 10 pounds raises intraocular pressure and must be avoided after cataract surgery.

options.text: "My vision should keep improving over the next 4 to 6 weeks."
options.rationale: Correct. Best vision is reached 4 to 6 weeks after surgery.

questions.takeaway: After cataract surgery avoid anything that raises intraocular pressure. That means no bending, no straining and no lifting more than 10 pounds.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: you are looking for the unsafe statement. Check each activity against intraocular pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Dark glasses, reporting pain and the 4 to 6 week timeline are all correct.
A 25-pound lift raises IOP.

elimination.verdict: C. It breaks the 10-pound limit.

questions.stem: A patient receiving furosemide has a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which assessment finding does the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Constipation and abdominal distention
options.rationale: A real finding in hypokalemia and not the one that kills. Smooth muscle slows along with everything else.

options.text: Shallow respirations with a weak cough
options.rationale: Hypokalemia weakens every muscle including the diaphragm and the intercostals. Respiratory muscle weakness is the finding that turns a laboratory value into an emergency.

options.text: Generalized fatigue and leg weakness
options.rationale: Expected and important, and it is the background against which you look for the breathing.

options.text: Prominent U waves on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: The classic electrocardiogram change in hypokalemia, and it belongs in the report. It is still not the finding that takes priority over ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Weakness is a respiratory finding until you rule it out. Hypokalemia, hypermagnesemia and hyponatremia all weaken the muscles that breathe.
questions.strategy: Every option is a genuine finding in hypokalemia. The question is which one threatens the airway and breathing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one option is about breathing.

steps.action: Note that U waves are tempting
steps.detail: They are the textbook sign, which is exactly why they are offered.

steps.action: Cut the gut and the fatigue
steps.detail: Both are expected and neither is immediately dangerous.

elimination.verdict: Shallow respirations. Assess the breathing, not just the grip.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium of 7.1 mEq/L with peaked T waves. The prescriber orders IV calcium gluconate. The patient asks what it will do. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: It will lower your potassium level quickly
options.rationale: The single most reliable near-miss distractor in this chapter. Calcium does not change the potassium at all.

options.text: It will protect your heart while we work on lowering the potassium
options.rationale: Calcium raises the threshold potential of cardiac cells, which stabilizes the membrane against the arrhythmia. It buys time and treats nothing.

options.text: It will help your kidneys excrete the extra potassium
options.rationale: Excretion is what a cation exchange resin or dialysis does. Calcium has no role in elimination.

options.text: It will move the potassium into your cells for storage
options.rationale: That is insulin with dextrose, or a beta agonist. Those shift potassium; calcium does not.

questions.takeaway: IV calcium in hyperkalemia protects the heart and changes the level not at all. Shifting is insulin and dextrose; removing is a resin or dialysis.
questions.strategy: Three options describe real hyperkalemia treatments. Only one of them is what calcium actually does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stabilize, shift, remove. Three different jobs.
It stabilizes.
Lowering, excreting and shifting all belong to other drugs.

elimination.verdict: Cardiac protection while another drug does the lowering.

questions.stem: A patient has been receiving potassium replacement for two days and the serum potassium remains 3.0 mEq/L. Which laboratory value does the nurse check next?

options.text: Serum magnesium
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes the kidney waste potassium and blocks it from staying in the cell. Potassium will not come up while the magnesium is low, no matter how much you give.

options.text: Serum albumin
options.rationale: Albumin matters for interpreting a calcium level, not a potassium one.

options.text: Serum phosphorus
options.rationale: Phosphorus moves inversely with calcium. It has no direct role in potassium replacement failing.

options.text: Serum chloride
options.rationale: Chloride tracks sodium and acid-base status. It does not explain refractory hypokalemia.

questions.takeaway: When a level will not respond to correction, the first question is which related electrolyte nobody checked. Potassium will not correct while magnesium is low.
questions.strategy: The stem is not asking about hypokalemia. It is asking why a correct treatment is not working.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two days of replacement with no movement.
Magnesium, every time.
Albumin and phosphorus belong to a different pairing.

elimination.verdict: Magnesium. Read labs as a set, not one line at a time.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old patient developed hypocalcemia one day after a total thyroidectomy. The total calcium was 7.6 mg/dL. The nurse administered IV calcium as prescribed. Two hours later the nurse reassesses. Which findings indicate that the hypocalcemia has not resolved and needs follow up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Carpal spasm when the blood pressure cuff is inflated
options.rationale: This is a positive Trousseau sign. Low calcium still leaves the nerves firing too easily.

options.text: Tingling and numbness around the mouth and in the fingertips
options.rationale: Paresthesia is usually the earliest complaint. Its persistence shows the nerves are still overexcitable.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Brisk reflexes mean nerve and muscle remain overexcitable.

options.text: Prolonged QT interval on the cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Low calcium lengthens the QT. A QT that stays long means the risk for dysrhythmia continues.

options.text: Deep bone pain with flank pain from a kidney stone
options.rationale: These belong to high calcium. They do not show that low calcium persists.

options.text: Constipation with decreased bowel sounds
options.rationale: This is a slowed gut, which fits high calcium. Low calcium causes cramping with diarrhea.

questions.takeaway: Low calcium excites nerve and muscle: tingling, brisk reflexes, positive Trousseau and Chvostek signs, tetany and a prolonged QT. High calcium sedates them. If the excitable findings remain after treatment, the problem has not resolved.
questions.strategy: Two options belong to the opposite imbalance. Ask of each finding whether it sounds excitable or sluggish. Only the excitable findings show the low calcium persists.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium excites. High calcium sedates.
Spasm, tingling, brisk reflexes and a long QT still point to low calcium.
Stones, bone pain and constipation belong to high calcium.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L, ascites, 3+ pitting edema and a weight gain of 4 kg this week. Which intervention does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL/hr
options.rationale: Saline into a fluid-overloaded hyponatremic patient makes both problems worse. The sodium is low because there is too much water, not too little salt.

options.text: Fluid restriction with daily weights
options.rationale: This is dilutional hyponatremia. The sodium is diluted by retained water, so removing water is what raises the number.

options.text: Encouraging salty broths and adding salt to meals
options.rationale: Adds sodium to a patient who is already retaining water and will retain more with it.

options.text: Rapid infusion of 3% sodium chloride over two hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures or coma, given slowly and with close monitoring. Correcting fast causes osmotic demyelination.

questions.takeaway: Find the volume status before you treat the sodium. A low sodium with edema and weight gain is too much water, and the treatment is restriction rather than replacement.
questions.strategy: Two options add sodium and one adds volume. The edema and the weight gain tell you which direction the patient needs to move.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ascites, 3+ edema and 4 kg of gain.
Adding fluid to an overloaded patient.
Sodium follows water in, and there is already too much water.

elimination.verdict: Fluid restriction. Hyponatremia is not automatically a sodium deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia becomes drowsy, and the nurse finds absent patellar reflexes with a respiratory rate of 10. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion
options.rationale: Reflexes go first, then respirations, then rhythm. The progression has already reached breathing, and the first action is to stop what is causing it.

options.text: Administer calcium gluconate as the antidote
options.rationale: Calcium is the antidote and it comes after stopping the infusion. Giving the antidote while the drug keeps running is treating around the cause.

options.text: Notify the prescriber of the assessment findings
options.rationale: Necessary and not first. Notification follows the action that stops the harm.

options.text: Place the patient on continuous pulse oximetry
options.rationale: Monitoring a patient who is being poisoned does not stop the poisoning.

questions.takeaway: Hypermagnesemia progresses reflexes, then respirations, then rhythm. Checking the patellar reflex before each hour of infusion is how you catch it before the breathing.
questions.strategy: Three of the four options are correct actions and only one of them removes the cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.

steps.action: Note that the antidote is tempting
steps.detail: It is right and it is second.
Both follow the intervention.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion, then calcium gluconate, then notify.

questions.stem: A patient has a total calcium of 7.8 mg/dL with a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL. The patient has no tingling, no spasm and a normal QT interval. How does the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The patient has significant hypocalcemia and needs replacement now
options.rationale: Treating the number instead of the patient. Nothing in the assessment supports a functional deficit.

options.text: The low albumin has lowered the total calcium without lowering the active calcium
options.rationale: Roughly half of serum calcium travels bound to albumin. Less albumin means less bound calcium and a lower total, while the ionized fraction that actually does the work is unchanged.

options.text: The result is a laboratory error and should be redrawn
options.rationale: The two values are consistent with each other, which is the opposite of an error.

options.text: The patient is developing hyperparathyroidism
options.rationale: That raises calcium rather than lowering it.

questions.takeaway: Low albumin lowers the total calcium without lowering the calcium that is working. Check the albumin, or ask for the ionized calcium, before treating a number.
questions.strategy: The absence of symptoms is the finding the question is built on. A truly low ionized calcium would show itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Calcium is reported with albumin for a reason.
No tingling, no spasm, normal QT.
Nothing functional is wrong.

elimination.verdict: A dilutional artifact of low albumin. Ask for an ionized calcium.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient with a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L after prolonged fever and poor intake. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor level of consciousness at least every four hours
options.rationale: Hypernatremia pulls water out of brain cells. Neurologic change is the earliest and most important finding.

options.text: Anticipate a hypotonic intravenous solution prescribed to run slowly
options.rationale: The water deficit is replaced gradually. Correcting a high sodium too quickly pulls water into brain cells and causes cerebral edema.

options.text: Institute seizure precautions
options.rationale: Both extremes of sodium change brain cell volume and both can produce seizures.

options.text: Offer oral fluids on a schedule rather than waiting for the patient to ask
options.rationale: Thirst is blunted in older adults and unreliable as a guide. A schedule works where waiting does not.

options.text: Correct the sodium to normal within the first eight hours
options.rationale: Rapid correction in either direction causes harm. Down too fast swells the brain; up too fast damages myelin.

options.text: Restrict free water until the sodium normalizes
options.rationale: This patient is short of water, not carrying too much. Restriction would worsen it.

questions.takeaway: Both sodium extremes are brain problems, and both are corrected slowly. Fast down causes cerebral edema; fast up causes osmotic demyelination.
questions.strategy: Two options are written to sound decisive. Speed is the trap in every sodium question.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A high sodium here means a water deficit.
Monitoring, seizure precautions, scheduled fluids.
Rapid correction is never the right option.
Wrong direction for a water deficit.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C and D.

questions.stem: Two hours after an intravenous infusion was started, a patient reports that the site feels tight. The nurse finds the area around the catheter cool, pale and swollen, with the swelling spreading outward from the insertion point. What does the nurse do?

options.text: Apply warm compresses and continue the infusion at a slower rate
options.rationale: Warmth is for phlebitis. Continuing any rate keeps pushing solution into tissue.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and elevate the extremity
options.rationale: Cool, pale, swollen and spreading is infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

options.text: Massage the area to disperse the fluid and reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Massage forces more solution into the tissue and can worsen the injury.

options.text: Aspirate from the catheter and flush with 10 mL of normal saline to confirm patency
options.rationale: A flush adds volume to tissue that already has too much, and patency is not the question. A catheter can flush perfectly while it sits outside the vein.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration runs cool and spreads around the site. Phlebitis runs warm and follows the vein. A streak or a palpable cord is always phlebitis.
questions.strategy: The temperature and the direction of spread are the two cues that separate the two complications, and the stem gives you both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That rules out phlebitis and infection.
Not along the vein, so not a cord.
Both belong to the other diagnosis or make this one worse.
Patency is not safety.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration. Stop, remove, elevate, and do not compress.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews four patients on a medical unit. Each has one abnormal electrolyte. Patient 1 is 49 years old and had parathyroid surgery yesterday. Patient 2 is 72 years old with kidney failure and has been taking a magnesium-based laxative. Patient 3 is 67 years old with kidney disease and takes an ACE inhibitor with spironolactone. Patient 4 is 58 years old with metastatic cancer.
questions.stem: For each patient's findings, indicate whether they reflect an overexcitable state or a slowed state.

rows.text: Patient 1: serum calcium 7.4 mg/dL with carpal spasm and a prolonged QT
rows.rationale: Hypocalcemia. Less calcium at the membrane lets nerves fire too easily, so tetany develops.

rows.text: Patient 2: serum magnesium 4.8 mEq/L with facial flushing and absent deep tendon reflexes
rows.rationale: Hypermagnesemia. Magnesium depresses nerve and muscle activity. Reflexes go first, then breathing, then the heart rhythm.

rows.text: Patient 3: serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L with tall peaked T waves and abdominal cramping
rows.rationale: Hyperkalemia. Cells respond to weaker stimuli, so cardiac and smooth muscle become irritable.

rows.text: Patient 4: serum calcium 12.6 mg/dL with lethargy, constipation and diminished reflexes
rows.rationale: Hypercalcemia. Extra calcium at the membrane means a stronger stimulus is needed, so everything slows.

questions.takeaway: Calcium and magnesium act as brakes on the membrane. Low levels make cells excitable while high levels slow them. Potassium is the opposite, because high potassium makes cells excitable.
questions.strategy: Potassium inverts the pattern, which is why it is placed third. Sort calcium and magnesium by the rule first. Then handle potassium on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Apply the calcium and magnesium rule
steps.detail: Low excites. High sedates.
High potassium excites. Low potassium weakens.

steps.action: Check the findings against the label
steps.detail: Spasm and peaked T waves are excitement. Absent reflexes, lethargy and constipation are slowing.

elimination.verdict: Two overexcitable and two slowed. Potassium is the one that breaks the pattern.

questions.stem: A patient has lost an estimated 1200 mL of blood during surgery and has a blood pressure of 88 over 52 with a pulse of 118. While blood is being crossmatched, which solution does the nurse expect to infuse?

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia and for expanding intravascular volume. It also carries risks of cell dehydration and hypernatremia that are unnecessary when an isotonic fluid will do the job.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so most of the infused water leaves the vasculature and enters cells. A fluid that moves water out of that space is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
