options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does expand intravascular volume by pulling water out of cells, and it is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Using it here treats the volume at the cost of dehydrating cells for no reason.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic at 273 mOsm/L, so infused volume stays in the extracellular space and expands circulating volume without shifting water into or out of cells. Volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation are the listed uses for isotonic fluids.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhage empties the vascular compartment, so the fluid that fixes it is the one that stays there. That is the definition of isotonic.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with a hemoglobin of 6.8 g/dL is ordered 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Consent is on file and baseline vital signs are recorded. The charge nurse sees one nurse read the blood bank record aloud while the second nurse listens and says, "Matches." What is the charge nurse's best action?

options.text: Stop the process and have each nurse independently check the label against the ID band, ABO/Rh type, unit number and expiration date
options.rationale: Two-nurse verification means two independent checks. The second nurse exists to catch the first nurse's error. She cannot do that if she never looks at the label or the band.

options.text: Let them proceed because both nurses will sign the transfusion record
options.rationale: Signing documents that verification happened. It does not replace it. Two signatures on a flawed check record the flaw twice.

options.text: Let them proceed because the nurse reading aloud is the one who will start the infusion
options.rationale: Who hangs the unit does not change how the check was done. This adds a condition that has nothing to do with the flaw.

options.text: Let them proceed once the patient states her name and date of birth
options.rationale: Patient participation confirms identity and is good practice. ABO/Rh type, unit number and expiration are checked against documents, not the patient's memory.

questions.takeaway: Two-nurse verification means two independent checks, not one check with a witness. An incompatible transfusion is a life-threatening sentinel event.

questions.stem: A nurse has scrubbed the insertion site with chlorhexidine using friction for 30 seconds. Which action next would require the nurse to repeat the skin preparation?

options.text: Waiting for the antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the catheter
options.rationale: Complete air drying is what allows the antiseptic to exert its full antimicrobial effect. This is the required step, not an error.

options.text: Palpating the vein once more to confirm its position before inserting
options.rationale: Repalpation means touching the cleansed skin with an unsterile finger. Vein position is confirmed before the prep, not after.

options.text: Applying the tourniquet above the site before cleansing
options.rationale: The tourniquet distends the vein to make it visible and palpable. Before, which is the correct order and does not touch the prepared skin.

options.text: Choosing a 20 gauge catheter for the planned infusion
options.rationale: Twenty gauge is the standard adult size, suitable for most medications and fluids. This is a reasonable decision about a different part of the procedure.

questions.takeaway: The prep is only as good as what happens after it. Drying completely and not touching the site are the two steps that preserve the work the scrub did.

questions.stem: A patient has a midline catheter placed for a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours
options.rationale: An antibiotic is a non-vesicant medication with an osmolarity well within peripheral limits. Antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration therapy are the listed indications.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr
options.rationale: Normal saline is isotonic at 308 mOsm/L. Yes, it is one of the named indications.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition at 60 mL/hr
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a highly concentrated solution of dextrose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins, and trace elements. Parenteral nutrition is explicitly excluded from midline use and requires central access, because its osmolarity far exceeds the peripheral limit and would damage the vein.

options.text: Morphine sulfate 2 mg intravenously every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: Morphine is an analgesic and is not a vesicant. Analgesics are listed among the appropriate therapies.

questions.takeaway: A midline is a long peripheral catheter, not a central line. Its tip ends below the axilla, so it obeys peripheral rules no matter how far up the arm it was inserted.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an intravenous site and finds the surrounding skin is cool and pale with moderate swelling. The drip rate has slowed and no blood return is obtained. Which complication has occurred?

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall itself, producing pain, redness, warmth, a streak along the vein, and a palpable cord. Inflammation raises local temperature, so a cool site points away from phlebitis even though both complications look alarming.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: Infiltration is IV fluid leaking out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Fluid sitting in the interstitium makes the skin cool and pale and produces edema, the catheter is no longer in the vessel so there is no blood return, and the resistance of the tissue slows the drip rate.

options.text: Hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood leaking into tissue at the insertion site, producing bruising, swelling, and tenderness. Swelling is shared between the two, which is what makes this worth checking rather than dismissing.

options.text: Thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a clot forming in or around the catheter, producing a swollen, painful limb and a decreased flow rate. A clot slows flow, and it does not push fluid into the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Cool and pale means fluid has left the vein. Warm and red with a cord means the vein wall is inflamed. Both begin with stopping the infusion and removing the catheter.

questions.stem: While a nurse is changing the injection cap on a patient's central venous catheter, the patient suddenly reports chest pain and severe shortness of breath. The blood pressure falls to 84 over 48 and a churning murmur is audible over the precordium. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Position the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract so it cannot be pumped into the lungs. It manages the air already inside while clamping prevents more.

options.text: Administer 100 percent oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen improves saturation and helps the trapped air be reabsorbed. It is part of the response and it does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Clamp the catheter tubing
options.rationale: Clamping closes the pathway between room air and the venous system. Stopping the source is the first action because every additional second adds volume to the embolus, and the remaining steps treat what has already entered.

options.text: Activate the rapid response team
options.rationale: A rapid response brings additional expertise to the bedside. Calling is essential and it is not the first action when a one-second intervention stops the cause.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, and a mill-wheel murmur during line manipulation is air embolism. Clamp, position in left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response, and give 100 percent oxygen.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has had a nontunneled subclavian central venous catheter for 9 days. It was placed in the ICU. He is now on a medical unit eating a regular diet. His IV antibiotics were completed yesterday. His only infusion is saline at a keep-open rate. Which nursing action most directly reduces his risk of a catheter-related bloodstream infection?

options.text: Change the transparent dressing today
options.rationale: Dressing care is required maintenance. It does not shorten how long the line stays in.

options.text: Ask the provider whether the catheter is still necessary and request removal
options.rationale: Dwell time is a primary CRBSI risk factor. Every extra day raises risk. He no longer has a reason for central access, so removal is the strongest action.

options.text: Flush each lumen with saline before and after every access
options.rationale: Flushing maintains patency. It does not remove the source of risk.

options.text: Label the tubing with the date and time it was hung
options.rationale: Labeling supports timely tubing changes. It does not address dwell time.

questions.takeaway: Ask every day whether the central line is still necessary. The line that is no longer needed is the one that infects the patient.

questions.stem: An RN is working with an LPN and an assistive personnel (AP) on a medical unit. State law and facility policy allow LPNs to perform routine infusion care. Which task can the RN appropriately delegate?

options.text: LPN: start the first unit of packed red blood cells after the two-person check
options.rationale: Class lists initiating blood products as RN only. The first 15 minutes carry the highest reaction risk and need RN judgment.

options.text: LPN: hang a new heparin infusion bag and program the pump
options.rationale: Heparin is a high-alert drug. Class reserves high-alert IV drugs for the RN.

options.text: AP: check the IV site for infiltration and remove the catheter if it looks puffy
options.rationale: Deciding whether a site is infiltrated is assessment. Removing the catheter is an intervention based on it. Neither belongs to the AP.

options.text: LPN: flush an established saline lock before and after an IV antibiotic
options.rationale: Flushing established lines is delegable to the LPN in class. It is routine maintenance of a line the RN has already set up.

questions.takeaway: The RN keeps initial assessment, blood product initiation, high-alert drugs, interpretation and teaching. Routine maintenance goes to the LPN and data collection goes to the AP. The RN stays accountable for all of it.
questions.strategy: Look for the word that moves a task to the RN: start, high-alert, assess or decide. Tasks that continue what the RN has already set up are the ones that can go.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The first unit of blood and a new heparin bag stay with the RN.
Deciding a site is infiltrated requires RN assessment.
Flushing an established line can be delegated to the LPN.

elimination.verdict: D. The LPN flushes the established saline lock.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with pneumonia is on day 3 of IV therapy through a 20 gauge catheter in the right forearm. The prescription is 0.9% sodium chloride with 20 mEq potassium chloride at 100 mL per hour. IV antibiotics will continue for four more days. At 0800 the site was clean and dry. At 1000 the patient reports burning along the arm. The nurse finds redness and warmth over the vein with a red streak running 5 cm up the forearm. A firm cord is palpable along the vein. The infusion runs freely with good blood return. Temperature is 37.4 C, down from 38.2 C yesterday. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Slow the infusion to 50 mL per hour and reassess the site in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing the rate keeps the irritating solution flowing into an inflamed vein. The slide intervention for phlebitis starts with stopping the infusion.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress and start a new line in the left arm
options.rationale: This is phlebitis. The red streak and palpable cord show an inflamed vein wall. The potassium is a likely chemical irritant. You stop, remove and apply warm moist heat. Therapy must continue, so the new site goes in the other arm, away from the damaged vein.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and start a new line in a hand vein below the current site
options.rationale: Removal is right. The new site is wrong. The slide lists sites distal to prior phlebitis as contraindicated because fluid entering below the inflamed vein must travel through it.

options.text: Flush the catheter with 10 mL of saline to confirm patency before deciding on removal
options.rationale: Patency is not the question. Blood return is already good. A patent catheter can still be sitting in an inflamed vein. Flushing adds more irritation.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis means stop, remove and apply warm moist heat. When you restart, choose a site that does not route fluid through the damaged vein.
questions.strategy: Two options remove the catheter. The tie breaker is where the new line goes. Ask which direction the fluid will travel from the new site.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord with good blood return is phlebitis, not infiltration.

steps.action: Cut the options that keep the line
steps.detail: Slowing the rate and flushing both leave the inflamed vein in use.
A hand vein below the site sends fluid through the inflamed vein. The other arm avoids it.

elimination.verdict: Stop, remove, warm moist compress and restart in the opposite arm.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old receiving TPN through a PICC in the left arm for two weeks reports that the left arm aches. At 0800 the upper arm circumference was 29 cm. At 1400 it is 32 cm. The right arm measures 28 cm. The pump has alarmed for downstream occlusion twice this shift. When the nurse attempts a saline flush, there is resistance. The insertion site has no redness or drainage. The dressing is dry and intact. Temperature is 37.0 C, heart rate 84, blood pressure 124/78, respirations 16, SpO2 97% on room air. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Flush the PICC with a 10 mL syringe using steady firm pressure to clear the occlusion
options.rationale: Flushing against resistance can rupture the catheter or push a clot into the circulation. The PICC teaching slide is clear: do not use the line if resistance is felt.

options.text: Stop the infusion, avoid flushing against resistance and notify the provider of a suspected catheter-related thrombosis
options.rationale: A swollen, painful limb with a rising circumference and a falling flow rate is the slide picture of thrombosis. You stop using the line and report. The provider decides on imaging, anticoagulation, or removal. Stopping TPN suddenly can drop the glucose, so hang D10W peripherally per protocol and check the glucose.

options.text: Draw two sets of blood cultures and anticipate IV antibiotics
options.rationale: This is the CRBSI response. She has no fever, chills, hypotension, or mental status change, so infection does not explain the swelling or the occlusion.

options.text: Elevate the arm, apply a warm compress and restart the TPN at a lower rate
options.rationale: Elevation is reasonable comfort care. Restarting the infusion through a line with a suspected clot is not safe. A slower rate does not treat the cause.

questions.takeaway: A swollen, painful limb plus a slowing line points to thrombosis. Stop using the catheter, never force a flush and call the provider.
questions.strategy: First decide which complication fits. Normal vital signs rule out infection. Then pick the action that stops harm without forcing the line.

steps.detail: Circumference rose 3 cm in six hours on the PICC side only.
Limb swelling, pain and reduced flow fit thrombosis. Normal temperature argues against CRBSI.
Firm flushing against resistance risks rupture or embolism.

elimination.verdict: Stop the infusion, do not flush against resistance and report suspected thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old reports that headlight glare has made night driving impossible and that colors look faded. She denies pain and says it came on over about two years. Which condition do these findings suggest?

options.text: Open-angle glaucoma
options.rationale: Glaucoma takes peripheral vision first and is painless, which is why the two get confused. Halos and peripheral loss point at the nerve; glare and faded color point at the lens, and plenty of clients have both conditions at once.

options.text: Cataract
options.rationale: Painless, gradual, bilateral, with glare, poor night vision and faded color. The clouding lens scatters light and filters out color.

options.text: Retinal detachment
options.rationale: Sudden, with flashes, floaters and a curtain across part of the field. Nothing here is sudden.

options.text: Angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Sudden, painful, with a red eye and a cloudy cornea. Halos appear here too, but the pain, the redness and the abrupt onset are what make it an emergency, and none of that fits a two-year history.

questions.takeaway: Cataract is painless, gradual, with glare, poor night driving and faded color. The lens is the problem, so the whole field is hazy rather than a piece of it missing.
questions.strategy: Two options are glaucoma and they are there to be separated. Sort by speed first, then by which part of the field is affected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two years is gradual, which cuts detachment and angle-closure.

steps.action: Ask which part of the field
steps.detail: Everything is hazy, not the edges.
Glare and faded color are lens complaints.

elimination.verdict: Cataract. Halos and peripheral loss would have pointed at the nerve instead.

questions.stem: A patient with open-angle glaucoma says he stopped his latanoprost because "it wasn't doing anything and my eyes feel fine." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Let me arrange for a different drop that will work better for you."
options.rationale: Accepts a false premise. The drop was working; the disease has no symptoms to relieve.

options.text: "Open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms until it is late. The drops protect the vision you still have."
options.rationale: Names the reason adherence failed. In a silent disease, feeling no different is the drug working, and lost vision never returns.

options.text: "You should restart it right away or you could go blind by next month."
options.rationale: Frightening and inaccurate about the timeline. Fear-based teaching tends to reduce adherence rather than improve it.

options.text: "Many people find these drops uncomfortable. Would you like something for that?"
options.rationale: Answers a complaint he did not make. He said the drop was ineffective, not that it bothered him.

questions.takeaway: When a client says a drug was not doing anything, ask what they expected it to do. For a preventive drug in a silent disease, feeling no different is the drug working.
questions.strategy: One option agrees with him, one frightens him, one answers a different complaint. Only one corrects the belief that caused the behavior.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He thinks no symptom means no benefit.

steps.action: Cut the agreement and the scare
steps.detail: Neither changes the belief.
He never mentioned discomfort.

elimination.verdict: Explain the silent disease. That conversation is the intervention.

questions.stem: A patient arrives reporting sudden severe eye pain, nausea, blurred vision and halos. The eye is red and the cornea looks cloudy. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply a cool compress and place the patient in a darkened room
options.rationale: Comfort measures for an emergency. The pressure keeps rising while you do them.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately and prepare for urgent pressure-lowering treatment
options.rationale: Acute angle-closure glaucoma. The optic nerve is being damaged by the hour, and permanent vision loss follows within hours without treatment.

options.text: Instill the patient's usual glaucoma drops and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Routine maintenance drops will not lower a pressure of this magnitude, and waiting 30 minutes costs vision.

options.text: Administer an antiemetic and reassess the pain
options.rationale: Treats a symptom of the emergency. The nausea is caused by the intraocular pressure.

questions.takeaway: Sudden, painful, red, with a cloudy cornea and halos is angle-closure glaucoma, and it is an emergency. Laser peripheral iridotomy is the definitive first-line treatment.
questions.strategy: Three options are comfort measures. The word sudden in an eye question almost always means emergency.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pain plus sudden in an eye is an emergency until proven otherwise.

steps.action: Cut the compress and the antiemetic
steps.detail: Symptom relief for a pressure problem.
Maintenance therapy will not touch this.

elimination.verdict: Notify now. Vision is lost in hours, not days.

questions.stem: A patient calls the clinic reporting that a shower of new floaters appeared this morning, with flashes of light at the edge of vision and a shadow across part of the field. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient to be seen today as an emergency
options.rationale: Flashes, floaters and a curtain are retinal detachment until proven otherwise, and time to treatment determines how much vision is saved.

options.text: Instruct the patient to avoid activities that jar the head while arranging transport
options.rationale: Reducing further traction on the retina is reasonable while arrangements are made.

options.text: Reassure the patient that floaters are common with age and to watch for changes
options.rationale: Floaters alone can be benign. Floaters with flashes and a field defect are not, and this is the reassurance trap.

options.text: Ask whether the vision loss is painful
options.rationale: Useful discrimination. Detachment is painless, and pain would point toward a different emergency such as angle-closure.

options.text: Advise the patient to use over-the-counter lubricating drops and call back in a week
options.rationale: Treats it as dryness and delays care by a week, by which time central vision may be involved.

options.text: Ask about recent eye trauma, eye surgery or high myopia
options.rationale: All three are named risk factors for detachment and help establish how likely this is.

questions.takeaway: Flashes, floaters and a curtain equal retinal detachment. It is sudden, painless, and still an emergency.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options are both calm and both delay. Any option that sends a sudden visual change home to watch and wait is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flashes, floaters, curtain.

steps.action: Keep the urgent and diagnostic actions
steps.detail: Same-day care, limited jarring, pain question, risk factors.
Reassurance and lubricating drops.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D and F.

questions.stem: A patient is discharged after cataract extraction with an intraocular lens. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to reinforce?

options.text: "Expect your best vision by tomorrow morning."
options.rationale: Vision improves gradually and stabilizes at about four to six weeks. Promising overnight results sets the patient up to think something has gone wrong.

options.text: "Avoid bending at the waist, straining and lifting more than 10 pounds."
options.rationale: All three raise intraocular pressure, and a pressure spike in a freshly operated eye risks the wound and the lens position.

options.text: "Wear the eye patch continuously for the first two weeks."
options.rationale: Shielding is typically at night and during naps, per the surgeon. Continuous patching is not the standard instruction.

options.text: "Stop the antibiotic drops once the redness resolves."
options.rationale: Drops are completed as prescribed. Stopping when it looks better is the same error as stopping an antibiotic course early.

questions.takeaway: After any eye surgery the governing principle is never raise the intraocular pressure. Bending, straining, lifting, coughing and vomiting are all on the list.
questions.strategy: One option promises a timeline, one shortens a treatment, one overstates a precaution. Only one names the mechanism that causes the complication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pressure is what damages a fresh eye.
Best vision comes at four to six weeks.
Courses are finished.
Not the standard.

elimination.verdict: Avoid anything that raises pressure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted with a headache. In ambient light both pupils are 3 mm, equal and round. When the nurse shines a penlight into each eye in turn, both pupils constrict briskly each time. Before documenting PERRLA, what should the nurse do next?

options.text: Repeat the light test in a darkened room to confirm the response
options.rationale: The light response is already shown in both eyes. Repeating it adds nothing and still does not test the A.

options.text: Have him look at a distant point and then at the nurse's finger moving toward his nose
options.rationale: This tests accommodation. The nurse watches for pupil constriction with convergence as the target comes close. It is the only letter of PERRLA not yet tested.

options.text: Document PERRLA because the pupils are equal, round and reactive
options.rationale: Charting the A without testing it documents an assessment that was not done.

options.text: Measure his visual acuity with a Snellen chart
options.rationale: Acuity is a separate test. It does not complete the pupil assessment.

questions.takeaway: PERRLA ends with accommodation. Far target first, then a finger moving toward the nose. Look for constriction with convergence.
questions.strategy: Match each finding in the stem to a letter of PERRLA. The letter with no finding is the next step.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Equal, round, reactive to light, accommodation.
Size and shape given. Light response given for both eyes.
Accommodation is untested.

elimination.verdict: B. Test the A before you chart it.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma is newly prescribed timolol eye drops. Which teaching point is most important?

options.text: "Shake the bottle vigorously before each dose."
options.rationale: Applies to suspensions and is not the safety issue here.

options.text: "Press on the inner corner of your eye for a minute after the drop goes in."
options.rationale: Punctal occlusion blocks the tear duct so the drug stays in the eye rather than draining into the nose and being absorbed systemically. Timolol is a beta blocker and can cause bronchospasm.

options.text: "Store the drops in the refrigerator between doses."
options.rationale: A storage detail rather than a safety one, and it is not universally required.

options.text: "Stop the drops if your vision becomes blurred right after instillation."
options.rationale: Brief blurring after a drop is expected and not a reason to stop a sight-preserving medication.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma drops are systemic drugs. The eye holds one drop and the rest is absorbed through the nasal mucosa, skipping the liver. Beta blockers can cause bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm.
questions.strategy: The patient's asthma is in the stem for a reason. Ask which option protects the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is the only comorbidity given.
Timolol is a beta blocker.

steps.action: Cut the storage and shaking options
steps.detail: Neither touches systemic absorption.
Expected and transient.

elimination.verdict: Punctal occlusion, and the drop belongs on the medication reconciliation.

questions.stem: A construction worker arrives with a metal fragment protruding from the right eye after a grinding injury. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Gently remove the fragment and irrigate the eye with sterile saline
options.rationale: Never remove a protruding object. Removing it can extrude intraocular contents and blind the eye.

options.text: Stabilize the object, shield both eyes, and arrange urgent ophthalmology evaluation
options.rationale: The object stays where it is, the eye is shielded rather than patched, and both eyes are covered because the uninjured eye tracking causes the injured one to move.

options.text: Apply a pressure patch to the injured eye to control bleeding
options.rationale: Pressure on a penetrated globe forces contents out. Shielding is not patching.

options.text: Send the patient for an MRI to determine the depth of the fragment
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated when a metal fragment is suspected, because the magnet can move it. X-ray or CT is used instead.

questions.takeaway: Never remove a protruding object, never apply pressure, shield both eyes, and no MRI when metal is suspected. Imaging is X-ray or CT.
questions.strategy: Three options involve doing something to the eye. In penetrating eye trauma, the correct action is almost always to protect and refer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The object is not the nurse's to remove.
Pressure extrudes contents.
Contraindicated with metal.
Covering only one leaves the injured eye tracking.

elimination.verdict: Stabilize, shield both eyes, refer urgently.

questions.stem: At a community health fair the nurse reviews four clients. None has a family history of eye disease. Which client has reached a glaucoma risk threshold taught in class that calls for earlier screening?

options.text: A 42-year-old African American man with no visual symptoms
options.rationale: African American clients meet the risk threshold at age 40. Open-angle glaucoma is often silent until late, so no symptoms does not mean no disease.

options.text: A 52-year-old Hispanic woman with no visual symptoms
options.rationale: Hispanic and Latino clients meet the risk threshold at age 60. At 52 with no other listed risk she has not reached it.

options.text: A 25-year-old who wears contact lenses and has a red, painful eye
options.rationale: This points to a corneal abrasion or infection, which needs prompt care for a different reason. It is not a glaucoma risk factor.

options.text: A 35-year-old office worker who reports eyestrain after long computer use
options.rationale: This is digital eyestrain. Teach the 20-20-20 rule. It is not a glaucoma risk.

questions.takeaway: Glaucoma risk: age 60 and older, African American 40 and older, Hispanic or Latino 60 and older, family history. The threshold is lower where the disease starts earlier.
questions.strategy: Two options describe real eye problems that belong to other conditions. One names a risk group below its threshold. Match each age to its threshold.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A cornea problem.
Digital eyestrain.
Hispanic at 52 is under 60. African American at 42 is over 40.

elimination.verdict: A. The only client past a glaucoma threshold.

questions.scenario: A 71-year-old man is seen in clinic for diabetes follow-up. He mentions he has stopped driving at night because of glare, and that he has started seeing rings around streetlights. He has filled his prescribed eye drops once in six months. Last recorded intraocular pressures were 26 mm Hg right and 24 mm Hg left. On confrontation testing he does not see your fingers until they are well inside his peripheral field bilaterally. His A1c is 9.1% and his blood pressure is 158/92.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Have him demonstrate instilling a drop, and teach punctal occlusion
options.rationale: Adherence is the problem in front of you, and technique is the part a nurse can fix in the room. Punctal occlusion also reduces systemic absorption.

options.text: Explain that the drops protect remaining vision in a disease with no symptoms
options.rationale: Names the belief that caused him to stop. Without this, better technique on a drug he does not believe in changes nothing.

options.text: Refer him for cataract evaluation for the glare and night driving
options.rationale: Reasonable on the surface and it misses the thing destroying his optic nerve. He may well have a cataract too, and it is not the priority today.

options.text: Document the missed doses and address adherence at the next visit
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. Every month of nonadherence costs visual field that does not come back.

options.text: Uncontrolled open-angle glaucoma with nonadherence to therapy
options.rationale: Painless, gradual, halos, raised pressures and peripheral field loss. The nonadherence is why it is uncontrolled.

options.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: That is sudden, painful, with a red eye and a cloudy cornea. Nothing here is acute.

options.text: Diabetic retinopathy
options.rationale: A real risk with an A1c of 9.1% and it does not explain a pressure of 26 or the pattern of peripheral loss.

options.text: Age-related macular degeneration
options.rationale: Macular disease takes central vision first. His loss is peripheral.

options.text: Intraocular pressure at follow-up
options.rationale: The direct measure of whether therapy is working. Target is at or below about 21 mm Hg.

options.text: Visual field testing results over time
options.rationale: Field loss is what the treatment exists to stop. Stability is success; further loss means the plan is failing.

options.text: Snellen visual acuity in each eye
options.rationale: Central acuity stays normal in open-angle glaucoma until very late, so it will look reassuring while the disease progresses.

options.text: Absence of eye pain at follow-up
options.rationale: Open-angle glaucoma is painless throughout. Comfort tells you nothing, and believing it is exactly why he stopped the drops.

questions.takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma is silent, takes peripheral vision first, and lost vision never returns. Evaluate it with pressure and visual fields, never with acuity or comfort.
questions.strategy: Two of the parameters will look normal while the disease progresses. Ask which measurement would actually change if the treatment failed.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Peripheral loss with raised pressure names the condition.
One filled prescription in six months.
Both stay normal until the disease is advanced.

elimination.verdict: Fix the adherence and the belief behind it, and follow pressure and fields.

questions.stem: During a Weber test the patient reports the sound is louder in the left ear. A Rinne test on the left shows bone conduction lasting longer than air conduction. How does the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Normal hearing bilaterally
options.rationale: Normal is equal on Weber and air conduction outlasting bone on Rinne. Neither is present.

options.text: Conductive hearing loss in the left ear
options.rationale: Weber lateralizes toward a conductive loss, and bone beating air means sound cannot get in through the usual route. Both tests point at the same ear for the same reason.

options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
options.rationale: A sensorineural loss makes Weber lateralize away, to the good ear, and air would still beat bone.

options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear
options.rationale: That would make Weber lateralize to the left, which fits, and the Rinne would show air beating bone on the left. It does not.

questions.takeaway: Weber lateralizes toward a conductive loss because the blocked ear hears less competing room noise, so the bone-conducted tone sounds louder there. It lateralizes away from a sensorineural loss because that ear cannot process sound however it arrives. Bone beating air means a conductive block.
questions.strategy: The Weber result alone is ambiguous, because it fits a conductive loss on the left or a sensorineural loss on the right. The Rinne is what settles it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Louder on the left. Two explanations fit.
Bone beats air on the left, which is a block.
Both tests name the left ear and name conduction.

elimination.verdict: Conductive loss on the left. Cerumen, fluid, perforation or otosclerosis.

questions.stem: A patient on day three of gentamicin and furosemide reports new ringing in both ears. The creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Document the tinnitus and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Documenting instead of acting. By the time hearing loss is measurable, aminoglycoside damage is often permanent.

options.text: Notify the prescriber of the tinnitus together with the rising creatinine
options.rationale: Both drugs are ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Tinnitus is the early warning of ototoxicity, and the rising creatinine is the same injury in a second organ.

options.text: Reassure the patient that ringing is a common and harmless side effect
options.rationale: It is common and it is not harmless. Reassurance here delays the only action that can prevent permanent loss.

options.text: Hold the next dose of gentamicin and continue the furosemide
options.rationale: The recognition is right and holding a drug is a prescriber decision. It also leaves the second ototoxic drug running.

questions.takeaway: Tinnitus is the early warning of ototoxicity, not the injury. An aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic is worse than either alone, and the ear and the kidney go down together.
questions.strategy: One option waits, one reassures and one exceeds scope. Only one reports the two findings as a single problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ear and kidney, same two drugs.
Both delay.
A prescriber decision, and it misses the diuretic.

elimination.verdict: Notify now, with the creatinine, and ask about trough levels.

questions.stem: A child with acute otitis media has been crying with ear pain for two days. This morning the parent reports the pain stopped suddenly and there is yellow drainage on the pillow. What does the nurse conclude?

options.text: The antibiotic has taken effect and the infection is resolving
options.rationale: The emotionally compelling answer, and the family will have already reached it. Nothing about the infection was treated by what happened.

options.text: The tympanic membrane has perforated and the finding must be reported
options.rationale: Pressure built until the drum gave way. The pain stops because the pressure is released, and the drainage is the contents of the middle ear.

options.text: The child has developed external otitis in addition to the middle ear infection
options.rationale: External otitis produces pain with movement of the pinna, not sudden relief with purulent drainage from behind the drum.

options.text: The drainage is normal cerumen loosened by the fever
options.rationale: Cerumen is waxy and brown, and a fever does not liquefy it into purulent drainage.

questions.takeaway: Otitis media progresses retracted, red, bulging, perforated, and the pain stops when it ruptures. Sudden relief with drainage is perforation, not recovery.
questions.strategy: The relief is real and the family will present it as good news. Ask what changed physically.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It built for two days and then stopped abruptly.
A rupture.
Antibiotics do not produce sudden relief with new purulent drainage.

elimination.verdict: Perforation. Document the drainage, notify, and the antibiotic course still finishes.

questions.stem: A patient with impacted cerumen and a suspected tympanic membrane perforation asks the nurse to flush the wax out. What is the nurse's response?

options.text: Irrigate gently with body-temperature water to avoid dizziness
options.rationale: Temperature control is a real technique point and it does not make irrigation safe here.

options.text: Explain that irrigation is not done when a perforation is suspected, and notify the provider
options.rationale: Irrigating past a perforated drum drives contaminated fluid into the middle ear and spreads the infection.

options.text: Instill a ceruminolytic and then irrigate after 15 minutes of softening
options.rationale: The softening step is correct in general, and it does not remove the contraindication.

options.text: Use a cotton-tipped applicator to remove the visible wax first
options.rationale: Swabs push wax deeper and risk injuring an already compromised drum.

questions.takeaway: Never irrigate with a suspected perforation or active otitis media, never with vegetable matter, and never a live insect. Ceruminolytic first, then removal by the provider.
questions.strategy: Three options are safer versions of the same forbidden action. A contraindication is not cancelled by good technique.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Suspected perforation.
Warm water, softening first and swabs are still going in.
Doing an unsafe thing more carefully is the recurring distractor.

elimination.verdict: Do not irrigate. Notify.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for an 80-year-old with presbycusis. Which communication technique by the nurse requires correction?

options.text: Facing the patient directly at eye level with the light on the nurse's own face
options.rationale: Appropriate. A large part of what a hearing-impaired person understands is read from lips and expression. Standing in front of a window makes your face a silhouette.

options.text: Lowering the pitch of the voice while speaking at a moderate pace
options.rationale: Appropriate. Presbycusis takes the high frequencies first. Lowering pitch moves your voice into the range still intact.

options.text: Raising the voice to a near shout so the words carry
options.rationale: Needs correction. Shouting raises pitch into exactly the range that has been lost. It also distorts the words.

options.text: Rephrasing a sentence that was not understood rather than repeating it
options.rationale: Appropriate. Different words carry different frequencies. Repeating the same words louder rarely works.

questions.takeaway: Face them, lower your pitch, slow down, cut the background noise, rephrase and verify with teach-back. Never shout.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong technique. Shouting is the reflex everyone has and the thing that makes it worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the one technique that fails.
High frequencies are gone.

steps.action: Find the one that raises pitch
steps.detail: Shouting raises pitch and distorts. The rest work with a high-frequency loss.

elimination.verdict: C. Shouting pushes the voice into the range that is lost.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged on the first day after a stapedectomy. Which instruction does the nurse emphasize?

options.text: "Your hearing should be back to normal by the time you get home."
options.rationale: Hearing improves over about four to six weeks. Promising an immediate result makes a normal recovery look like a failure.

options.text: "Ask for help when you get up, and avoid straining, nose-blowing and air travel."
options.rationale: Vertigo risk is high right after surgery, and every one of those activities raises middle ear pressure against a fresh prosthesis.

options.text: "Irrigate the ear canal daily to prevent a wax buildup."
options.rationale: Nothing goes into a postoperative ear canal, and irrigation after middle ear surgery is contraindicated.

options.text: "A drooping mouth on the operative side is expected for a few days."
options.rationale: Facial asymmetry means facial nerve injury, because CN VII runs right past the surgical field. That is reported, never normalized.

questions.takeaway: After a stapedectomy: assist ambulation because vertigo risk is high, avoid anything that raises middle ear pressure, watch CN VII, and expect hearing to improve over four to six weeks.
questions.strategy: One option normalizes a complication, one promises a timeline, one puts fluid in a fresh surgical field. The correct one is the only one about safety.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Falling from vertigo.
That is CN VII injury and gets reported.
Never in a postoperative canal.
Four to six weeks, not immediately.

elimination.verdict: Assist ambulation and avoid pressure-raising activities.

questions.stem: A patient with Meniere disease is admitted during an acute attack with severe vertigo, vomiting and nystagmus. Which nursing action takes priority?

options.text: Encourage oral fluids to replace losses from vomiting
options.rationale: Fluid is not the intervention here, and sodium restriction is the dietary principle in this disease.

options.text: Keep the side rails up, the call light in reach, and instruct the patient to lie still
options.rationale: The priority is preventing injury. Movement worsens the vertigo, and a fall during an attack is the realistic harm.

options.text: Ambulate the patient in the hall to prevent deconditioning
options.rationale: Movement during an acute attack is what causes the injury. Vestibular rehabilitation happens between attacks, not during one.

options.text: Place the patient in a brightly lit room for orientation
options.rationale: Light and visual stimulation worsen vertigo. A darkened quiet room is what helps.

questions.takeaway: Meniere is a safety diagnosis. The classic triad is vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss, and the fall is the emergency, not the vital sign changes.
questions.strategy: Nothing here threatens the airway, so the ABCs do not decide it. Safety and risk reduction does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safety, not ABCs.
Both make vertigo worse.
Sodium restriction is the dietary rule.

elimination.verdict: Injury prevention: rails, call light, lie still, darkened room.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with Meniere disease is taught what to change at home. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will follow a low-sodium diet."
options.rationale: Correct. Sodium drives fluid retention. The disease is excess endolymph. Sodium restriction is the first lifestyle intervention.

options.text: "I will not drive or climb ladders when an attack could occur."
options.rationale: Correct. Tumarkin drop attacks come without warning, so the environment has to be safe in advance rather than relying on the patient to notice symptoms.

options.text: "I will drink more fluids to dilute the fluid in my inner ear."
options.rationale: The problem is too much fluid, not fluid that is too concentrated. Adding volume works against the treatment.

options.text: "My diuretic will reduce the amount of fluid in my inner ear."
options.rationale: Correct. Diuretics lower endolymph volume, which is the mechanism of the disease.

questions.takeaway: Low sodium, avoid triggers, fall precautions, diuretics. Surgery is last resort and labyrinthectomy costs the hearing on that side.
questions.strategy: One statement sounds like sensible hydration advice. Ask whether more fluid helps a disease of too much fluid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Need for further teaching means you want the wrong statement.
Excess endolymph distending the labyrinth.

steps.action: Keep everything that removes fluid or prevents falls
steps.detail: Low sodium, diuretic, safety.
More fluid adds volume to a disease of too much fluid.

elimination.verdict: C, increasing fluids.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man worked 30 years in a loud factory. Audiometry shows sensorineural hearing loss. His hearing aids helped very little. The nurse explains how a cochlear implant differs from a hearing aid. Which statement by the patient shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: "The implant is a stronger hearing aid, so it will just make everything louder."
options.rationale: This shows a misunderstanding. The implant is a different mechanism, not more amplification.

options.text: "The implant goes around the damaged part of my inner ear and sends the signal straight to the nerve."
options.rationale: This is correct. A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged cochlea and stimulates the nerve directly. That is why it can help when amplification cannot.

options.text: "My hearing aids failed because they were not fitted right. A refit would fix my nerve damage."
options.rationale: Fit matters. A perfect fit still only amplifies sound. It does not repair the cochlea or nerve.

options.text: "Hearing aids work best for nerve damage. Implants are for blockages like earwax."
options.rationale: This is reversed. Hearing aids help conductive loss more. Cochlear implants are for sensorineural loss.

questions.takeaway: Hearing aids amplify and help conductive loss more than sensorineural loss. Cochlear implants are for sensorineural loss. They bypass the damaged cochlea and stimulate the nerve directly.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that names what each device actually does. Statements that confuse the devices or blame the fitting show teaching is still needed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensorineural from noise. The cochlea is damaged.
Aids for nerve damage is backwards.
Amplification and refitting do not bypass the cochlea.

elimination.verdict: B. Amplify versus bypass is the whole concept.

questions.nursesNote: 0830: Patient is 74, admitted yesterday with pyelonephritis, receiving IV gentamicin and furosemide. Reports new bilateral ringing in the ears that began overnight. Asks the nurse to repeat questions twice and turns the left ear toward the speaker. No prior history of hearing difficulty and wears no hearing aids. Nursing assistant reports the patient was unsteady walking to the bathroom this morning. Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, up from 0.9 on admission. Temperature 37.2 C. Blood pressure 124/72. Lungs clear. Reports flank pain improved from 7 to 3 out of 10.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate a developing drug toxicity.

segments.text: Receiving IV gentamicin and furosemide
segments.rationale: An aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic. Both are ototoxic and both are nephrotoxic, and together they are worse than either alone.

segments.text: New bilateral ringing in the ears that began overnight
segments.rationale: Tinnitus is the earliest sign of ototoxicity and precedes measurable hearing loss.

segments.text: Asks the nurse to repeat questions twice and turns the left ear toward the speaker
segments.rationale: Behavioral cues of hearing loss, and they are new. Behavior is assessment data.

segments.text: Unsteady walking to the bathroom this morning
segments.rationale: CN VIII carries hearing and balance together, so vestibular symptoms belong in the same picture rather than being filed as deconditioning.

segments.text: Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, up from 0.9 on admission
segments.rationale: The same drugs damaging the same two organs. A rising creatinine in this patient is also an ear warning.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2 C
segments.rationale: Normal, and evidence the infection is responding.

segments.text: Blood pressure 124/72
segments.rationale: Normal and unrelated.

segments.text: Flank pain improved from 7 to 3 out of 10
segments.rationale: The pyelonephritis is improving. A reassuring finding that has nothing to do with the toxicity.

questions.takeaway: When a new symptom appears in a patient on a known toxic drug, the drug is your first hypothesis, not your last. Aging, deconditioning and anxiety are the three explanations that get older adults hurt.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or improving and are there to reward you for reading the whole note. Everything else converges on two drugs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Gentamicin and furosemide.
Ringing, repeating, unsteadiness, and a creatinine that nearly doubled.
Temperature, blood pressure and improving flank pain.

elimination.verdict: Five findings, all pointing at ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity from the same two drugs. The negative hearing history is context that makes the change new, not a manifestation you highlight.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. The patient sits at the side of the bed unassisted for three minutes, reaches across midline, and shakes the nurse's hand. With both feet flat on the floor and the knees below hip level, the patient straightens each knee and points the toes. When asked to rise, the patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. Which mobility level does this patient have?

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Level 3 is assigned when the patient fails the stand test, which checks lower-extremity strength for standing. The patient passed the first two tests and failed the third, which means there is some lower-extremity strength but not enough to progress toward walking.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Level 1 is assigned when the patient fails the sit and shake test, which checks trunk strength and seated balance. The first test was passed, so Level 1 is ruled out by the stem.

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Level 2 is assigned when the patient fails the stretch and point test, which checks lower-extremity strength and stability. The second test was passed as well.

options.text: Level 4, minimum or standby assist
options.rationale: Level 4 requires passing the walk test, which checks standing balance and gait by having the patient march in place and advance a foot. You cannot skip a failed test to reach a higher level.

questions.takeaway: The tool is a sequence of four tests, and the level is named by the first test the patient cannot complete. Sit and shake, stretch and point, stand, walk.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old patient is on postoperative day 2 after abdominal surgery. The nurse is completing the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. The patient sat unassisted for 3 minutes, reached across midline and shook the nurse's hand. The patient then extended each knee and pointed the toes. Before asking the patient to rise toward standing, which finding is most important for the nurse to act on?

options.text: The patient used a front-wheeled walker at home before surgery
options.rationale: An assistive device may be used during the stand test, so this information shapes how the test is set up. It does not tell the nurse whether it is safe to begin.

options.text: The patient is oriented to self only today and drifts in and out of the conversation
options.rationale: Orientation to self only with fluctuating attention suggests delirium, an acute confusion with a physical cause. The slides direct the nurse to consider cognition, orientation and delirium before the stand test. Standing is the first step that puts the patient's weight on the legs. A patient who cannot follow directions may stand before being ready.

options.text: Seated heart rate is 88 beats per minute and blood pressure is 128/76
options.rationale: These values are within expected limits for a seated patient. They support moving forward rather than stopping.

options.text: The handshake grip was firm in both hands
options.rationale: Grip was sampled during the first level of the tool. It reflects upper body strength and says nothing about judgment or leg strength.

questions.takeaway: Strength and judgment fail separately. A patient whose legs pass the test while the thinking does not may stand without waiting for help, so the nurse checks cognition before level 3.

questions.stem: A patient has left-sided weakness after a stroke. The patient can raise the left arm about halfway toward shoulder height and then cannot lift it any further. Which exercise does the nurse use to maintain shoulder mobility?

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the arm through the whole arc
options.rationale: Passive range of motion means someone else moves the joint while the patient's muscle does nothing. Taking over the whole arc wastes the muscle activity the patient still has, and passive work maintains flexibility without building strength.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the patient raising the arm through the full arc unaided
options.rationale: Active range of motion means the patient performs the entire movement alone. The joint would never reach full range, and stiffness would develop in the part that is never used.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the patient raising the arm as far as possible and the nurse completing the movement
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion means the patient moves the joint as far as they can and the nurse supplies the remainder. The muscle works through the portion the patient controls, which preserves strength, and the joint still reaches full range, which preserves flexibility.

options.text: Isometric exercise, with the patient tightening the shoulder muscles without moving the joint
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. Isometric work builds static strength and joint stability and does nothing for range.

questions.takeaway: Whenever a patient can contribute any part of a movement, they do that part. Active-assistive is the choice that keeps muscle working and still carries the joint through full range.

questions.stem: A patient has a long arm cast after a forearm fracture and will wear it for six weeks. The patient asks how to avoid losing strength in that arm. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Move the elbow and wrist through their full range several times daily
options.rationale: Range of motion carries a joint through its arc. Joints above and below a cast are exercised where they are free, and the joints inside it are immobilized on purpose while the bone heals.

options.text: Lift a light hand weight with the casted arm
options.rationale: Lifting a weight through an arc is isotonic exercise, in which the muscle contracts while the joint moves. This is the correct exercise for building dynamic strength and the wrong one for a limb that must stay still.

options.text: Rest the arm completely until the cast is removed
options.rationale: Complete rest means no muscle activity at all. Resting sounds protective and guarantees the outcome the patient asked how to avoid.

options.text: Tighten and release the muscles inside the cast without moving the joints
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement. It increases static strength and builds joint stability, and it can be used safely around painful or healing tissue, so the muscle keeps working for the six weeks the joint cannot.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise is the answer when a joint must not move. The muscle can still be loaded, so strength and joint stability survive the period of immobilization.

questions.stem: A patient walks the length of the hallway with a nurse. Which findings indicate that the patient exceeded activity tolerance? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient becomes light-headed and reaches for the handrail
options.rationale: Dizziness is a listed tolerance parameter and it signals that perfusion to the brain has dropped. A patient who needs the handrail to stay upright is at the point where the activity becomes a fall.

options.text: Heart rate remains 118 ten minutes after returning to the chair
options.rationale: Recovery is the last item on the list of things to evaluate and the one most often skipped. A sustained elevation says the patient did more than the cardiovascular system could absorb, even if the walk itself looked acceptable.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 92 during the walk and returns to 80 within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is judged by the response to activity and by the recovery afterward. This is the body working correctly, not failing.

options.text: Oxygen saturation falls from 96 percent to 87 percent during the walk
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Oxygenation is one of the listed tolerance parameters, and a drop of nine points into the eighties means demand has outrun the patient's ability to supply it.

options.text: The patient stops twice and says it is hard to catch a breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea is the subjective sense of not getting enough air. Having to stop is the functional version of the same finding.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20 and settles back to 16 after three minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is one of the tolerance parameters. A modest increase during walking that resolves on sitting is the expected response.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and the ability to recover afterward. Rises during exertion are expected; what matters is how large they are and whether they resolve.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a neurovascular assessment on a patient six hours after surgical repair of an ankle fracture. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Capillary refill of four seconds in the toes with new numbness of the foot, compared with two seconds and normal sensation on the other side
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressure on the nail bed, normally under three seconds, and numbness is loss of sensation. Absent or diminished pulses, a cool or pale extremity, new numbness, and sudden loss of movement are all findings to report.

options.text: Moderate swelling at the surgical site
options.rationale: Swelling is fluid accumulating in injured tissue. What would concern you is swelling that is rapid or increasing quickly, and the stem describes neither.

options.text: Bruising visible along the lateral ankle
options.rationale: Bruising is blood that has escaped into the tissue from the injury and the surgery. It is an expected finding after a fracture and its repair.

options.text: Pain rated 5 of 10 that decreases after the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Pain is one of the neurovascular parameters. This pain responded to the ordered dose, which is the reassuring version of the finding.

questions.takeaway: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, and pain, and it is always compared side to side. Two abnormal findings in the same limb with a normal opposite side is the pattern that gets reported.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile in bed for two weeks following a spinal cord injury. The nurse finds that both feet rest with the toes pointed downward and the ankles can no longer be brought to a neutral position. Which complication has developed?

options.text: Bone demineralization
options.rationale: Bone demineralization is the loss of mineral from bone that is not being loaded. It shows on imaging or in calcium studies, not as a joint that will not move.

options.text: Foot drop, which is a plantar flexion contracture
options.rationale: A contracture is the permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility, and plantar flexion is the toes-pointed position of the ankle. That is foot drop, and it is prevented by maintaining neutral alignment, performing range of motion, and using supportive devices.

options.text: Muscle atrophy
options.rationale: Atrophy is the shrinking of muscle that is not being used. This patient almost certainly has atrophy too, and atrophy does not lock a joint in a fixed position, which is what the stem describes.

options.text: Venous stasis
options.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs because the muscle pump has stopped working. It raises the risk of thrombus formation and presents as swelling or as a clot, not as a rigid ankle.

questions.takeaway: Contractures are permanent shortening, so prevention is the whole intervention. Range of motion, neutral alignment, and supportive devices are scheduled rather than offered when there is time.

questions.stem: A patient is on bed rest after spinal surgery. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds at both lung bases with no adventitious sounds, notes that the patient's cough is weak, and finds that the oxygen saturation has fallen from 97 to 92 percent. The temperature is 36.8 C. Which complication is developing?

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue. It has not yet.

options.text: Thrombus formation in the legs
options.rationale: A thrombus is a clot forming in a vein where blood has stopped moving. Thrombus is a genuine risk for this patient and is not what these findings describe.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of small airways and alveoli that are not being inflated. Diminished sounds without adventitious sounds means air is not reaching the area rather than moving through something.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance means the body is breaking down more protein than it takes in. It is a metabolic effect of immobility, not a respiratory one.

questions.takeaway: Flat positioning reduces lung expansion, a weak cough leaves secretions in place, and the dependent bases collapse first. Atelectasis is the step before pneumonia, not the same thing.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old patient has been on prescribed bed rest for 6 days after a pelvic fracture. The patient has a weak cough and spends most of the day lying flat. The patient has begun resting with the toes pointed. The nurse plans care for the next shift. For each nursing action, indicate the complication of immobility it is intended to prevent.

rows.text: Sits the patient upright and has the patient cough and deep breathe every two hours
rows.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli that are not being inflated. Sitting upright expands the lungs. Coughing and deep breathing move the retained secretions that build up when a patient with a weak cough stays flat.

rows.text: Applies sequential compression devices and has the patient perform leg exercises
rows.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs once the muscle pump stops working. Compression devices and leg exercises keep blood moving out of the legs, which is what prevents a clot from forming.

rows.text: Takes every joint through its full arc twice daily
rows.rationale: A contracture is permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility. Range of motion is the direct prevention.

rows.text: Repositions the patient on a schedule and lifts rather than drags during the move
rows.rationale: Pressure, friction and shear are the three mechanical forces that injure skin. All three reduce circulation to the tissue. The schedule limits time under pressure. Lifting instead of dragging removes friction and shear.

rows.text: Raises the head of the bed in stages and has the patient sit at the edge of the bed before standing
rows.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in blood pressure when the patient moves upright, so the brain briefly receives too little blood. Gradual position changes give the circulation time to adjust before the patient bears weight.

rows.text: Positions a supportive device against the soles of the feet to hold the ankles in neutral alignment
rows.rationale: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture in which the ankle sets with the toes pointed. This patient already rests that way. A supportive device holds the ankle in neutral alignment so the contracture cannot form.

questions.takeaway: Immobility damages seven systems through three mechanisms: stasis of fluids, pressure on tissue and disuse of muscle, bone and joint. Name the mechanism and the matching intervention follows.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 22-year-old soccer player twisted the left knee during a game 2 hours ago. The knee is swollen and the patient cannot fully straighten it. The patient reports that the knee gives way when bearing weight. Pedal pulses are strong and equal.

The nurse anticipates that the first study ordered to show whether a bone is broken is [[1]].

The imaging shows no fracture. Three days later the knee still gives way. The nurse anticipates that the study best able to show a torn ligament is [[2]].

A fracture is still suspected because pain persists at one spot on the bone even though the imaging looked normal. The study that may reveal it is [[3]].

options.text: an x-ray
options.rationale: An x-ray passes radiation through tissue and shows dense structures clearly. It is the first study for a possible broken bone because it answers that question quickly.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography builds cross-sectional images and gives more detail of bone than a plain film. It earns its place with complex fractures once a fracture is known or strongly suspected.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound uses sound waves to assess tendons, muscles, fluid collections and some joint abnormalities. Bone reflects the sound, so it is not the study for a suspected fracture.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissue best. It is the right study for a different question about this knee.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography is the detailed bone study. This is the near miss, because both this and the correct answer are cross-sectional and both sound like more information than an x-ray.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, such as occult fractures, infection or tumors. A ligament tear does not show up on a bone scan.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is best for soft tissue such as muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, spinal structures and bone marrow. Instability that persists after a clear x-ray points to ligament rather than bone.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density and is used to assess osteoporosis. It tells how strong bone is over time rather than what tore today.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity. Injured bone is metabolically active. Occult means present but not visible on ordinary imaging, which is exactly this situation.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density. It reports how dense the bone is, which is a different question from whether this bone is cracked.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography provides more detailed bone images and is useful for complex fractures. This is the strongest distractor, because more detail sounds like the way to find something that is hiding.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles, fluid collections and some joint abnormalities. Sound does not pass through bone well enough to find a hidden fracture.

questions.takeaway: Match the study to the tissue and to the question. Use x-ray for a suspected break and computed tomography for detail on bone. Use magnetic resonance imaging for soft tissue, a bone scan for a fracture nothing else has shown and a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan for density.

questions.stem: A patient has 5 of 5 muscle strength in both legs but sways and grabs the bedrail when standing with eyes closed. Which system is most likely impaired?

options.text: Skeletal muscle strength
options.rationale: Already measured as full. Strength is not the failing component.

options.text: Joint range of motion
options.rationale: Limits how far a joint moves. It does not produce instability at rest in standing.

options.text: Bone density
options.rationale: Affects fracture risk, not postural control.

options.text: Proprioception and balance
options.rationale: Proprioception is awareness of body position without looking. Losing vision removes the backup, so the sway appears.

questions.takeaway: Strength and balance fail separately. A strong patient can still be unsafe to walk.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old patient with chronic low back pain sits slumped in a bedside chair with the hips slid forward. After 20 minutes the patient reports aching in the low back and says, "I'm worn out just sitting here." The nurse repositions the patient with the hips at the back of the seat and the feet flat on the floor. A pillow supports the lumbar curve. Which finding 1 hour later best shows that the repositioning achieved its purpose?

options.text: The patient is still sitting upright and says the back ache has eased and the tiredness is gone
options.rationale: Proper alignment minimizes stress on joints and reduces fatigue. Less ache and less tiredness in the same position are the outcomes alignment is meant to produce. The posture also held, which shows the support was adequate.

options.text: The patient ate the whole lunch tray
options.rationale: Appetite is not an outcome of alignment. Eating well is a good sign that has no link to how the spine is positioned.

options.text: The patient has slid forward again but says the chair is comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort alone does not confirm alignment. The posture that caused the strain has returned, so the intervention has not held and the patient needs repositioning with more support.

options.text: The patient's heart rate rose from 76 to 94 beats per minute while sitting
options.rationale: A rising heart rate while resting in a chair suggests effort or distress. It is the opposite of the reduced fatigue that good alignment produces.

questions.takeaway: Proper alignment promotes efficient movement, minimizes stress on joints, reduces fatigue and improves balance. Evaluate it by checking that the posture held and that the strain it caused has eased.

questions.stem: During the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool, a patient cannot sit at the side of the bed unassisted and is unable to reach across midline. Which level applies?

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient sits successfully but cannot extend the leg and point the toes.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Failing the sit and shake test means trunk strength and seated balance are inadequate. The assessment stops here.

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. This patient never reached that test.

options.text: Level 4, minimum assist
options.rationale: Requires advancing a step, which is three tests away.

questions.takeaway: You stop at the first test the patient cannot complete, and that failure names the level.

questions.stem: A patient is unconscious after a traumatic brain injury and cannot initiate any movement. Which exercise maintains joint flexibility?

options.text: Active range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to move the joint. This patient cannot initiate movement.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to start the movement so the nurse can complete it.

options.text: Passive range of motion
options.rationale: The nurse moves the joint entirely. It maintains flexibility and prevents contractures when the patient can contribute nothing.

options.text: Isometric exercise
options.rationale: Requires voluntary muscle contraction.

questions.takeaway: Passive is correct only when the patient cannot contribute. It maintains flexibility and builds no strength.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches an 80-year-old patient about the musculoskeletal changes expected with aging. Which statement by the patient shows that further teaching is needed?

options.text: "My muscles will get smaller as I age, so staying active matters."
options.rationale: Expected. Muscle tissue atrophies with age, which contributes to weakness and slower movement. This statement shows accurate understanding.

options.text: "I may not be able to bend my joints as far as I used to."
options.rationale: Expected. Range of motion decreases as joint cartilage loses elasticity. This statement is accurate.

options.text: "The cartilage in my joints will become more elastic as I get older."
options.rationale: Synovial joint cartilage becomes less elastic and compressible with age. The patient has the direction reversed, so this statement needs correction.

options.text: "My bones may get thinner, which raises my risk of breaking one."
options.rationale: Expected. Osteopenia or osteoporosis develops as bone density falls. This statement is accurate.

questions.takeaway: Muscle, bone and cartilage all lose something with age. These are expected changes rather than disease, although they still raise the risk of falls and fractures.
questions.strategy: The stem asks which statement shows a need for more teaching, so look for the one that is false. Every expected aging change in this system is a loss, so the statement describing a gain is the error.

steps.detail: "Further teaching is needed" means pick the incorrect statement.
Smaller muscles, less joint motion and thinner bones are all losses.
More elastic cartilage is the only gain.

elimination.verdict: C.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a casted arm and cannot palpate the radial pulse. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the finding and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Delays confirmation of whether blood is reaching the hand.

options.text: Elevate the arm above the level of the heart
options.rationale: Raising a limb that may already be underperfused reduces arterial inflow further.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to improve circulation
options.rationale: Does not address a possible obstruction and delays the assessment.

options.text: Use a Doppler to check for flow, then compare with the other arm
options.rationale: A Doppler detects flow that cannot be felt. Comparing sides turns an uncertain finding into a clear one.

questions.takeaway: Absent or diminished pulses is a red flag. Confirm with Doppler and always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wants to begin an exercise program. Which modification does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Shorter sessions paced to the patient's tolerance with rest periods
options.rationale: Activity plans are modified rather than cancelled in chronic illness, and tolerance sets the pace.

options.text: Avoid all physical activity to conserve oxygen
options.rationale: Inactivity worsens deconditioning and breathlessness over time.

options.text: High-intensity intervals to build endurance quickly
options.rationale: Exceeds tolerance and risks severe dyspnea.
