options.rationale: Feeding can be delegated once swallowing is confirmed safe.

options.text: Give the patient sips of water to see how well she swallows.
options.rationale: This is a swallow assessment.

options.text: Feed the patient now because she is hungry.
options.rationale: Feeding before a swallow screen risks aspiration.

questions.takeaway: The RN does the swallow screen. Assistive personnel can feed only after the screen is passed.
questions.strategy: Assessment stays with the RN. Look for the option that keeps it there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and C are both swallow assessments.
D skips the screen.
B has the RN confirming first.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old patient is 24 hours after an ischemic stroke. At 0800 the patient was calm and oriented. At 1000 the nurse reassesses the patient. Which finding, if present, is the earliest sign of increased intracranial pressure?

options.text: Pupils 6 mm, fixed and nonreactive
options.rationale: Fixed, dilated pupils are a late sign.

options.text: Restless and pulling at the gown. Unsure of the day.
options.rationale: Declining LOC, including restlessness and new confusion, is the earliest sign of increased ICP.

options.text: BP 182/70 with heart rate 50
options.rationale: Rising BP with a widened pulse pressure and bradycardia is part of the Cushing triad, a late sign.

options.text: Arms extended and rotated outward with feet pointed down
options.rationale: Decerebrate posturing is a late sign that indicates brainstem involvement.

questions.takeaway: The earliest sign of increased ICP is a change in LOC. Fixed pupils, posturing and the Cushing triad are late.
questions.strategy: "Earliest" means pick the subtlest change, not the most dramatic.

steps.detail: Fixed pupils, posturing and the Cushing pattern are late.
Restlessness and new confusion show a change in LOC from the 0800 baseline.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old patient with increased ICP after a hemorrhagic stroke becomes harder to arouse. Four hours ago the vital signs were BP 138/82, heart rate 84 and respirations 16 and regular. Which new set of vital signs should the nurse recognize as the Cushing triad?

options.text: BP 88/50, heart rate 128, respirations 30 and shallow
options.rationale: Hypotension with tachycardia suggests shock, not rising ICP.

options.text: BP 186/74, heart rate 48, respirations irregular
options.rationale: Rising BP with a widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing is the brainstem's late response to high ICP.

options.text: BP 170/96, heart rate 118, temperature 39.2 C
options.rationale: The heart rate is rising, not falling. This is not the Cushing pattern.

options.text: BP 84/48, heart rate 52, skin warm and dry
options.rationale: Hypotension with bradycardia does not fit the Cushing triad. In the triad the BP rises with a widened pulse pressure.

questions.takeaway: Cushing triad: rising BP with a widening pulse pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing. It is a very late sign. Act immediately.
questions.strategy: BP goes up while the heart rate goes down. That opposite movement is the clue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypotension in A and D points to shock, not ICP.
C has a rising heart rate.
B has high BP with a wide pulse pressure, a low heart rate and irregular breathing.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with increased ICP who needs a bath, linen change, suctioning, and repositioning. What is the best plan?

options.text: Do all of the care at once so the patient can rest afterward.
options.rationale: Back-to-back care can spike ICP.

options.text: Space the care out with rest periods between activities.
options.rationale: Clustering raises ICP. Spacing care keeps pressure down.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed flat during care.
options.rationale: HOB up per protocol, often 30 degrees, helps venous drainage.

options.text: Suction every hour to keep the airway clear.
options.rationale: Suction only when needed; suctioning raises ICP.

questions.takeaway: With high ICP you space out care. This is the opposite of the usual rule to cluster care.
questions.strategy: Watch for a usually correct rule that flips for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clustering is usually right, but not with high ICP.
Flat HOB and routine suctioning raise ICP.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes arrives with slurred speech and confusion. Blood glucose is 52 mg/dL. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Prepare the patient for a fibrinolytic.
options.rationale: Symptoms may be from hypoglycemia, not stroke.

options.text: Treat the hypoglycemia per protocol, then reassess the neurologic status.
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia mimics stroke. Correct it and recheck.

options.text: Complete the NIHSS before treating the glucose.
options.rationale: Delays a quick, reversible fix.

options.text: Give a regular meal tray.
options.rationale: Swallowing is not confirmed, and the glucose needs faster treatment.

questions.takeaway: Low glucose looks exactly like a stroke. Check glucose promptly, treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess.
questions.strategy: Fix the reversible cause before starting treatment for the scary diagnosis.

steps.detail: Glucose of 52 explains the symptoms.
A gives a clot buster before the mimic is ruled out.
D ignores swallow safety.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient's spouse says she went to bed feeling fine at 2300 and woke him at 0630 unable to lift her right arm. What is her last known well time?

options.rationale: That is when the symptoms were found.
The last time she was known to be normal.

options.text: The time she arrived in the ED
options.rationale: Arrival time does not start the clock.

options.text: Unknown, so she cannot be treated
options.rationale: LKW is known: 2300.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last moment the patient was known to be normal, not when symptoms were discovered.
questions.strategy: For wake-up strokes, LKW is bedtime.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0630 is discovery; 2300 is last known normal.
Arrival time and 'unknown' are both wrong here.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: During an alteplase infusion, the patient reports a sudden severe headache and vomits. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Give an antiemetic and continue the infusion.
options.rationale: These symptoms suggest bleeding in the brain.

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider immediately.
options.rationale: Severe headache with nausea and vomiting may mean intracranial bleeding.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate by half.
options.rationale: A partial dose still risks worsening a bleed.

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Waiting delays action on a possible bleed.

questions.takeaway: Bleeding is the main danger of a clot buster. Severe headache, acute hypertension, nausea, or vomiting: stop the infusion and call.
questions.strategy: When a drug could be causing harm, stop it first.

steps.action: Link the symptom to the drug
steps.detail: Clot busters cause bleeding; headache and vomiting suggest brain bleed.
A and C keep the drug running; D waits.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient is a candidate for alteplase. The BP is 196/112 mmHg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Start alteplase now because time is brain.
options.rationale: BP must be below 185/110 before the drug.

options.text: Give an antihypertensive such as labetalol as ordered, then start alteplase once BP is below 185/110.
options.rationale: High BP raises bleeding risk with a clot buster.

options.text: Cancel alteplase permanently because the BP is too high.
options.rationale: BP can be lowered first.

options.text: Lower the BP to below 120 systolic quickly.
options.rationale: A sudden large drop reduces brain perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Before a clot buster, BP must be below 185/110. After it, keep BP below 180/105 for 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Look for the option that meets the threshold safely rather than skipping or abandoning treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A ignores the limit; C gives up; D drops BP too far too fast.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with a right hemisphere stroke keeps trying to get out of bed without help and says, "I'm fine, I can walk." What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Teach the patient to use the call light.
options.rationale: The patient is impulsive and unaware of deficits.

options.text: Turn on the bed alarm and provide close supervision.
options.rationale: Right hemisphere damage causes impulsivity, poor judgment, and unawareness of deficits: high fall risk.

options.text: Use a communication board.
options.rationale: Language is usually intact with right hemisphere stroke.

options.text: Apply wrist restraints.
options.rationale: Not the least restrictive option.

questions.takeaway: Right brain stroke: impulsive, poor judgment, unaware of deficits, left neglect. Safety measures must not rely on the patient's judgment.
questions.strategy: Match the hemisphere to its behavior, then choose the least restrictive safety measure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Impulsive, unaware of deficits.

steps.action: Remove options that rely on judgment
steps.detail: A relies on the patient remembering.
Restraints are a last resort.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with a left hemisphere stroke looks at a cup and says, "I want... the... thing... drink," and becomes frustrated. The patient follows commands correctly. How should the nurse describe this?

options.text: Dysarthria
options.rationale: Dysarthria is slurred speech with the right words.

options.text: Expressive aphasia
options.rationale: Understands but cannot get the words out; frustration is common.

options.text: Receptive aphasia
options.rationale: The patient follows commands, so understanding is intact.

options.text: Unilateral neglect
options.rationale: Neglect is ignoring one side.

questions.takeaway: Expressive (Broca) aphasia: understands, struggles to speak, often frustrated. Receptive (Wernicke): fluent speech that makes little sense, poor understanding.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions: does the patient understand, and are the words right?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Follows commands, so not receptive.
Missing words, so not dysarthria.

elimination.verdict: Expressive aphasia is correct.

questions.stem: A patient has left homonymous hemianopsia after a stroke. Which intervention should the nurse include?

options.text: Place the meal tray on the patient's left side.
options.rationale: The left field is lost; the patient won't see it.

options.text: Teach the patient to turn the head side to side to scan the environment.
options.rationale: Scanning makes up for the lost half of the visual field.

options.text: Patch one eye, alternating every 2 to 4 hours.
options.rationale: That treats diplopia.

options.text: Keep the room dark to reduce stimulation.
options.rationale: Does not help field loss and increases fall risk.

questions.takeaway: Homonymous hemianopsia: the same half of the visual field is lost in both eyes. Teach scanning and place items in the intact field.
questions.strategy: Match the intervention to the specific deficit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Left half of the view is gone in both eyes.
A puts food in the blind field.
C is for double vision.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient had 40 minutes of left arm numbness and slurred speech that fully resolved. He says, "It's gone now, so I'll just go home." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "That's fine, since there's no permanent damage."
options.rationale: A TIA is a warning of a coming stroke.

options.text: "A TIA is a warning sign that a stroke may follow, so we need to evaluate the cause now."
options.rationale: TIA needs urgent evaluation and treatment of the cause.

options.text: "Take an aspirin at home and call if it happens again."
options.rationale: Delays evaluation.

options.text: "Your symptoms were probably from anxiety."
options.rationale: Dismisses a neurologic event.

questions.takeaway: A TIA is temporary with no permanent damage, but it is an emergency warning of a coming stroke.
questions.strategy: Resolved symptoms are not a reason to relax.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.detail: Temporary dysfunction, warning of stroke.
A, C, and D all minimize the risk.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient suddenly reports "the worst headache of my life," vomits, has a stiff neck, and is becoming drowsy. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Thrombotic ischemic stroke
options.rationale: Usually gradual, with LOC preserved and no severe headache.

options.text: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
options.rationale: Sudden severe headache, vomiting, stiff neck, and falling LOC are classic for SAH.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack
options.rationale: TIA symptoms resolve and do not include this headache.

options.text: Migraine
options.rationale: Does not explain a stiff neck and falling LOC.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhagic stroke: sudden severe headache, vomiting, declining LOC, sometimes seizures. SAH adds a stiff neck and light sensitivity.
questions.strategy: A sudden severe headache plus declining LOC points to a bleed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Worst headache of my life.
Stiff neck, vomiting, drowsiness.
Ischemic strokes rarely cause this headache.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient received alteplase 2 hours ago. Which findings should the nurse report immediately? Select all that apply.

options.text: New severe headache
options.rationale: May signal bleeding in the brain.

options.text: Blood in the urine
options.rationale: Sign of bleeding.

options.text: Bleeding at the IV site that continues despite pressure
options.rationale: Uncontrolled bleeding. Minor oozing is first managed with direct pressure.

options.text: BP 192/108 mmHg
options.rationale: Above the 180/105 limit after a clot buster.

options.text: Worsening arm weakness
options.rationale: New or worse neuro deficit may signal bleeding.

options.text: BP 164/92 mmHg
options.rationale: Within the post-treatment goal of below 180/105.

questions.takeaway: After a clot buster, bleeding is the major concern. Report headache, neuro decline, BP above 180/105, and any bleeding.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into bleeding, neuro decline, BP above limit, or within goal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Headache, hematuria, IV site bleeding despite pressure, worsening weakness.
192/108 is above; 164/92 is within goal.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are correct.

questions.stem: The nurse is supervising a nursing student who is caring for a 49-year-old patient with increased ICP. The nurse reviewed ways to prevent further rises in ICP. Which action by the student shows the teaching was effective?

options.text: The student flexes the patient's hips sharply while repositioning
options.rationale: Sharp hip flexion raises intra-abdominal and chest pressure. It blocks venous outflow from the skull. The student needs more teaching.

options.text: The student suctions the patient every hour on a schedule
options.rationale: Suctioning raises ICP. Suction only when needed, with oxygen before and after.

options.text: The student keeps the patient's head midline and neutral with the head of the bed elevated
options.rationale: A midline head keeps the neck veins open so venous blood can drain from the skull. Elevating the head of the bed per protocol also helps drainage.

options.text: The student lowers the head of the bed flat so the patient can rest
options.rationale: A flat bed slows venous drainage. The head of the bed is elevated per protocol, often 30 degrees.

questions.takeaway: Keep venous drainage open and avoid pressure spikes. Elevate the head of the bed, keep the head midline, avoid sharp flexion and straining, space out care and keep the room calm.
questions.strategy: For each action, ask whether it helps blood drain out of the skull or raises pressure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sharp hip flexion and scheduled suctioning raise ICP.
A flat bed slows venous outflow.
A midline head with the bed elevated keeps the neck veins open.

elimination.verdict: C shows the teaching was effective.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for two patients admitted with stroke. Patient 1, age 72, had a left hemisphere stroke. Patient 2, age 65, had a right hemisphere stroke. For each finding the nurse notes, indicate which patient it most likely belongs to.

rows.text: Cannot find the word for "cup" and becomes frustrated
rows.rationale: Aphasia is a language problem. Language lives in the left hemisphere.

rows.text: Eats only the food on the right side of the tray
rows.rationale: Ignoring the left side is left neglect, which follows right hemisphere damage.

rows.text: Moves slowly and asks for help before each step
rows.rationale: Patients with left hemisphere strokes tend to be slow and cautious.

rows.text: Tries to climb out of bed alone and says, "Nothing is wrong with me"
rows.rationale: Right hemisphere damage impairs judgment and awareness of deficits. This causes impulsive behavior.

rows.text: Right hand grip is weak
rows.rationale: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body.

rows.text: Cannot add up the cost of a meal or read the menu
rows.rationale: Reading, writing and math are left hemisphere functions.

questions.takeaway: Left brain damage causes language and logic problems, right-sided weakness and cautious behavior. Right brain damage causes spatial and judgment problems, left neglect and impulsive behavior.
questions.strategy: Remember that motor and sensory findings appear on the side opposite the damaged hemisphere.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Word finding, reading and math point to the left hemisphere.
Neglect and impulsivity point to the right hemisphere.
Weakness appears opposite the damaged hemisphere.

elimination.verdict: Left: rows 1, 3, 5 and 6. Right: rows 2 and 4.

questions.stem: A patient is 36 hours after a large ischemic stroke. At 0800 she was alert and oriented. At 1000 she is restless and confused, reports a worsening headache, and has vomited once. BP 168/88, HR 84, SpO2 93%. Which condition is the patient most likely experiencing?

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Possible, but it would not explain a worsening headache. Check glucose, but it is not the most likely picture.

options.text: Increased intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Declining LOC, headache, and vomiting in the first 72 hours after stroke point to rising ICP.

options.text: Transient ischemic attack
options.rationale: TIA symptoms resolve. She has had a completed stroke and is getting worse.

options.text: Expected post-stroke fatigue
options.rationale: New confusion is never expected fatigue.

questions.takeaway: Risk of increased ICP is highest in the first 72 hours after a stroke. Earliest sign is a drop in LOC. Prevent hypoxia and keep venous drainage open.
questions.strategy: Put the cues together with the timing. One option explains all three findings in the highest-risk window.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New confusion is never expected fatigue.

steps.action: Reject what does not fit the timeline
steps.detail: A TIA resolves. This patient is getting worse after a completed stroke.
Hypoglycemia can confuse but does not explain a worsening headache with vomiting.
LOC decline, headache and vomiting 36 hours after stroke mean rising ICP.

elimination.verdict: B. Increased intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews four patients with stroke symptoms. Which patient meets the criteria to start fibrinolytic therapy now?

options.text: Noncontrast CT shows an intracerebral hemorrhage. Last known well was 1 hour ago. BP is 170/95.
options.rationale: A clot buster in a bleeding brain makes the bleed worse. It is given only for ischemic stroke.

options.text: Noncontrast CT shows no bleeding. Last known well was 3 hours ago. BP is 176/98.
options.rationale: Ischemic stroke with bleeding ruled out by CT, inside the 4.5 hour window from last known well, with BP below 185/110.

options.text: Noncontrast CT shows no bleeding. Last known well was 3 hours ago. BP is 192/114.
options.rationale: The BP must be below 185/110 before the drug starts. Antihypertensives come first, then the drug if the BP comes down.

options.text: Noncontrast CT shows no bleeding. She woke with symptoms after going to bed normal 9 hours ago. BP is 160/90.
options.rationale: Last known well is bedtime, not when the symptoms were found. That is far outside the standard 4.5 hour window. Later treatment needs advanced imaging.

questions.takeaway: Clot buster: ischemic only, CT first, within 4.5 hours of LKW, BP below 185/110.
questions.strategy: Every criterion protects against bleeding. Check each patient against all of them. Two options fail on a single number.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Never hemorrhagic. Cut A.
LKW is the last normal moment. Bedtime 9 hours ago is outside 4.5 hours. Cut D.
192/114 is above 185/110. Cut C until it is lowered.

elimination.verdict: B.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old with atrial fibrillation was found by her husband at 0900 with right arm weakness and garbled words. She went to bed normal at 2230. Blood glucose is 58 mg/dL. She asks repeatedly for a drink of water. Her husband is at the bedside. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Treat the low blood glucose per protocol, then reassess her neurologic status
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and must be treated first. It can cause weakness and slurred speech that look exactly like a stroke.

options.text: Give small sips of water because she is alert and thirsty
options.rationale: Nothing by mouth until a swallow screen. New one-sided weakness with a speech change means aspiration risk. Thirsty does not mean give water.

options.text: Report 0900 to the stroke team as the time of onset
options.rationale: 0900 is when she was found. Her last known well is 2230, the time she went to bed normal. That decides whether a clot buster or clot removal is possible.

options.text: Obtain a complete history of her medications and past illnesses before she goes to CT
options.rationale: Asking about anticoagulants matters because of the atrial fibrillation, but a full history must not delay care. The reversible mimic comes first.

questions.takeaway: Stroke: treat mimics like low glucose, keep NPO until a swallow screen and time the stroke from last known well (2230 here).
questions.strategy: Before you treat this as a stroke, fix what could be causing the symptoms. A glucose of 58 is reversible in minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Water before a swallow screen risks aspiration.
Onset is timed from last known well at 2230, not from 0900.
Treat the glucose before a full history.

elimination.verdict: A. Correct the mimic first, then reassess.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a family about stroke warning signs using BE FAST. Which statement by a family member requires further teaching?

options.text: "If one side of his face droops, I'll call 911."
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: "If his symptoms go away, we can wait until morning to see the doctor."
options.rationale: Incorrect. Symptoms that go away may be a TIA, still an emergency.

options.text: "I should note the time he was last normal."
options.rationale: Correct. T is time.

options.text: "Sudden trouble with balance or vision is a warning sign."
options.rationale: Correct. B and E.

questions.takeaway: BE FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time. Symptoms that go away still need emergency care.
questions.strategy: Find the one statement that delays care.

steps.detail: Face, time, balance, eyes are all correct.
Waiting until morning after resolved symptoms.

elimination.verdict: B requires further teaching.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is 48 hours after a large right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke. HOB is at 30 degrees. At 0800 she was alert, oriented to person and place and following commands. BP 146/84, HR 88, RR 18 and regular. At 1000 she reports her headache is "getting worse" and is oriented to person only. At 1200: BP 178/70, HR 60, temperature 37.2 C, right pupil 5 mm and sluggish, left pupil 3 mm and brisk. Which interpretation of the 1200 findings is correct?

options.text: The heart rate of 60 is within the normal range and needs no follow-up
options.rationale: 60 is inside the normal range. It fell from 88 while BP rose. That pairing points to brainstem pressure, so it needs follow-up.

options.text: The pupil changes are expected after a right hemisphere stroke
options.rationale: A pupil that is larger and slower on one side means pressure on the third cranial nerve. Herniation may be starting. It is not an expected finding.

options.text: The temperature of 37.2 C is a fever that is worsening her brain injury
options.rationale: Normal. Fever would worsen brain injury. This value is not a fever.

options.text: The widening pulse pressure with a falling heart rate suggests the Cushing triad is forming
options.rationale: The systolic rose while the diastolic fell. Her pulse pressure widened from 62 to 108. HR fell from 88 to 60. That pattern is part of the Cushing triad.

questions.takeaway: ICP shows up first as a change in LOC and a worse headache. Late signs are a widening pulse pressure, a falling heart rate and an unequal pupil. A heart rate of 60 can still be a warning when it was 88 two hours ago.
questions.strategy: Read every value against her 0800 baseline, not against the normal range. The HR of 60 is the trap. It is normal on its own and alarming as a trend.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0800 is her normal. Every later value is compared to it.
Pulse pressure went from 62 to 108 and HR went from 88 to 60.
A normal HR that is falling while BP rises is not reassuring.
A unilateral dilated sluggish pupil is never expected. 37.2 C is not a fever.

elimination.verdict: D, the Cushing triad forming.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old received alteplase for an acute ischemic stroke. The infusion ended at 1230. It is now 1500. Her NIHSS was 9 on arrival and is 6 now. BP trend: 1400 was 172/98, 1430 was 178/100, 1500 is 184/102. HR 84. SpO2 97% on room air. She failed her bedside swallow screen at 1100. Her home medications include daily aspirin. Which action is the nurse's priority at 1500?

options.text: Notify the provider about the blood pressure of 184/102
options.rationale: The limit after the drug is 180/105. The systolic is above 180, so it crosses the line even though the diastolic does not. High pressure after a clot buster raises the risk of a brain bleed.

options.text: Continue neuro checks and vital signs every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Correct schedule. The infusion ended 2.5 hours ago, so she is in the 30-minute window. Continuing routine checks does not act on a value that already crossed the limit.

options.text: Hold her home aspirin until a follow-up CT shows no bleeding
options.rationale: Correct. No aspirin or anticoagulants for 24 hours and until a follow-up CT shows no bleeding. Holding a drug prevents a future risk. The pressure is a risk now.

options.text: Request a nasogastric tube so her oral medications can be given
options.rationale: NG tubes are held until she is stable. Passing a tube through the nose can cause bleeding that is hard to stop. She stays NPO for now.

questions.takeaway: For 24 hours after a clot buster, you watch for bleeding and avoid anything that can start one. That means no tubes, no catheters and no antiplatelets. It also means a call when BP rises above 180/105.
questions.strategy: The BP rose slowly across three readings. Each reading looks close to the last one. Compare the newest value to the 180/105 limit, not to the reading before it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is 2.5 hours past a clot buster. Bleeding is the main risk.
An NG tube waits until she is stable.

steps.action: Check the numbers against the limits
steps.detail: 184 is above 180 systolic. Routine checks and holding aspirin do not answer that.

elimination.verdict: A. Call about the BP above 180 systolic.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old arrives in the ED 70 minutes after her daughter watched her develop sudden left facial droop and left arm weakness. She is drowsy, with slurred speech. BP 198/108, HR 92, RR 20, SpO2 95%. She takes metformin for type 2 diabetes. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should occur.

options.text: Assess airway, breathing and circulation
options.rationale: First. Stroke can weaken the muscles that protect the airway. Nothing else matters if she cannot breathe or protect her airway.

options.text: Check a fingerstick blood glucose
options.rationale: Second. Low glucose causes weakness and slurred speech that look exactly like a stroke. It takes seconds and it changes the whole plan if it is low.

options.text: Transport for a noncontrast CT of the head
options.rationale: Third. The CT rules out bleeding. No one can decide on a clot buster until it does.

options.text: Give IV labetalol as prescribed to lower BP below 185/110
options.rationale: Fourth. Her BP is lowered only because she is now a clot buster candidate. Without that decision, the BP would be allowed to run high to keep the brain perfused.

options.text: Give the alteplase bolus over 1 minute and start the infusion on a pump
options.rationale: Last. The drug is safe only after bleeding is ruled out and the BP is below the limit.

questions.takeaway: ABCs, rule out the mimic, rule out the bleed, get the BP under the line, then give the clot buster. Each step makes the next one safe.
questions.strategy: The high BP pulls you toward lowering it first. You lower it only after the CT shows she is a clot buster candidate. Before that, a high BP helps keep the brain perfused.

steps.detail: She is drowsy, so airway protection is the first question.
She has diabetes. Hypoglycemia can look exactly like this stroke.
The CT decides whether a clot buster is possible.
The BP is lowered to below 185/110 only to make the drug safe. The drug goes last.

elimination.verdict: Airway, glucose, CT, labetalol, alteplase.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with atrial fibrillation is on day 3 after an embolic ischemic stroke. She was not a clot buster candidate. A continuous heparin infusion was started yesterday. Her NIHSS has been 4 and stable for two days. At 1400 she reports a sudden severe headache and vomits. She is now difficult to arouse. NIHSS is 11. BP 188/96, HR 74. Most recent aPTT was above the target range. Blood glucose 142 mg/dL. She has not had a bowel movement in 3 days. Which interpretation and response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: A new embolic stroke from atrial fibrillation; give the scheduled aspirin to prevent another embolus
options.rationale: A defensible guess, since she has atrial fibrillation. Embolic strokes usually do not cause a severe headache with vomiting. She is also anticoagulated. An antiplatelet adds to the bleeding risk. Her embolic risk is real and it is not what is happening now.

options.text: Hemorrhagic transformation of the ischemic stroke; stop the heparin infusion, notify the provider or rapid response team immediately and prepare her for an emergency noncontrast CT of the head
options.rationale: The vessel walls in the stroke area are weak. On heparin with a high aPTT, a sudden headache, vomiting and a falling LOC after days of stability point to bleeding into the infarct. Heparin with a high aPTT keeps a bleed going, so stopping it and calling for help are done together, right now. Only imaging shows whether this is a bleed. The treatment plan depends on it.

options.text: Rising intracranial pressure from straining; give the prescribed stool softener and encourage fluids
options.rationale: Nothing in the data shows she strained. Having no bowel movement in 3 days does not explain a sudden severe headache, vomiting and an NIHSS jump from 4 to 11 while she is on heparin with a high aPTT. Preventing straining is a good ICP measure. It is the right action at the wrong time, and it does nothing for an active bleed.

options.text: A transient ischemic attack; keep the heparin running and wait for the CT result before positioning her
options.rationale: A TIA resolves. Her deficits are getting worse and her LOC is falling. Heparin with a high aPTT keeps a bleed going, so it must be stopped, not continued. Positioning for airway protection is immediate. It never waits for imaging.

questions.takeaway: An ischemic stroke can turn into a bleed. A sudden headache or decline after days of stability is not just the stroke. Stop the anticoagulant, call for help and get a CT. Then follow her LOC with the NIHSS along with her BP, pulse pressure and heart rate trend.
questions.strategy: Atrial fibrillation makes a new embolic stroke tempting. The tie breaker is the pattern. Severe headache, vomiting and falling LOC in a patient on heparin with a high aPTT point to bleeding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She was stable for two days. The sudden headache and vomiting are new.
She is on heparin and her aPTT is above target.

steps.action: Test both halves of each option
steps.detail: A adds an antiplatelet to a bleed. C is a true ICP measure at the wrong time. D names a problem that resolves and delays airway positioning.

steps.action: Pick the option that stops the bleed and confirms it
steps.detail: Stop the heparin, call for help and prepare for CT.

elimination.verdict: Hemorrhagic transformation; stop heparin, notify and prepare for CT.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old arrives 14 hours after his last known well with left arm weakness and slurred speech. The CT shows no hemorrhage. The stroke team determines he is not a candidate for a clot buster or clot removal. He is admitted for an acute ischemic stroke. At 1600 his blood pressure is 198/104, heart rate 82, SpO2 96%. It was 204/108 at 1200. His NIHSS is unchanged from admission. A PRN antihypertensive is available. A new graduate nurse says, "His pressure is way too high. I'll give the PRN to get him under 140." Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Give it now. The goal after any stroke is a systolic pressure below 140."
options.rationale: A rapid drop starves the tissue that is still alive around the stroke. That tissue depends on pressure for flow. A target of 140 is not the early goal for an untreated ischemic stroke.

options.text: "Hold the PRN. Without a clot buster, his pressure is allowed to run high to keep the brain perfused. We report if it passes the protocol limit or his neuro checks worsen."
options.rationale: Permissive hypertension. Without a clot buster the pressure may run up to about 220 systolic. Any lowering is gradual. His pressure is trending down on its own and his neuro status is stable.

options.text: "Give it only enough to get him below 185/110."
options.rationale: 185/110 is the ceiling before a clot buster can be given. He is not receiving one, so that threshold does not apply.

options.text: "Call the provider now because the pressure is above 180/105."
options.rationale: 180/105 is the limit for 24 hours after a clot buster. He did not get one. Applying the wrong threshold leads to unnecessary lowering.

questions.takeaway: Blood pressure targets in stroke depend on treatment. Below 185/110 before a clot buster, below 180/105 after one. Allow up to about 220 systolic when none was given.
questions.strategy: Three of the options quote real stroke numbers. Ask which number belongs to this patient's treatment path.

steps.detail: Ischemic, imaging done, no clot buster given.
The pre-treatment and post-treatment numbers do not apply to him.
His pressure is falling on its own and his neuro checks are stable.

elimination.verdict: Hold the PRN and allow permissive hypertension with close monitoring.

questions.scenario: A nurse in the emergency department receives report on six patients with stroke symptoms. Imaging is pending for each.
questions.stem: For each patient finding, indicate the type of stroke it most suggests.

rows.text: Weakness worsened in steps over several hours; she had two brief episodes of arm numbness last month; she stayed awake and alert
rows.rationale: Gradual, stepwise onset with preserved LOC and prior TIAs fits a clot growing on plaque.

rows.text: Atrial fibrillation; sudden right-sided weakness that was at its worst the moment it began
rows.rationale: A clot from the heart travels and lodges suddenly. The deficit is maximal at onset.

rows.text: Sudden severe headache with vomiting followed by deepening lethargy
rows.rationale: Bleeding raises ICP quickly. Headache, vomiting and falling LOC are the hemorrhage pattern.

rows.text: A seizure at the onset of symptoms
rows.rationale: Blood irritates the cortex. Seizures are usual with hemorrhage and not with thrombotic or embolic stroke.

rows.text: Long history of atherosclerosis and high cholesterol; awoke with weakness and is fully alert
rows.rationale: Atherosclerosis builds the plaque where thrombi form. Deficits are often noticed on waking, and LOC is preserved.

rows.text: Recent cocaine use followed by sudden loss of consciousness
rows.rationale: Cocaine causes sudden severe hypertension that can rupture a vessel.

questions.takeaway: Onset and LOC separate the types. Stepwise with alert LOC is thrombotic. Sudden and maximal is embolic. Headache, vomiting, seizures and falling LOC are hemorrhagic. The CT still decides.
questions.strategy: For each row ask two questions. How fast did it start? Is the patient still awake?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stepwise points to thrombotic. Sudden and maximal points to embolic or hemorrhagic.
A falling LOC with headache or seizure points to hemorrhage.
Atrial fibrillation suggests embolic. Atherosclerosis suggests thrombotic. Cocaine suggests hemorrhage.

elimination.verdict: Thrombotic, embolic, hemorrhagic, hemorrhagic, thrombotic, hemorrhagic.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old patient with increased ICP after a stroke was restless with a GCS of 12. The nurse elevated the head of the bed to 30 degrees, positioned the head midline, applied oxygen for an SpO2 of 91% and spaced out care. Which finding 2 hours later shows the interventions were effective?

options.text: GCS 14, the patient rests quietly and pupils are equal and brisk
options.rationale: A rising GCS, less restlessness and unchanged pupils show LOC is improving. Declining LOC is the earliest sign of rising ICP, so improving LOC is the best sign that pressure is coming down.

options.text: BP 184/70, heart rate 50 and irregular respirations
options.rationale: This is the Cushing triad, a very late sign of rising ICP. The nurse must act immediately.

options.text: GCS 12 with a new report of severe headache and projectile vomiting
options.rationale: Headache and vomiting are signs of increased ICP. The patient is not improving.

options.text: SpO2 97% and the right pupil is now 5 mm and sluggish
options.rationale: Oxygenation improved, but a new unequal, sluggish pupil shows neurologic decline that needs immediate follow up.

questions.takeaway: The best measure of whether ICP interventions worked is LOC, trended with the GCS. Improved oxygenation alone does not prove success if other neuro findings worsen.
questions.strategy: Pick the option where every finding improved. Reject any option that has one new sign of rising ICP.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: B is the Cushing triad.
C has headache and vomiting with no GCS change.
D has better SpO2 but a new pupil change, which is a decline.
A shows a higher GCS, calm behavior and stable pupils.

elimination.verdict: A shows the interventions were effective.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old patient is going home after a TIA. The nurse teaches the patient's wife how to recognize a stroke. Which statement by the wife shows the teaching was understood?

options.text: "His symptoms went away last time, so if they come back I'll wait an hour to see if they pass."
options.rationale: A TIA is a warning of a coming stroke, not a false alarm. Waiting wastes treatment time.

options.text: "If his face droops, his arm gets weak or his speech changes suddenly, I will call 911 and note the time he was last normal."
options.rationale: The wife uses BE FAST correctly. She knows to call 911 and to record the last known well time, which starts the treatment clock.

options.text: "If he has trouble speaking at night, I'll drive him to his doctor's office in the morning."
options.rationale: Stroke symptoms are an emergency. Waiting until morning can make him ineligible for a clot buster.

options.text: "If he gets weak, I'll write down the time I found him and give him some water to drink."
options.rationale: The time found is not the last known well. Nothing should be given by mouth until a swallow screen is done.

questions.takeaway: Stroke signs are sudden: balance, eyes, face, arm and speech changes. Time means call 911 and record when the patient was last known well. A TIA is a warning, not a false alarm.
questions.strategy: Look for the statement that treats sudden symptoms as an emergency and uses the correct time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and C both wait instead of calling 911.
D records when the symptoms were found, not the last known well time.
D also gives water before a swallow screen.

elimination.verdict: B shows the teaching was understood.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old admitted with a GI bleed has a hemoglobin of 7.1 g/dL, down from 11.8 g/dL on admission. SpO2 is 99% on room air. Heart rate 118, respirations 24, blood pressure 102/64. She is pale, her capillary refill is 4 seconds. She feels dizzy when she sits up. A student says, "Her oxygen is fine because her saturation is 99%." Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: "The saturation is falsely high because pale skin interferes with the sensor."
options.rationale: Pallor is not on the list of pulse oximetry errors. Poor circulation, movement, cold fingers, nail polish and placement are. Blaming the device dismisses a real problem.

options.text: "Her hemoglobin is nearly full of oxygen, but she has too little hemoglobin to carry enough oxygen to her tissues."
options.rationale: Saturation is a percentage of the hemoglobin she has. With a hemoglobin of 7.1 each cell is full, yet the total oxygen delivered is low. Her fast heart rate and dizziness are the tissues asking for more. This is decreased oxygen carrying capacity.

options.text: "Her rapid breathing shows the problem is ventilation, so we should coach her to take slow deep breaths."
options.rationale: Her airway and ventilation are working. Her fast breathing is compensation for poor oxygen delivery. Slowing it would take away that compensation.

options.text: "A nonrebreather mask will correct the problem by raising the oxygen in her blood."
options.rationale: Her blood oxygen is already normal. Oxygen therapy treats hypoxemia. It does not fix hypoxia caused by missing hemoglobin. She needs the cause treated.

questions.takeaway: An open airway and a normal SpO2 do not guarantee oxygenation. Ventilation, diffusion and perfusion all need enough hemoglobin to deliver oxygen to the tissues.
questions.strategy: Anchor on the hemoglobin trend first. Once you see it falling, the 99% becomes a percentage of too little.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hemoglobin fell from 11.8 to 7.1 g/dL. That is lost carrying capacity.
Tachycardia, dizziness and slow capillary refill say tissues are short on oxygen.
Pallor does not fool the sensor. Her ventilation works. Oxygen does not replace hemoglobin.

elimination.verdict: Too little hemoglobin to carry enough oxygen, even at 99%.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with pneumonia has a prescription for oxygen by simple face mask at 6 L/min. On rounds the nurse finds the flowmeter set at 3 L/min. The patient says the mask feels stuffy and hot. SpO2 is 93%, respirations 24, heart rate 96. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Switch to a nasal cannula at 3 L/min so the patient is more comfortable
options.rationale: Changing the device and the dose is outside the prescription. Comfort matters. Ask the provider before changing the device.

options.text: Leave the flow at 3 L/min because the SpO2 is above 90%
options.rationale: A saturation that looks acceptable does not make an unsafe setting safe. At 3 L/min the mask keeps collecting exhaled air.

options.text: Obtain an arterial blood gas to check for carbon dioxide retention
options.rationale: Getting a gas is not a nursing decision here and it delays the fix. Correct the setting first, then reassess.

options.text: Increase the flow to the prescribed 6 L/min and reassess the patient
options.rationale: A simple mask needs at least the minimum prescribed flow to flush exhaled CO2 out of the mask. At low flow the patient rebreathes CO2, which also explains the stuffy feeling. Correcting the flow matches the order and fixes the hazard.

questions.takeaway: A simple mask run below its minimum flow becomes a CO2 trap. Use the ordered device at the ordered setting, then watch the response.
questions.strategy: Two options sound kind or reassuring. Neither follows the order. The stuffy feeling is a clue to rebreathing, not a reason to lower the dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Compare the setting with the order
steps.detail: 3 L/min is below the prescribed 6 L/min.
A simple mask at low flow means rebreathing exhaled CO2.

steps.action: Pick the action in scope that fixes it
steps.detail: Set the ordered flow, then reassess.

elimination.verdict: Increase to the prescribed 6 L/min and reassess.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old comes to the clinic for an annual visit. She smoked 1.5 packs a day for 30 years and quit 8 years ago. She worked 20 years in a shipyard before retiring. She says, "I've coughed up a little white phlegm every morning for years. That's just my smoker's cough." She also says she now sits on a stool halfway through her shower to catch her breath. Last year she did not need to. Which finding does the nurse explore further first?

options.text: Her 45 pack-year smoking history
options.rationale: 1.5 packs a day for 30 years is 45 pack-years. It is an important risk factor to document. It describes her risk. It does not tell you her lungs changed this year.

options.text: Her morning cough with a small amount of white sputum
options.rationale: Abnormal and long-standing. Nothing about it has changed, so it is her baseline.

options.text: Needing to rest halfway through her shower
options.rationale: A new loss of activity tolerance in a daily task tells you the disease is progressing now. Ask when it started, what else she has stopped doing and how far she can walk.

options.text: Her past employment in a shipyard
options.rationale: Past work matters because lung damage can show up decades later. It is a risk factor, like the pack-years. It is not a change in her status.

questions.takeaway: In a respiratory history, a new change in sleep or daily activities is the finding that tells you the patient is getting worse.
questions.strategy: Three options are risk factors or baseline. Only one is new. When two answers feel important, ask which one is changing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Risk factor, baseline or new change.
Pack-years and shipyard work are both history.
The cough has been the same for years.

elimination.verdict: The new need to rest in the shower.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 70-year-old with COPD whose SpO2 is 91% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, unchanged all shift, who is speaking in full sentences
options.rationale: Abnormal numbers and stable. He is at his baseline and talking comfortably.

options.text: A 45-year-old on postoperative day 1 with rhonchi over the large airways that clear after coughing
options.rationale: Secretions that respond to coughing. Encourage coughing and deep breathing. This can wait a few minutes.

options.text: A 58-year-old who started an IV antibiotic 20 minutes ago and now has a hoarse voice and a high-pitched sound on inspiration heard without a stethoscope
options.rationale: Hoarseness plus a harsh inspiratory sound is stridor. It means the upper airway is narrowing, here most likely from an allergic reaction. This airway can close within minutes.

options.text: An 80-year-old with pneumonia who has a temperature of 38.3 C and rust-colored sputum, with SpO2 of 93% on 2 L/min
options.rationale: Expected findings for his diagnosis. His oxygenation is acceptable. He needs care soon, after the airway threat.

questions.takeaway: Stridor is an upper airway emergency. Airway problems outrank abnormal but stable breathing and expected infection findings.
questions.strategy: Each patient has something abnormal. The tie breaker is expected versus unexpected, then stable versus unstable. Only one finding is new and threatens the airway.

steps.detail: Stable baseline, expected secretions, new airway sound, expected infection.
Stridor is a narrowing upper airway.
It started 20 minutes after a new drug, so it may be getting worse.

elimination.verdict: The patient with new stridor after the antibiotic.

questions.nursesNote: 1000: 55-year-old, postoperative day 2 after abdominal surgery. Respirations 28, using neck muscles on inspiration. Speaks in 3 to 4 word phrases. Trachea midline. Bronchial breath sounds heard over the trachea. Vesicular breath sounds in the left base. Crackles in the right lower lobe that do not clear with coughing, new since 0800. Right side of the chest rises less than the left. Incision pain 3 out of 10 with coughing, relieved by splinting with a pillow. Skin warm and pink.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

segments.text: Respirations 28, using neck muscles on inspiration
segments.rationale: A fast rate with accessory muscle use means her work of breathing is high. She is tiring.

segments.text: Speaks in 3 to 4 word phrases
segments.rationale: Ability to speak is part of the immediate assessment. Short phrases mean she does not have the breath for a full sentence.

segments.text: Trachea midline
segments.rationale: Normal. A shifted trachea would be the emergency.

segments.text: Bronchial breath sounds heard over the trachea
segments.rationale: Loud, high sounds are expected over the trachea. They sound harsh. That is where they belong.

segments.text: Vesicular breath sounds in the left base
segments.rationale: Soft, low sounds at the bases are normal.

segments.text: Crackles in the right lower lobe that do not clear with coughing, new since 0800
segments.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways. They are new and do not clear, which after surgery points toward pneumonia or fluid.

segments.text: Right side of the chest rises less than the left
segments.rationale: Unequal expansion means the right lung is not filling well. It fits with the crackles on the same side.

segments.text: Incision pain 3 out of 10 with coughing, relieved by splinting with a pillow
segments.rationale: Expected after abdominal surgery and controlled. Splinting is the right technique.

segments.text: Skin warm and pink
segments.rationale: Normal color. Cyanosis is a late sign, so pink skin does not rule out a problem. The finding itself needs no follow-up.

questions.takeaway: Work of breathing, speech, new adventitious sounds and asymmetry need follow-up. Bronchial sounds over the trachea and vesicular sounds at the bases are normal.
questions.strategy: The note mixes in normal findings that sound alarming. Bronchial sounds over the trachea are the classic over-highlight. Know your normals.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rate, accessory muscles and phrase length are all abnormal.

steps.action: Match each sound to its location
steps.detail: Bronchial over the trachea and vesicular at the bases are expected.
New right crackles with less right expansion.

elimination.verdict: Rate with neck muscles, short phrases, new right crackles and unequal expansion.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old in an assisted living facility with a current influenza outbreak developed a severe headache, muscle aches, fatigue and loss of appetite about 20 hours ago. Temperature is 37.6 C. Heart rate 98, respirations 20, SpO2 95% on room air. She received her influenza vaccine two months ago. Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Wait to report until her temperature reaches 38.3 C, since influenza usually causes a high fever
options.rationale: Older adults often do not mount a high fever. Waiting for one uses up the window when an antiviral helps.

options.text: Notify the provider now about the symptoms and their onset time so an antiviral can be considered
options.rationale: Rapid onset of headache, muscle aches, fatigue and anorexia during an outbreak is influenza until proven otherwise. Antivirals may help if started within 24 to 48 hours of symptoms. She is at hour 20, so the clock matters.

options.text: Explain that her recent vaccine means this cannot be influenza
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents influenza or reduces its severity. It does not make infection impossible.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and reassess in 4 hours because her vital signs are stable
options.rationale: Comfort care is reasonable. Delaying the report still costs antiviral time. Stable vital signs do not change that.

questions.takeaway: For influenza, the onset time is a clinical fact you report. Antivirals work best within 24 to 48 hours. Older adults may never spike a high fever.
questions.strategy: The low temperature and the recent vaccine are both there to talk you out of reporting. Neither rules out influenza.

steps.detail: Rapid onset of classic flu symptoms during an outbreak.
20 hours into a 24 to 48 hour window.
Low fever and vaccination do not rule it out.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider now so an antiviral can be considered.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old admitted with pneumonia smokes one pack a day. The nurse has asked about his tobacco use and advised him clearly to quit. He says, "I know I should. I'm just not ready right now with everything going on at work." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Let's set your quit date for the day you go home. I'll ask about starting a nicotine patch today."
options.rationale: This jumps to Assist before Assess. He just told you he is not willing. A plan he did not agree to rarely works.

options.text: "Smoking is the reason you are in the hospital. Next time it could be much worse."
options.rationale: A fear message that ignores what he said. It tends to make people defensive, not ready.

options.text: "It sounds like this isn't the right time. I can leave you some information. I'd also like to hear whether cutting back feels possible."
options.rationale: Assess found he is not ready. For a patient who is not ready, you give information, listen for any interest in cutting back, then Arrange follow-up. This keeps the door open.

options.text: "That's your decision. I'll document that you declined counseling."
options.rationale: Respects his choice, then ends the conversation. It skips Arrange, so no one follows up.

questions.takeaway: The 5 As are Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist and Arrange. Assess readiness before you assist. If the patient is not ready, give information, listen and plan follow-up.
questions.strategy: Setting a quit date sounds like the most helpful answer. It is the right action at the wrong time.

strategies: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings

steps.action: Find the step you are on
steps.detail: Ask and Advise are done. He has answered Assess: not ready.

steps.action: Remove the pushy and the closed options
steps.detail: A quit date ignores his answer. Documenting a refusal ends the process.
It denies his feelings and does not build readiness.

elimination.verdict: Acknowledge, give information and explore cutting back.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old had a right thoracentesis 1 hour ago. 900 mL of fluid was removed. Heart rate was 88 before the procedure, 104 at 30 minutes and 122 now. Respirations went from 18 to 30 and shallow. He suddenly reports sharp right-sided chest pain and says he cannot get enough air. Breath sounds are diminished on the right. The dressing has a small spot of serous drainage. The site is sore. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Stay with him, raise the head of the bed, apply oxygen per protocol and call the provider or rapid response
options.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, rapid shallow breathing, rising heart rate and diminished breath sounds on the procedure side point to pneumothorax. Support breathing now and get help now.

options.text: Reinforce the dressing and assess the puncture site for bleeding
options.rationale: A small serous spot and a sore site are expected. The site is not what is failing.

options.text: Encourage him to cough and take deep breaths to help the lung expand
options.rationale: Useful in routine recovery. It does not address a collapsing lung and can worsen his distress.

options.text: Give the prescribed PRN analgesic for pleuritic pain and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Treats the pain and waits 30 minutes while the likely cause gets worse.

questions.takeaway: After a thoracentesis or lung biopsy, sudden dyspnea with rising heart rate and absent or diminished breath sounds on that side means pneumothorax. Stay, support breathing and escalate.
questions.strategy: The dressing and the pain are real findings placed there to pull you toward the site. Look at the trend in heart rate and breathing first.

steps.detail: Heart rate 88 to 104 to 122 and respirations 18 to 30.
Sudden one-sided pain, air hunger and diminished sounds on the right.
Oxygen, upright position and help come before the dressing or pain relief.

elimination.verdict: Stay, sit him up, apply oxygen and call for help.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old is on day 2 after a hip repair. Her SpO2 was 96% at 0800, 94% at 1400 and 92% at 2000 on room air. Respirations rose from 16 to 22. At 2100 she is restless and keeps trying to get out of bed. Her daughter says, "Mom always gets a little mixed up at night. It's just her age." Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Dim the lights, reorient her and let her daughter stay at the bedside
options.rationale: Helpful for night-time confusion. It assumes the cause before checking her breathing.

options.text: Perform a full respiratory assessment and report the falling SpO2 with the new restlessness
options.rationale: Older adults have a blunted response to low oxygen. Restlessness or confusion may be the first sign you see. Her SpO2 is still above 90%, yet it has fallen all day while her rate climbed. The trend plus the behavior change needs assessment and a report.

options.text: Apply a bed alarm and recheck the SpO2 in 4 hours because it is still above 90%
options.rationale: A bed alarm addresses falls, not the cause. Waiting 4 hours ignores a steady decline.

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative so she can rest safely overnight
options.rationale: Sedating a patient who may be hypoxic can depress breathing further and hide the warning sign.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult, new restlessness or confusion may be hypoxia. A value that is still normal but falling steadily needs action.
questions.strategy: The daughter's explanation is the trap. Any change from baseline is assessed first. It is never assumed to be aging.

steps.detail: SpO2 96 to 94 to 92 and respirations 16 to 22 over 12 hours.
New restlessness in a patient with a blunted hypoxia response.
Reorienting, alarms and sedation all skip the cause.

elimination.verdict: Assess her breathing and report the trend with the restlessness.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old with peripheral vascular disease is in a cool procedure room. The pulse oximeter on her finger reads 84% with an irregular, flat waveform. She is alert and speaking in full sentences. Respirations are 16 and unlabored. Her lips and oral mucosa are pink. Her hands are cold. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
options.rationale: This treats the number without checking the patient. Nothing about her breathing or color suggests an SpO2 of 84%.

options.text: Call the rapid response team
options.rationale: Escalation is for a patient who looks unstable. This patient looks well, so verify first.

options.text: Assess her breathing and color, then warm her hand or move the sensor to an earlobe and recheck
options.rationale: Poor circulation and cold extremities both cause inaccurate readings. The flat waveform confirms a poor signal. Correlate the reading with the patient before you act on it.

options.text: Document the reading as artifact and continue routine monitoring
options.rationale: You cannot call a reading artifact until you have a good signal. Documenting it without rechecking could miss real hypoxemia.

questions.takeaway: Pulse oximetry is accurate only with a good signal. Correlate every reading with the patient. Fix the causes of error before you treat or dismiss the number.
questions.strategy: The two extreme options are opposite errors. One treats the monitor and one ignores it. The answer verifies.

steps.action: Compare the monitor with the patient
steps.detail: Alert, full sentences, pink lips and a normal rate do not fit 84%.
Cold hands, vascular disease and a flat waveform.
Warm or move the sensor and recheck.

elimination.verdict: Assess the patient and get a reliable reading first.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with severe pneumonia has received oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min for 40 hours. SpO2 has stayed at 99% to 100%. She now reports a burning pain under her breastbone and a dry, hacking cough. The nurse hears new fine crackles. She says she feels more short of breath. Her prescribed SpO2 goal is 95% or higher. Which action is best?

options.text: Report the findings as possible oxygen toxicity and ask about titrating to the lowest concentration that meets the SpO2 goal
options.rationale: High oxygen concentrations for more than 24 to 48 hours can injure the lungs. Early signs are substernal pain, dry cough, dyspnea and crackles. Her saturation is well above the goal, so she can likely tolerate less.

options.text: Increase the oxygen by switching to high-flow nasal cannula at a higher concentration
options.rationale: The dyspnea tempts you to give more. More oxygen is the likely cause of the new symptoms.

options.text: Give a PRN antacid for the burning pain and continue the current oxygen
options.rationale: Treats the chest burning as indigestion and leaves the cause in place.

options.text: Encourage incentive spirometry every hour and continue the current oxygen
options.rationale: Helpful for lung expansion. It does not address prolonged high oxygen.

questions.takeaway: Use the lowest oxygen concentration that meets the prescribed goal. Prolonged high concentration causes toxicity and absorption atelectasis.
questions.strategy: A saturation of 100% when the goal is 95% is a cue, not a comfort. It tells you there is room to come down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nonrebreather at 15 L/min for 40 hours.
Substernal burning, dry cough, crackles and dyspnea fit oxygen toxicity.
99% to 100% against a goal of 95% means she can be weaned.

elimination.verdict: Report possible oxygen toxicity and titrate to the lowest effective concentration.

questions.scenario: A 52-year-old is admitted on day 4 of COVID 19. The nurse reviews findings from the past 12 hours. SpO2 on room air was 95% at 0600, 92% at 1200 and 89% at 1800.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with COVID 19 and can be monitored, or requires prompt escalation.

rows.text: Loss of smell since day 2
rows.rationale: A recognized symptom of COVID 19, though less common than other cues. It does not signal deterioration.

rows.text: Two loose stools today
rows.rationale: GI symptoms are common and may even come first. Watch hydration. This alone does not need escalation.

rows.text: SpO2 trend on room air of 95%, 92% and 89%
rows.rationale: A steady fall to below 90% signals impaired gas exchange. The trend matters as much as the last number.

rows.text: Respirations up from 20 to 28, speaking in short phrases
rows.rationale: Rising rate and effort mean the breathing pattern is failing to keep up.

rows.text: Temperature 38.1 C with muscle aches
rows.rationale: Fever and myalgia are typical cues of the illness.

rows.text: Newly unsure of the date and slow to answer
rows.rationale: A change in mental status can mean poor oxygen delivery to the brain. It is a deterioration cue.

rows.text: Fatigue and a reduced appetite
rows.rationale: Common with viral illness. Encourage nutrition and rest.

questions.takeaway: COVID 19 causes many uncomfortable symptoms that are expected. A falling SpO2 trend, rising work of breathing and a change in mental status are the cues you escalate.
questions.strategy: Sort by body system. Symptoms that make the patient miserable are expected. Findings that show oxygenation or the brain failing are escalated.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Smell loss, GI upset, fever, aches and fatigue.
SpO2 falling and respirations rising.
New confusion is a deterioration cue.

elimination.verdict: Escalate the SpO2 trend, the rising work of breathing and the new confusion.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with asthma arrived 1 hour ago with loud wheezes in all fields. He has received two nebulizer treatments. Now his wheezes are barely audible and air movement is faint throughout. Respirations are 34, he answers only by nodding. He is becoming drowsy. SpO2 is 88%. A student says, "His wheezing is much better." How does the nurse interpret these findings?

options.text: The treatments are working, since the wheezing has decreased
options.rationale: Quieter wheezes would be good news only if he were breathing easier. He is breathing faster, cannot speak and is getting drowsy.

options.text: He is moving very little air and is tiring, which is an emergency
options.rationale: Wheezes need airflow. When they fade while effort, speech and alertness worsen, the airways are so tight that little air moves. Silent breath sounds are on the list of findings that need immediate intervention.

options.text: He is drowsy from the nebulizer medication and should be allowed to rest
options.rationale: Nebulizer bronchodilators tend to cause jitteriness and a fast heart rate. Drowsiness with an SpO2 of 88% points to falling oxygen and rising CO2.

options.text: His airways have narrowed less, so the fast rate is likely from anxiety
options.rationale: Anxiety does not explain drowsiness, faint air movement or an SpO2 of 88%.

questions.takeaway: A silent chest is worse than a wheezing one. Fading wheezes with worsening effort, speech and alertness means almost no air is moving.
questions.strategy: The student's comment invites you to read one finding alone. Read the sound together with the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pair the sound with the patient
steps.detail: Quieter chest, faster rate, no speech, drowsy.
Wheezes need air moving. Less air means less sound.
SpO2 of 88% confirms he is failing.

elimination.verdict: Little air movement and tiring. Emergency.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old started bupropion 3 weeks ago to help him quit smoking. His mother calls the clinic. She says he has stayed in his room for several days and told her, "What's the point of any of this?" Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Explain that low mood is common during nicotine withdrawal and should pass in a few weeks
options.rationale: Withdrawal can cause irritability and low mood. That is true. It is exactly why this option is dangerous. Bupropion carries a warning for suicidal thoughts in young adults, so this must not be dismissed.

options.text: Advise switching from bupropion to a nicotine patch
options.rationale: A reasonable later question for the provider. It does not address his safety today.

options.text: Encourage him to join a smoking cessation support group next week
options.rationale: Counseling helps quitting. It does not respond to a possible suicide risk.

options.text: Assess him directly for suicidal thoughts and notify the provider today
options.rationale: Bupropion has a black box warning for suicidal thinking, especially in young adults. Social withdrawal, a hopeless statement and a behavior change must be assessed and reported right away.

questions.takeaway: Families of patients on bupropion are taught to report mood or behavior changes right away. A hopeless statement is a safety issue first and a cessation issue second.
questions.strategy: The withdrawal option is technically true and not the priority. When safety and comfort compete, safety wins.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bupropion carries a suicidality warning in young adults.
Withdrawal from family and a hopeless statement.
Assess for suicidal thoughts and report today.

elimination.verdict: Assess for suicidal thoughts and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is 6 hours after abdominal surgery with a morphine PCA. SpO2 is 97% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. The nurse counts respirations at 8 per minute and shallow. He opens his eyes only to a firm shoulder shake, then drifts off. His wife says, "He's finally sleeping comfortably." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min to protect his saturation
options.rationale: His saturation is fine. The problem is ventilation. More oxygen can keep the SpO2 high while CO2 keeps rising.

options.text: Stimulate him, keep him awake, stop the PCA per protocol and notify the provider
options.rationale: Slow, shallow breathing that he can barely be roused from is opioid-induced respiratory depression. Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation or CO2, so the 97% is falsely reassuring. Keep him breathing and remove the cause.

options.text: Recheck his SpO2 and respiratory rate in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting 30 minutes with a rate of 8 lets CO2 continue to build.

options.text: Let him sleep because his pain is finally controlled
options.rationale: This agrees with the family and ignores the rate and his level of consciousness.

questions.takeaway: Pulse oximetry measures saturation, not ventilation or CO2. A sedated patient can read 98% while CO2 climbs. Count the respirations and check how easily the patient wakes.
questions.strategy: The SpO2 of 97% is there to reassure you. The respiratory rate and the arousal decide the question.

steps.detail: SpO2 97% on oxygen does not show CO2.
Rate of 8, shallow, rousable only to a shake.
Stimulate, stop the opioid and get help.

elimination.verdict: Stimulate him, stop the PCA and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with heart failure is being discharged after community-acquired pneumonia. His home plan includes a fluid restriction of 1.5 L per day. Which statement indicates the need for further teaching?

options.text: "I'll drink at least 3 liters of water every day to keep my mucus thin."
options.rationale: 3 L a day is the pneumonia teaching unless fluids are restricted. He is restricted to 1.5 L, so 3 L could push him into heart failure. The exception decides this item.

options.text: "I'll get my pneumonia and flu vaccines when my provider says it's time."
options.rationale: Vaccination is a core prevention measure.

options.text: "I'll stay out of big crowds during flu season."
options.rationale: Correct prevention teaching.

options.text: "I'll do my deep breathing and coughing several times a day and walk around the house."
options.rationale: Coughing, turning, moving and deep breathing help prevent another pneumonia.

questions.takeaway: Standard pneumonia teaching includes 3 L of water daily. That advice applies only when the patient has no fluid restriction.
questions.strategy: Every option is standard teaching for pneumonia. Read the stem for the detail that makes one of them wrong for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: You are looking for the wrong statement.
Heart failure with a 1.5 L restriction.
Only the 3 L statement conflicts with the restriction.

elimination.verdict: The plan to drink 3 liters a day.

questions.stem: A nurse makes a home visit to a 71-year-old who uses oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: The oxygen cylinder is stored upright in a wheeled stand
options.rationale: Securing cylinders prevents them from falling and damaging the valve. This is correct.

options.text: A water-based gel is used on her dry nostrils
options.rationale: Water-based products are safe with oxygen and help with dryness.

options.text: The patient rubs a petroleum-based vapor rub on her chest at bedtime
options.rationale: Petroleum products are flammable in an oxygen-rich environment and sit right under the oxygen flow. Easy to miss because it looks like an ordinary cold remedy.

options.text: An "Oxygen in use" sign is posted on the front door
options.rationale: Correct fire safety practice.

questions.takeaway: Keep oxygen away from flames and smoking. Keep petroleum-based products away from the face and chest. Water-based lubricants are the safe choice.
questions.strategy: Look for the petroleum product hiding in something familiar. Vapor rub does not look like a fire hazard until you think about what it is made of.

steps.detail: Flame, smoking or petroleum near oxygen.
Vapor rub is petroleum-based.
Secured cylinder, water-based gel, posted sign.

elimination.verdict: The petroleum-based vapor rub.

questions.scenario: A 76-year-old with type 2 diabetes is on day 4 after a hip repair. At 0800 she was oriented x3 with BP 142/84. At 1400 she knows only her name. Temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 112, respirations 28, BP 98/58, SpO2 89% on room air. Coarse crackles in the right lower lobe. WBC 15,800/mm3. Lactate 3.1 mmol/L.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen as prescribed
options.rationale: Improving gas exchange is the first goal of the pneumonia plan. Upright positioning helps the lungs expand.

options.text: Obtain blood and sputum cultures, then give the first antibiotic dose promptly as prescribed
options.rationale: Cultures before the first dose keep results accurate. Prompt antibiotics are how you prevent sepsis from progressing.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.rationale: She is not on a restriction and her blood pressure is falling. Restricting fluids worsens perfusion.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until culture results return
options.rationale: Cultures take days. Waiting lets the infection spread.

options.text: Keep her flat in bed to reduce oxygen demand
options.rationale: Lying flat makes breathing harder. Rest is good and it is done sitting up.

options.text: Hospital-acquired pneumonia with signs of early sepsis
options.rationale: Onset after 48 hours in hospital, crackles, low SpO2 and a high WBC point to pneumonia. Falling BP, fast heart rate, new confusion and a raised lactate are sepsis cues.

options.text: Postoperative delirium from pain medication
options.rationale: Explains confusion only. It does not explain crackles, hypoxemia or a high lactate.

options.text: Pulmonary edema from fluid overload
options.rationale: Overload raises the blood pressure. Hers is falling. The crackles are also on one side.

options.text: Hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Diabetes makes it worth checking. It does not explain fever, crackles, high WBC or hypoxemia.

options.text: SpO2 trend with respiratory rate and work of breathing
options.rationale: Tells you whether gas exchange is improving.

options.text: Blood pressure, mental status and lactate
options.rationale: Tell you whether sepsis is progressing or responding.

options.text: Hemoglobin A1C
options.rationale: Reflects three months of glucose control. It will not change during this event.

options.text: Incision appearance
options.rationale: Worth routine checks. It is not the source of this problem.

questions.takeaway: The pneumonia plan is to improve gas exchange, prevent airflow obstruction and prevent sepsis. In an older adult, new confusion and a falling BP may be the loudest cues, even with a low fever.
questions.strategy: The low temperature and the diabetes are there to pull you toward delirium or hypoglycemia. Only one condition explains every cue.

steps.action: Pick the condition that explains every cue
steps.detail: Lungs, blood pressure, brain and labs all fit pneumonia with early sepsis.

steps.action: Choose actions for gas exchange and sepsis
steps.detail: Upright with oxygen. Cultures, then antibiotics.
Oxygenation for the lungs. Blood pressure, mental status and lactate for sepsis.

elimination.verdict: HAP with early sepsis; oxygen upright, cultures then antibiotic; oxygenation trend and perfusion markers.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old had a bronchoscopy with biopsy 2 hours ago. The nurse reviews the latest findings. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Coughing up about 30 mL of bright red blood in the last 15 minutes
options.rationale: Bleeding is a biopsy complication. Bright red blood in a measurable amount is active bleeding, not streaking. It can block the airway.

options.text: Sputum streaked with small amounts of blood
options.rationale: Expected after a biopsy. Monitor it.

options.text: A sore throat with a hoarse voice
options.rationale: Expected after a scope has passed through the throat.

options.text: Gag reflex not yet returned, so she has not been given anything to drink
options.rationale: Correct care. She stays NPO until the gag reflex returns.

questions.takeaway: After a bronchoscopy with biopsy, streaked sputum is expected and frank bleeding is not. Keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns.
