questions.strategy: Two options mention blood. The amount and the color decide which one is expected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Streaks, sore throat and an absent gag reflex are expected early.
Streaks versus 30 mL of bright red blood.
Active bleeding can fill the airway.

elimination.verdict: The 30 mL of bright red blood.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old with a history of heart failure has received IV fluid at 150 mL/hr for 2 days for dehydration. Her weight is up 1.8 kg since admission. The nurse auscultates her lungs. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider now?

options.text: Soft, low-pitched sounds heard over both lung bases
options.rationale: Vesicular sounds. Normal at the bases.

options.text: Medium-pitched sounds heard near the sternum
options.rationale: Bronchovesicular sounds. Normal in that location.

options.text: Coarse sounds over the trachea and large airways that clear after she coughs
options.rationale: Rhonchi from secretions. They cleared with coughing, so the nurse manages them with coughing and deep breathing.

options.text: Fine crackles in both bases that remain after coughing, new since yesterday
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid in the airways. They are new and they do not clear. They fit her weight gain on steady IV fluids. With her heart failure history, the fluid rate needs review now.

questions.takeaway: Crackles mean fluid, wheezes mean narrowed airways and rhonchi mean secretions. New crackles that do not clear in a patient receiving IV fluids are a report-now finding.
questions.strategy: The rhonchi are abnormal too. What tips it is that they cleared with coughing while the crackles did not. They also match the weight gain and the IV rate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vesicular at the bases and bronchovesicular near the sternum.
Rhonchi cleared. Crackles persisted.
Weight up 1.8 kg on IV fluids with heart failure.

elimination.verdict: New crackles that persist after coughing.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia is newly confused. On room air her SpO2 is 86% and her RR is 28 with accessory muscle use. The nurse raises the head of the bed and applies a nasal cannula at 4 L/min as ordered. Which finding 30 minutes later best shows the oxygen therapy is effective?

options.text: SpO2 95% with RR 20 and unlabored. She is oriented as she was at baseline
options.rationale: Saturation, work of breathing and mental status have all improved. Correlating the number with the patient is how you confirm a response to oxygen.

options.text: SpO2 96% but she is now hard to wake with RR 10
options.rationale: This is deterioration. Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation or CO2. A drowsy patient breathing slowly needs immediate assessment.

options.text: She says the nasal cannula feels comfortable
options.rationale: Comfort matters for adherence. It says nothing about her oxygenation.

options.text: SpO2 95% on a cold finger while she is still restless and using accessory muscles
options.rationale: Cold extremities can make the reading inaccurate. Restlessness and accessory muscle use show she is still struggling.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate oxygen therapy by the patient and the number together. Better SpO2, easier breathing and a return to baseline mental status mean it worked.
questions.strategy: Three options show a good SpO2 or a good report. Only one shows the patient improving in every cue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: RR 10 and accessory muscle use are not improvement.
It is not an oxygenation finding.
Only A improves SpO2, RR and mental status together.

elimination.verdict: A. Treat the patient, not the number.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a 30 pack-year history. He is ready to quit. The plan combines counseling, a nicotine patch and bupropion. The nurse completes the Assist step of the 5 As. Which statement by the patient shows he needs further teaching?

options.text: "I'll use the patch and go to my counseling sessions, not just one or the other."
options.rationale: Correct. Combining counseling with medication is the recommended strategy.

options.text: "If a craving gets bad, I can smoke one cigarette while I have the patch on."
options.rationale: This needs follow up. Smoking while on nicotine replacement raises nicotine levels and the risk of stroke and heart attack.

options.text: "My wife will call the doctor if she notices my mood or behavior changing."
options.rationale: Correct. Bupropion carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts. Families should report behavior changes right away.

options.text: "The clinic will call me in the first week after my quit date."
options.rationale: Correct. Arrange is the last of the 5 As. Follow up starts in the first week after the quit date.

questions.takeaway: Nicotine replacement plus smoking stacks nicotine and raises cardiovascular risk. Teach the patient not to smoke while using NRT.
questions.strategy: Negative polarity: look for the unsafe statement. Three statements match the plan. One creates a risk.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that is wrong.
Combined treatment, family monitoring and early follow up are correct.
Smoking on the patch raises nicotine levels.

elimination.verdict: B. It is the only statement that puts him at risk.

skills.title: FSBS/Insulin Administration Check-Off

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receives 18 units of Humulin N subcutaneously at 0800. He eats breakfast at 0830 and lunch at 1230. The nurse plans when to monitor most closely for hypoglycemia from this dose. Which window is correct?

options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.

questions.takeaway: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. That wide peak is why NPH catches people off guard. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.
questions.strategy: The NPH peak is broad rather than sharp, so the risk is spread across a whole shift rather than concentrated in an hour.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours out.
NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.

questions.concept: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.

questions.stem: Before the 0730 medication round, the nurse restocks the unit's insulin bin. She inspects each vial and compares its appearance with the label. Which vials are expected to look clear? Select all that apply.

options.text: Humalog
options.rationale: Lispro is rapid-acting and comes as a clear solution. Cloudiness in this vial would mean something is wrong.

options.text: NovoLog
options.rationale: Aspart is rapid-acting and clear. Clear insulins do not need resuspending before you draw them up.

options.text: Humulin R
options.rationale: Regular insulin is short-acting and clear.

options.text: Novolin R
options.rationale: Regular insulin is short-acting and clear.

options.text: Humulin N
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension. It is cloudy by design and has to be rolled to mix it evenly before drawing.

options.text: Novolin N
options.rationale: This is also NPH and also cloudy. The cloudiness is the suspension, not spoilage.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting and regular insulins are clear. NPH is the cloudy one. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.
questions.strategy: Appearance is a first check on each vial. It narrows the field and never replaces reading the label, because two different insulins can look identical and act over completely different time courses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH, which is cloudy.
Humalog, NovoLog, Humulin R, and Novolin R are rapid-acting or regular. All are clear.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulins (Humalog, NovoLog) and regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) are clear. NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) is cloudy. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old newly started on insulin is preparing for discharge and demonstrates his technique to the nurse while explaining what he plans to do at home. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will not inject into my thigh right before I go for a walk."
options.rationale: Accurate. Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.

options.text: "I will roll the cloudy vial gently rather than shaking it."
options.rationale: Accurate. NPH is a suspension and shaking froths it.

options.text: "I will rotate between my abdomen, arm, and thigh so I never use the same area twice."
options.rationale: Anatomical site rotation is no longer recommended, because absorption differs by site and rotating between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate. One anatomical site is selected and rotation occurs within that region.

options.text: "If my glucose is under 70 and I can swallow, I take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the glucose is rechecked in 15 minutes.

questions.takeaway: One anatomical site, rotate within that region. Between-region rotation varies absorption dose to dose.
questions.strategy: This guidance changed, so the wrong statement is what patients were taught for years.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the outdated practice.
One site, rotate within it.
Rolling, rule of 15, and exercise are correct.

elimination.verdict: C is the statement needing correction: rotate within one region, not between regions.

questions.stem: Lunch trays arrive on the unit at 1200. A student is caring for several patients who are eating normally and have insulin ordered around lunch. She shows the nurse her planned time for each patient's insulin. Which planned times are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Humalog at 1200, as the tray is set in front of him
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes. It is given just before or with the meal.

options.text: NovoLog at 1200, with the meal
options.rationale: Also rapid-acting with an onset of 10 to 30 minutes. It is timed to food in front of the patient.

options.text: Humulin R at 1130
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes. It is given about 30 minutes before the meal.

options.text: Novolin R at 1130
options.rationale: Also regular insulin. Giving it 30 minutes ahead matches its action to the meal.

options.text: Lantus at 1130, so it covers the lunch meal
options.rationale: Lantus is long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak. Its timing is not tied to food.

options.text: Levemir with lunch, since it is the largest meal of the day
options.rationale: Levemir is also long-acting basal insulin. It is not matched to carbohydrate intake.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting goes with the meal. Regular goes about 30 minutes before. Long-acting basal is not timed to food at all.
questions.strategy: Sort each product by class first. The class sets the timing, so a correct time for the wrong class is still a wrong plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting goes at 1200. Regular goes at 1130.
Lantus and Levemir are basal insulin. They are not timed to lunch.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulin is given just before or with the meal. Regular insulin is given about 30 minutes before. Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A nurse withdraws a dose from a vial labeled Humulin N. The solution is uniformly cloudy. The vial is within date and has been refrigerated. Which action is correct?

options.text: Return the vial to the pharmacy
options.rationale: Cloudiness is the normal appearance of this product.

options.text: Draw the dose without mixing
options.rationale: An unmixed suspension delivers an unpredictable dose.

options.text: Roll the vial gently between the palms
options.rationale: NPH is an intermediate-acting suspension and is expected to be cloudy. Rolling redistributes it before the dose is drawn.

options.text: Shake the vial until the particles dissolve
options.rationale: Shaking froths the suspension and makes an accurate dose difficult to draw.

questions.takeaway: The N in Humulin N and Novolin N stands for NPH. Intermediate-acting, cloudy, gently rolled before use. Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH, intermediate-acting insulin. Onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. Cloudy in appearance and gently rolled before use.
questions.strategy: Cloudy identifies exactly one class. If a vial is cloudy it is NPH, and any other insulin here is clear.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: N is NPH, intermediate-acting.
Cloudiness is the normal appearance of this product.
Shaking froths the suspension and makes an accurate dose difficult to draw.
An unmixed suspension delivers an unpredictable dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: NPH is an intermediate-acting suspension and is expected to be cloudy.

questions.concept: Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH, intermediate-acting insulin. Onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. Cloudy in appearance and gently rolled before use. The N stands for NPH.

questions.stem: An order reads Humulin R 8 units subcutaneously before meals. The nurse removes a vial labeled Humulin N from the cabinet and notices the discrepancy before drawing up the dose. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give half the Humulin N dose
options.rationale: Improvises a dose of the wrong insulin.

options.text: Give the Humulin N as drawn
options.rationale: The brand is shared and the class is not.

options.text: Return it and obtain Humulin R
options.rationale: The two differ in onset, peak, and duration. NPH given in place of regular would peak hours after the meal it was meant to cover.

options.text: Give both at the next meal
options.rationale: Administers an insulin that was never ordered.

questions.takeaway: Humulin R is regular and short-acting. Humulin R is regular and short-acting; Humulin N is NPH and intermediate-acting. The shared brand name is the trap. A shared brand name does not mean a shared class, and look-alike insulin names are a recognized cause of medication error.
questions.strategy: Look-alike names are a causes of insulin error. The brand tells you the manufacturer; the letter after it tells you what the drug does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Same brand family, different class.
The brand is shared and the class is not.
Improvises a dose of the wrong insulin.
Administers an insulin that was never ordered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the two differ in onset, peak, and duration.

questions.concept: Humulin R is regular and short-acting; Humulin N is NPH and intermediate-acting. A shared brand name does not mean a shared class, and look-alike insulin names are a recognized cause of medication error.

questions.stem: A nurse is called to a patient who seems unwell an hour after receiving mealtime insulin. She considers whether the presentation fits a falling blood glucose before checking. Which findings are consistent with hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shakiness and diaphoresis
options.rationale: Sympathetic responses, and they are usually the earliest warning.

options.text: Tachycardia
options.rationale: Part of the same adrenergic response.

options.text: Polyuria developing over the past two days
options.rationale: The picture of hyperglycemia, driven by osmotic diuresis, meaning sugar in the urine drags water out with it. It builds over days rather than minutes.

options.text: Irritability or anxiety
options.rationale: Correct, and it is often mistaken for a behavioral issue.

options.text: Deep, rapid respirations with a fruity odor
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations, meaning deep rapid breathing that blows off acid, and ketotic breath indicate ketoacidosis.

options.text: Warm, dry, flushed skin
options.rationale: Points to hyperglycemia. Hypoglycemia produces cool, clammy skin from the adrenergic response.

questions.takeaway: Shaky, sweaty, tachycardic, hungry, irritable, confused. Hypoglycemia comes on fast; hyperglycemia builds over days. Hypoglycemia presents as shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hunger, irritability or anxiety, confusion, and altered level of consciousness.
questions.strategy: Onset separates them as reliably as the symptoms do. Anything developing over minutes after insulin points at a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One hour after mealtime insulin.
Shaky, sweaty, tachycardic, hungry, anxious.
Polyuria and polydipsia are hyperglycemia over days.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Hypoglycemia presents as shakiness, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hunger, irritability or anxiety, confusion, and altered level of consciousness.

questions.stem: An order reads Novolin R 8 units subcutaneously before lunch. Meal trays arrive on the unit at 1200. The patient is eating normally and his 0700 glucose was 142 mg/dL. At what time should the dose be given?

options.rationale: Leaves the insulin acting after the food has been absorbed.
That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so a dose half an hour ahead matches its action to the meal.
Two hours ahead brings the insulin to its peak well before any carbohydrate arrives.

questions.takeaway: The R in Humulin R and Novolin R stands for Regular. Short-acting, given about 30 minutes before meals. Humulin R and Novolin R are regular, short-acting insulin. Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours.
questions.strategy: R for Regular and N for NPH is the most useful pair of letters to learn. Once you have that, the timing follows from the class.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: R is Regular, short-acting.
Two hours ahead brings the insulin to its peak well before any carbohydrate arrives.
That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Leaves the insulin acting after the food has been absorbed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so a dose half an hour ahead matches its action to the meal.

questions.concept: Humulin R and Novolin R are regular, short-acting insulin. Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. Given about 30 minutes before meals. The R stands for Regular.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to give a scheduled dose of insulin to a patient admitted two days ago. Insulin is a high-alert medication and she works through her checks before drawing it up. Which checks does she complete before administering? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the expiry date on the vial
options.rationale: Checking expiry applies to any medication and is not one of the specific checks before an insulin dose.

options.text: Establish the current blood glucose and whether it is safe to give insulin now
options.rationale: The value determines whether the dose goes ahead at all.

options.text: Review the insulin ordered, the dose, and any hold or notify parameters
options.rationale: Parameters exist precisely so the dose is not given automatically.

options.text: Determine whether the patient is eating and whether the timing fits the meal
options.rationale: A dose that was correct for a normal meal becomes too much when the meal is skipped or delayed, and that is a frequent cause of inpatient lows.

options.text: Confirm the patient has a working intravenous line
options.rationale: Insulin here is subcutaneous. An intravenous line is irrelevant to this administration.

options.text: Administer the dose before checking the glucose so the timing is not delayed
options.rationale: Reverses the order and removes the check that decides whether the dose is safe.

questions.takeaway: Patient, glucose, order, food, safety, then reassess. Incorrect type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Before insulin, check patient, glucose, order, food, safety, and reassessment plan.
questions.strategy: Every one of the four causes of inpatient hypoglycemia is caught by one of these checks, which is why the list exists in this order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Patient, glucose, order, food, safety.
Giving before checking removes the deciding check.

elimination.verdict: B, C and D are selected.

questions.concept: Before insulin, check patient, glucose, order, food, safety, and reassessment plan. Incorrect type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old receives Humulin R 10 units subcutaneously at 0730. He eats a full breakfast at 0800. His 0715 fingerstick glucose was 168 mg/dL. The nurse plans when to watch him most closely for shakiness, diaphoresis, and confusion from this dose. Which window does she choose?

options.rationale: This is past the peak. It is approaching the end of the 5 to 8 hour duration.
Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes. At this point it is barely working.
Regular insulin peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose. For a 0730 dose that places the risk window mid-morning.
This is about 12 hours out. It is well past the duration of this dose.

questions.takeaway: Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, a peak at 2 to 4 hours, and a duration of 5 to 8 hours. The peak is the window for hypoglycemia.
questions.strategy: Peak is the most useful number in the table. Onset tells you when to give it. Peak tells you when a low is most likely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humulin R is regular insulin, which peaks 2 to 4 hours after the dose.
That is still within the onset period.
That is past the peak.
That is past the 5 to 8 hour duration.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: 0930 to 1130 is 2 to 4 hours after a 0730 dose.

questions.concept: Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R): onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, duration 5 to 8 hours. The peak is the window for hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes is prescribed Humalog 6 units subcutaneously three times daily. His breakfast tray has just been placed in front of him. His fingerstick glucose is 138 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the dose now
options.rationale: Humalog is lispro, with an onset of 10 to 30 minutes, so it is timed to food already in front of him.

options.text: Give the dose after he finishes eating
options.rationale: Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.

options.text: Hold the dose and recheck the glucose
options.rationale: A glucose of 138 does not meet any hold parameter.

options.text: Give the dose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: That timing belongs to regular insulin, which has a slower onset.

questions.takeaway: Humalog is lispro and NovoLog is aspart. Both are rapid-acting, given just before or with the meal.
questions.strategy: Learn the brand and generic as a pair. Humalog and NovoLog both end in -log and both act fast, which is a usable hook.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humalog is lispro, rapid-acting.
That timing belongs to regular insulin, which has a slower onset.
Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.
A glucose of 138 does not meet any hold parameter.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: humalog is lispro, with an onset of 10 to 30 minutes, so it is timed to food already in front of him.

questions.concept: Humalog is lispro and NovoLog is aspart. Both are rapid-acting, with an onset of 10 to 30 minutes, a peak at 30 to 90 minutes, and a duration of 3 to 5 hours. Given just before or with meals.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a newly hired graduate the four insulin classes, because several products on the unit share a brand name and differ only by a letter. She then asks the graduate to sort the supply and explain each choice aloud. Which statements by the graduate show that the teaching was understood? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Humalog and NovoLog are rapid-acting."
options.rationale: Correct. Lispro and aspart have an onset of 10 to 30 minutes. That is why they are given with food in front of the patient.

options.text: "Humulin R and Novolin R are short-acting regular insulin."
options.rationale: Correct. The R stands for Regular.

options.text: "Humulin N and Novolin N are intermediate-acting NPH."
options.rationale: Correct. The N stands for NPH.

options.text: "Lantus and Levemir are long-acting basal insulin."
options.rationale: Correct. Glargine and detemir last 20 to 24 hours or more with no pronounced peak. That is what makes them basal insulin.

options.text: "Humulin R and Humulin N go in the same bin because they share a brand name."
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. The brand identifies the manufacturer's family. The letter identifies the class. R and N behave completely differently.

options.text: "Lantus goes with the rapid-acting insulins because it is clear."
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. Appearance does not determine class. Lantus is clear and long-acting.

questions.takeaway: Four classes by name: Humalog and NovoLog are rapid-acting. Humulin R and Novolin R are short-acting regular. Humulin N and Novolin N are intermediate-acting NPH. Lantus and Levemir are long-acting basal.
questions.strategy: The wrong statements each lean on a shortcut that fails. One uses the brand name. The other uses appearance. The letter after the brand carries the class. Clear covers three of the four classes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A, B, C, and D pair the product with its correct class.
Same brand with a different letter means a different class.
Clear does not mean rapid-acting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Four classes by name: Humalog and NovoLog are rapid-acting; Humulin R and Novolin R are short-acting regular; Humulin N and Novolin N are intermediate-acting NPH; Lantus and Levemir are long-acting basal.

questions.stem: A nurse obtains fasting glucose results on four patients at 0630: 48 mg/dL, 96 mg/dL, 164 mg/dL, and 212 mg/dL. All four are alert and oriented. Which result requires action first?

options.text: 212 mg/dL
options.rationale: Hyperglycemia requiring assessment and orders, and not the immediate emergency a low is.

options.text: 164 mg/dL
options.rationale: Within the target range.

options.text: 96 mg/dL
options.rationale: Within the common inpatient target range of 70 to 180.

options.text: 48 mg/dL
options.rationale: Below 70, and within ADA level 2 hypoglycemia at under 54. It is an immediate safety concern.

questions.takeaway: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range. Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia requiring assessment and review of orders. ADA levels: level 1 is 54 to 69 mg/dL, level 2 is under 54 mg/dL.
questions.strategy: A high glucose needs attention and a low glucose needs it now. When a stem offers both, the low wins on urgency every time.

steps.detail: One below 70, two in range, one above 180.
Within the common inpatient target range of 70 to 180.
Within the target range.
Hyperglycemia requiring assessment and orders, and not the immediate emergency a low is.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: below 70, and within ADA level 2 hypoglycemia at under 54.

questions.concept: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range. Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia requiring assessment and review of orders. ADA levels: level 1 is 54 to 69 mg/dL, level 2 is under 54 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old with type 2 diabetes is prescribed Lantus 20 units at bedtime and NovoLog 5 units with meals. He had asked why the bedtime dose is not timed to food. The nurse explains how each insulin works. Which statement by the patient shows that the teaching was understood?

options.text: "I only need the Lantus on nights when I skip dinner."
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. Basal insulin continues regardless of intake.

options.text: "The Lantus gives steady background coverage with no big peak, so it is not matched to my meals."
options.rationale: Correct. Glargine provides background coverage over 20 to 24 hours or more with no pronounced peak. That is why its timing is not tied to carbohydrate.

options.text: "The Lantus works just like my NovoLog. It just lasts longer."
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. NovoLog is rapid-acting with a defined peak. The two classes differ in more than duration.

options.text: "The Lantus peaks while I sleep, so that is when my sugar will drop the most."
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. Lantus has no pronounced peak. That is exactly why it is used for basal coverage.

questions.takeaway: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak, lasting 20 to 24 hours or more.
questions.strategy: No pronounced peak is the defining feature. It explains why basal insulin is not timed to meals. It also explains why it is not the insulin that causes a mealtime low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lantus is glargine, a long-acting basal insulin.
Lantus has no pronounced peak.
Basal insulin is not skipped based on meals.
NovoLog has a defined peak. Lantus does not.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: steady coverage with no pronounced peak is why Lantus is not timed to food.

questions.concept: Lantus is glargine and Levemir is detemir. Both are long-acting basal insulin with an onset of 1 to 2 hours, no pronounced peak, and a duration of 20 to 24 hours or more. Never mixed with other insulin types.

questions.stem: A point-of-care glucose is due on a patient whose hands are cold and who has been resting under a blanket. The meter and strips are at the bedside and the patient has just woken. Which actions reflect correct technique? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify the patient's identity before testing
options.rationale: The first of the checks, as with any procedure.

options.text: Wash and dry hands thoroughly before testing
options.rationale: CDC guidance, and drying matters because residual water dilutes the sample.

options.text: Warm the finger under hot running water to improve flow
options.rationale: Hot water is unnecessary and risks a burn. Warming gently or lowering the hand is sufficient.

options.text: Puncture the side of the fingertip
options.rationale: Less painful and yields a better sample than the pad, which has more nerve endings.

options.text: Squeeze the finger firmly to obtain an adequate sample quickly
options.rationale: Excessive squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid and produces an inaccurate result.

options.text: Wipe away the first drop and use the second
options.rationale: Applies to some devices by manufacturer instruction rather than as a universal rule.

questions.takeaway: Identify, wash and dry, check the meter and strips, use the side of the fingertip, and never squeeze hard. Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.
questions.strategy: The wrong option is the shortcut everyone takes when blood is slow to come. It changes the number you are about to act on.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Identity, hands, equipment, site, puncture.
Squeezing dilutes the sample with tissue fluid.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old injects his morning insulin into his thigh at 0700. He then takes a brisk 30-minute walk at 0730. His log shows a 0700 glucose of 146 mg/dL. On three mornings in a row he felt shaky during the walk with readings of 62 to 66 mg/dL. On days he rests after the injection he has no lows. Which explanation fits these findings?

options.text: The thigh absorbs insulin faster than the abdomen at rest
options.rationale: This reverses the two. The abdomen is the fastest site.

options.text: Exercise in the injected limb speeds absorption from that site
options.rationale: Walking works the thigh he injected. That speeds absorption from that site, so more insulin acts sooner than on rest days.

options.text: Site choice affects comfort only
options.rationale: Comfort matters. Absorption is the clinical reason the site is chosen deliberately.

options.text: Absorption is the same at every site
options.rationale: It differs by site. If it were the same, his rest days and walking days would not differ.

questions.takeaway: Abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. Exercise speeds absorption from the limb injected.
questions.strategy: Compare the walking days with the rest days. The only thing that changes is activity in the injected limb, so the explanation has to involve that limb.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The lows happen only when he walks after a thigh injection.
The pattern itself shows absorption varies.
The abdomen is fastest at rest.
The lows are a dosing effect, not a comfort issue.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: walking speeds absorption from the thigh he injected.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas and rotate sites per policy.

questions.stem: A student is preparing to give her first subcutaneous insulin injection and describes her plan to the nurse before approaching the patient. She has practiced in the skills laboratory and wants her technique checked. Which elements of her description are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat as appropriate for the site and needle length
options.rationale: Ensures the dose reaches subcutaneous tissue rather than muscle.

options.text: Insert the needle at a 90 degree angle
options.rationale: The typical angle for subcutaneous insulin, adjusted for the site and needle length.

options.text: Aspirate before injecting to check for blood return
options.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin administration.

options.text: Aspirate before injecting to confirm placement
options.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin administration.

options.text: Withdraw the needle at the same angle used for insertion
options.rationale: Pulling straight back out along the track you made avoids dragging the needle sideways through tissue.

options.text: Massage the site after withdrawing the needle
options.rationale: Massage alters absorption and is avoided after insulin injection.

questions.takeaway: Pinch, insert at 90 degrees, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold briefly, withdraw at the same angle, dispose immediately. Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle, and dispose in a sharps container immediately.
questions.strategy: Aspiration is the step students import from intramuscular technique. It is not part of subcutaneous insulin administration.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pinch, insert, inject, hold, withdraw, dispose.
Aspiration belongs to a different route.

elimination.verdict: A, B and E are selected.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle, and dispose in a sharps container immediately.

questions.stem: An order reads regular insulin 6 units subcutaneously before breakfast. The tray is expected in 30 minutes. The patient is alert, eating normally, and his fingerstick glucose is 156 mg/dL. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give the dose now
options.rationale: Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

options.text: Hold the dose until bedtime
options.rationale: Separates a mealtime insulin from the meal it covers.

options.text: Give the dose when the tray arrives
options.rationale: That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.

options.text: Give the dose after he has eaten half the meal
options.rationale: Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting goes just before or with the meal. Regular goes about 30 minutes before, because its onset is slower. Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.
questions.strategy: Match the onset to the food. The number to remember is not the duration but when the insulin starts working relative to when carbohydrate arrives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular, which is short-acting.
That timing belongs to rapid-acting insulin.
Leaves the insulin peaking after the carbohydrate has been absorbed.
Separates a mealtime insulin from the meal it covers.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes, so giving it half an hour before the tray matches its action to the food.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulin such as lispro or aspart has an onset of 10 to 30 minutes and is given just before or with meals. Regular insulin has an onset of 30 to 60 minutes and is given about 30 minutes before meals.

questions.stem: A patient is alert and swallowing safely. His fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. His rapid-acting insulin is due now and his breakfast tray has not arrived. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the scheduled insulin
options.rationale: Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. It would drive the glucose lower.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: A glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

options.text: Recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
options.rationale: The recheck follows treatment rather than replacing it.

options.text: Wait for the breakfast tray
options.rationale: Delays treatment while the glucose continues to fall.

questions.takeaway: Treat first, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then work out why it happened. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient. For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low.
questions.strategy: The scheduled insulin and the missing tray are both deliberate pressure. Neither changes the rule that a glucose under 70 is treated now.

steps.detail: 58, which is under 70.
Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.
The recheck follows treatment rather than replacing it.
Delays treatment while the glucose continues to fall.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: a glucose under 70 is treated before anything else, and he is conscious and able to swallow.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: During her morning insulin round a nurse is told the breakfast trays are delayed by an hour. Two of her patients are due rapid-acting insulin and one is due long-acting basal insulin. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hold the rapid-acting Humalog until the tray is actually in front of the patient
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin begins working in 10 to 30 minutes, so giving it an hour before food creates a low.

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose if there is any further delay
options.rationale: Reduced or delayed intake is a cause of inpatient hypoglycemia.

options.text: Notify the provider if the delay affects the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: The regimen was written around a meal schedule that has changed.

options.text: Give the Humalog now so the round stays on time
options.rationale: Prioritizes the schedule over the patient and produces the exact mismatch that causes hypoglycemia.

options.text: Give the patient's Lantus as scheduled
options.rationale: Long-acting basal insulin has no pronounced peak and is not timed to food, so a delayed tray does not change it.

options.text: Give a double dose of Humalog once the tray arrives to make up the delay
options.rationale: Doubling a mealtime dose has no basis and creates a serious hypoglycemia risk.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin waits for the meal. Basal insulin does not, because it is not matched to food. Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.
questions.strategy: This single scenario separates the two classes. If a delayed tray changes whether you give it, it is a mealtime insulin.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humalog is mealtime; Lantus is basal.
Convenience over the patient.
Doubling has no basis.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A nurse is to give 6 units of regular insulin and 14 units of NPH in one syringe. She has rolled the NPH vial and drawn up air. Which action comes next?

options.text: Inject air into the NPH vial without withdrawing insulin
options.rationale: Air is injected into the cloudy vial first, without drawing any insulin, so the clear vial is never contaminated with suspension.

options.text: Inject air into the regular vial and withdraw the regular insulin
options.rationale: The regular insulin is drawn later. Injecting air into the cloudy vial comes first.

options.text: Withdraw the NPH first since it is the larger dose
options.rationale: Dose size does not set the order. Clear is always drawn before cloudy.

options.text: Withdraw both doses into separate syringes and combine them
options.rationale: Transferring between syringes introduces error and an unnecessary break in the system.

questions.takeaway: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, draw cloudy. The clear vial must stay uncontaminated.
questions.strategy: The order protects the clear vial. If suspension enters it, every later dose drawn from that vial is altered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Air into cloudy first, without drawing.
Regular is drawn after the air step is complete.
Dose size is irrelevant, and combining syringes adds error.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: air into the NPH vial first.

questions.concept: NPH is intermediate-acting with an onset of 1 to 2 hours, a peak at 4 to 12 hours, and a duration of 14 to 24 hours. It is cloudy and is gently rolled before use. Rapid-acting and regular insulins are clear.

questions.stem: A patient taking glyburide is also prescribed metoprolol for hypertension. Which concern does the nurse identify?

options.text: The beta blocker will raise the blood glucose
options.rationale: Beta blockers have a modest and unpredictable effect on glucose. Losing the warning signs is the danger.

options.text: The beta blocker reduces absorption of the glyburide
options.rationale: No clinically meaningful absorption interaction between them.

options.text: The combination increases the risk of lactic acidosis
options.rationale: Lactic acidosis is a metformin concern, not a sulfonylurea one.

options.text: The beta blocker may mask the early warning signs of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The shakiness, sweating, and racing heart that warn of a low are adrenergic. A beta blocker blunts them, so the first sign may be confusion instead.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia. Sweating usually persists; shakiness and palpitations do not.
questions.strategy: Ask what the patient would normally feel first during a low, and what a beta blocker does to that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shaky, sweaty, palpitations. All adrenergic.

steps.action: Ask what a beta blocker blocks
steps.detail: The adrenergic response.
That belongs to metformin.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the warning signs are masked.

questions.stem: A patient who takes acarbose with each meal becomes hypoglycemic. Which does the nurse administer?

options.text: Table sugar dissolved in water
options.rationale: Sucrose has to be split into glucose and fructose first, and acarbose is blocking exactly that step. This is the trap.

options.text: A slice of bread
options.rationale: A complex carbohydrate needing digestion, and slower still.

options.text: A glass of milk
options.rationale: Lactose also requires breakdown, and milk raises glucose too slowly for an acute low.

options.text: Glucose tablets
options.rationale: Acarbose blocks the enzyme that breaks table sugar into absorbable glucose, so sucrose will not work. Glucose tablets need no digestion.

questions.takeaway: On acarbose or miglitol, treat hypoglycemia with glucose specifically. Sucrose and starch will not be absorbed.
questions.strategy: This is the one hypoglycemia scenario where the usual juice-or-sugar answer is wrong. The drug name in the stem is the signal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breakdown of complex sugars in the gut.
Both need the blocked enzyme.
Lactose also needs breakdown.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: glucose tablets.

questions.stem: A patient is starting empagliflozin. Which teaching does the nurse include?

options.text: Expect increased urination, and report burning or genital itching
options.rationale: SGLT-2 inhibitors work by dumping glucose into the urine. Sugar in the urine raises the risk of urinary and genital yeast infections.

options.text: This is a form of insulin taken by mouth
options.rationale: There is no oral insulin. Insulin is destroyed in the stomach.

options.text: Your urine should stay free of glucose on this medication
options.rationale: The opposite. Glucose in the urine is the mechanism, not a complication.

options.text: Take it only when the glucose reads above 200
options.rationale: It is taken on a schedule, not in response to a reading.

questions.takeaway: SGLT-2 inhibitors lower glucose by excreting it in the urine, which brings polyuria and a risk of urinary and yeast infections.
questions.strategy: Work out the mechanism from the drug class and the side effects follow from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose is excreted in the urine.
More urine, and sugar feeding organisms.
No such thing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: more urination, and report infection signs.

questions.stem: A patient on metformin is scheduled for a computed tomography scan with iodinated contrast. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give half the usual dose
options.rationale: Not a recognized approach. The decision is to hold or not, and it is the provider's.

options.text: Confirm with the provider that the metformin is held around the study
options.rationale: Contrast can impair kidney function, and metformin cleared by the kidneys accumulates. The build-up risks lactic acidosis.

options.text: Give the metformin with a full glass of water before the scan
options.rationale: Water does not protect the kidneys from the contrast or clear the drug faster.

options.text: No action, since metformin does not interact with contrast
options.rationale: It does, and this is one of the most tested medication-procedure interactions.

questions.takeaway: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast because contrast-related kidney impairment lets it accumulate and cause lactic acidosis.
questions.strategy: Ask what clears the drug and what the contrast does to that organ.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: By the kidneys.
Impair kidney function.
A well-known interaction.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm the hold with the provider.

questions.stem: A clinic nurse reviews patients who each take one oral antidiabetic agent alone. Each patient reports skipping lunch today. Which patients are at meaningful risk of hypoglycemia from their medication? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 66-year-old taking glipizide
options.rationale: Glipizide is a sulfonylurea. It pushes the pancreas to release insulin whether or not glucose is high, so a low can follow a skipped meal.

options.text: A 71-year-old taking glyburide
options.rationale: Glyburide is also a sulfonylurea with the same mechanism.

options.text: A 59-year-old taking glimepiride
options.rationale: Glimepiride is the third of the commonly used sulfonylureas.

options.text: A 54-year-old taking metformin
options.rationale: Metformin reduces liver glucose output and improves sensitivity. It does not force insulin release, so alone it rarely causes a low.

options.text: A 62-year-old taking sitagliptin
options.rationale: Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor. It acts through incretins, which work only when glucose is rising, so the risk is low.

options.text: A 68-year-old taking acarbose
options.rationale: Acarbose slows carbohydrate absorption rather than adding insulin. The risk alone is low, though it changes how a low must be treated.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia because they force insulin release regardless of the glucose level. Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, and acarbose do not.
questions.strategy: Sort by mechanism. Anything that pushes insulin out regardless of glucose can cause a low when a meal is skipped. Anything glucose-dependent is low risk alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does it force insulin release, or does it work only when glucose rises?
Glipizide, glyburide, and glimepiride force insulin release.
Metformin, sitagliptin, and acarbose do not force insulin release.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's insulin supply. Which observation requires follow-up?

options.text: The regular insulin appears clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is a clear solution. This is normal.

options.text: The NPH insulin appears cloudy
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension and is cloudy by design. It is rolled to mix it before drawing.

options.text: The insulin lispro appears clear
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is also clear. Normal.

options.text: The insulin glargine appears cloudy
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation, and the vial must not be used.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH should look cloudy. Every other insulin is clear, and cloudiness in a clear insulin means discard it.
questions.strategy: One insulin is meant to be cloudy. Any other cloudy vial is the finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH, and only NPH.
NPH cloudy, regular and lispro clear.
A cloudy glargine.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: cloudy glargine.

questions.stem: A patient wakes with a glucose of 240 mg/dL. Overnight readings show a fall to 48 mg/dL at 0300 followed by a rise. Which does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Somogyi phenomenon
options.rationale: An overnight low triggers counter-regulatory hormones, which drive the glucose up by morning. The high reading is the rebound from the low.

options.text: Insufficient evening basal insulin
options.rationale: That would produce a steady overnight rise, not a fall to 48 first.

options.text: An inaccurate morning meter reading
options.rationale: The overnight trend explains the morning value. Dismissing it as error loses the pattern.

options.text: Dawn phenomenon
options.rationale: Dawn is a morning rise from overnight growth hormone and cortisol, with no preceding low. The 0300 reading of 48 is what separates them.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi has an overnight low that rebounds. Dawn rises without a low. The 0200 to 0300 check is what distinguishes them.
questions.strategy: Both produce a high morning glucose, and the overnight reading is the only thing that separates them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 48 mg/dL at 0300.
Dawn has no preceding low.
One predicts a steady rise, one dismisses real data.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: Somogyi phenomenon.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes has influenza and is vomiting. Which sick-day instructions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep taking the insulin, even when not eating normally
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose through stress hormones. Stopping insulin during illness is how patients arrive in ketoacidosis.

options.text: Check the glucose every three to four hours
options.rationale: More often than usual, because illness makes the glucose unpredictable.

options.text: Test for ketones when the glucose stays above 240
options.rationale: Ketones signal that fat is being broken down for fuel and that ketoacidosis may be developing.

options.text: Take small sips of fluid frequently
options.rationale: Vomiting plus a rising glucose dehydrates quickly, and dehydration accelerates the whole process.

options.text: Stop the insulin until eating normally again
options.rationale: The single most dangerous sick-day error. Insulin need usually rises during illness.

options.text: Wait until the fever settles before contacting the provider
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting, ketones, or a glucose that will not come down need reporting rather than waiting.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: never stop insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, test ketones above 240, and keep fluids going.
questions.strategy: Two options tell the patient to wait or to stop. Ask what illness does to the insulin requirement.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: Stress hormones raise the glucose.
The need goes up, not down.
Vomiting with ketones is what needs reporting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A patient using an insulin pump reports the glucose has risen from 140 to 310 mg/dL over four hours and ketones are now present. Which does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: A faulty glucose meter
options.rationale: The ketones corroborate the reading. Two findings agreeing is not a meter fault.

options.text: The pump is delivering too much basal insulin
options.rationale: Too much would lower the glucose, not raise it, and would not produce ketones.

options.text: An expected rise after a high-carbohydrate meal
options.rationale: A meal does not produce ketones, and the rise would not continue over four hours.

options.text: An interruption in insulin delivery at the site or in the tubing
options.rationale: A pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin, with no long-acting reserve. An occlusion or dislodged cannula leaves the patient with no insulin at all within hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump patients have no long-acting insulin on board. An interruption produces hyperglycemia and ketones within hours.
questions.strategy: Ask what a pump does and does not deliver. The ketones are the finding that rules out a simple meal-related rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rapid-acting only, no basal reserve.
They indicate no insulin is reaching the patient.

steps.action: Cut the meal and meter options
steps.detail: Neither explains ketones.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an interruption in delivery.

questions.stem: A student is checking a 0730 fingerstick glucose on a 68-year-old with type 2 diabetes. She has verified the patient with two identifiers, washed and dried her hands, and confirmed the meter passed its control check. The patient's hands are cool, so she lowers his arm below heart level. As she opens the strip vial she sees the expiration date was last month. Which action should she take next?

options.text: Proceed with the test since the meter passed its control check
options.rationale: The control check shows the meter works. It says nothing about strips that are past their date, which can give an inaccurate reading.

options.text: Obtain an in-date vial of compatible strips before puncturing the finger
options.rationale: Strip compatibility and expiration are part of the pre-test check. An expired strip makes the number untrustworthy. Insulin decisions ride on that number.

options.text: Run the test and repeat it with a new strip only if the value is abnormal
options.rationale: Testing with a strip you already know is expired wastes a puncture and invites acting on a false number.

options.text: Raise the arm above heart level to improve blood flow
options.rationale: Lowering the hand below heart level helps blood pool in a cool finger. Raising it does the opposite.

questions.takeaway: Check the meter and the strips before the stick. A working meter cannot rescue an expired or incompatible strip.
questions.strategy: Two things are checked before the puncture: the meter and the strips. The stem confirms one and hands you a problem with the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The meter passed its control check. The strips are expired.
Lowering the hand improves flow. Raising it reduces flow.
The control check covers the meter only.
You do not run a test you already know is unreliable.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: replace the expired strips before the puncture so the value can be trusted.

questions.concept: Before a fingerstick: verify identity, wash and dry hands, check glucometer function, strip compatibility and expiration, and assess the site. Puncture the side of the fingertip and avoid excessive squeezing, which dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old admitted for cellulitis has fingerstick glucose values of 148 mg/dL at 0700 and 171 mg/dL at 1100. At 1630 the value is 194 mg/dL. He is alert, oriented, and eating about half of each meal. He reports no shakiness or sweating. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Document the value as within the inpatient target range
options.rationale: The inpatient target range is 70 to 180. A value of 194 is above it. The rising trend across the day makes it worth acting on.

options.text: Give 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: That treats a low. This patient is high, so extra carbohydrate would push the value further up.

options.text: Assess the patient and review the orders for glucose parameters
options.rationale: Above 180 is hyperglycemia, which calls for assessment and a review of the orders, including any correctional insulin. The steady climb from 148 to 194 adds weight to the finding.

options.text: Give an extra dose of the patient's mealtime insulin
options.rationale: Adding insulin that was never ordered is outside your scope and risks a low later in the evening.

questions.takeaway: Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia. You assess and review the orders. You do not treat it on your own or ignore it.
questions.strategy: Know the edges of the range. 180 is the top of the inpatient target. A value that keeps climbing across the day deserves attention even when he looks well.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 194 is above 180. The values have risen all day.
Carbohydrate treats a low, not a high.
194 is outside the 70 to 180 target.
An unordered insulin dose is outside scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: a value above 180 calls for assessment and a review of the orders.

questions.concept: Under 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia and an immediate safety concern. 70 to 180 mg/dL is the common inpatient target range. Above 180 mg/dL is hyperglycemia requiring assessment and review of orders.

questions.stem: At 0600 a 74-year-old on insulin has a fingerstick glucose of 61 mg/dL. He is awake, sweaty, and able to swallow, so the nurse gives 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. At 0615 the recheck is 66 mg/dL. He says he feels less shaky. His breakfast tray is due at 0730 with NovoLog 4 units ordered. Which action does the nurse take now?

options.text: Give another 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate
options.rationale: The value is still under 70, so treatment is repeated. Feeling better does not mean the glucose has recovered.

options.text: Recheck the glucose again in 15 minutes before treating
options.rationale: The recheck already happened and showed a persistent low. Another wait without treatment lets it fall further.

options.text: Document the improvement and wait for breakfast
options.rationale: The value is still hypoglycemic. The tray is over an hour away, which is too long to leave a low untreated.

options.text: Give the NovoLog early so it is working when breakfast arrives
options.rationale: Insulin is never given to a hypoglycemic patient. It would drive the glucose lower.

questions.takeaway: Treat, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still under 70. The number decides whether he is better. How he feels does not.
questions.strategy: The trap is his symptom report. A rise from 61 to 66 is movement in the right direction, but 66 is still a low.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 66 at the 15 minute recheck is still under 70.
Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.
A value under 70 is not left waiting for a tray.
The recheck is done. The next step is treatment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: the glucose is still under 70, so you repeat the fast-acting carbohydrate.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old is ordered Humalog 6 units with meals and Lantus 18 units daily at 0900. At 0800 his fingerstick glucose is 132 mg/dL. His breakfast tray is placed in front of him. He eats two bites, then says he feels nauseated and pushes the tray away. The nurse has not yet given either insulin. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Give the Humalog now since the tray was delivered
options.rationale: The tray being present is not the point. Food being eaten is. Rapid-acting insulin with no meal behind it creates a low.

options.text: Give half the Humalog dose to match the smaller intake
options.rationale: This improvises a dose that was never ordered. Dose changes come from the provider.

options.text: Hold the Humalog and notify the provider about the reduced intake
options.rationale: Reduced intake is a key cause of inpatient hypoglycemia. Holding the mealtime insulin and reporting the change lets the provider adjust the plan.

options.text: Hold both the Humalog and the Lantus until he can eat
options.rationale: Lantus is long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak. It is not timed to food, so a missed meal does not by itself stop it.

questions.takeaway: Mealtime insulin follows the meal the patient actually eats. Basal insulin is not matched to food.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the Humalog. The tiebreaker is the Lantus. Basal insulin does not depend on the meal, so holding it on that basis is wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He ate two bites. Humalog is mealtime. Lantus is basal.
Rapid-acting insulin with no food behind it causes a low.
A half dose is an unordered dose.
Lantus is not timed to food.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: hold the mealtime insulin and report the reduced intake.

questions.concept: Incorrect insulin type, dose, timing, and reduced intake are the key causes of inpatient hypoglycemia. Mealtime insulin is held until food is present; basal insulin is not timed to food.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing regular insulin 5 units and NPH insulin 12 units in one syringe. She has rolled the NPH vial, injected air into the NPH vial, then injected air into the regular vial. She has withdrawn the regular insulin to the 5 unit mark. She now inserts the needle into the NPH vial. To which mark on the syringe does she withdraw?

options.text: 12 units
options.rationale: This counts only the NPH dose and ignores the 5 units of regular insulin already in the barrel. The patient would receive 7 units of NPH.

options.text: 7 units
options.rationale: This subtracts instead of adding. The syringe already holds 5 units, so the NPH is added on top.

options.text: 17 units
options.rationale: The syringe already holds 5 units of regular insulin. Adding 12 units of NPH brings the total to 17.

options.text: She draws the NPH into a second syringe
options.rationale: The two insulins are ordered together in one syringe. Splitting them adds a second injection with no benefit.

questions.takeaway: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, draw cloudy. The final mark is the total of both doses.
questions.strategy: Once the clear insulin is in the barrel, the syringe keeps counting. You read the combined total when you draw the cloudy dose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 5 units of regular already in the syringe. 12 units of NPH to add.
The order is a single syringe.
7 subtracts the doses instead of adding them.
12 ignores the regular insulin already in the barrel.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: 5 plus 12 is 17 units.

questions.concept: When mixing, inject air into the cloudy NPH vial first, then into the clear vial. Draw the clear insulin first, then the cloudy, so the clear vial is never contaminated with suspension. Long-acting insulins are never mixed.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old receives NPH insulin twice daily. His record shows injections given in the abdomen for the past week. Before today's 0800 dose the nurse inspects his abdomen. She finds a small bruise at yesterday's injection spot in the left lower abdomen. The rest of the abdomen is intact. Which site should she choose?

options.text: An intact spot on the abdomen away from the bruise
options.rationale: One anatomical site is kept and rotation happens within that region. Moving away from the bruise keeps absorption consistent while avoiding damaged tissue.

options.text: The center of the bruise, since it marks the usual site
options.rationale: Bruised tissue is avoided because absorption from it is unreliable.

options.text: The thigh, to give the abdomen time to heal
options.rationale: Moving between regions changes the absorption rate from dose to dose. The rest of the abdomen is intact and still usable.

options.text: The same left lower abdominal area, just at the edge of the bruise
options.rationale: This stays in damaged tissue. Rotation within the site means moving to a clearly intact spot.

questions.takeaway: Stay in one anatomical site and rotate within it. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas.
questions.strategy: The thigh looks kind because it rests the abdomen. It fails because switching regions changes absorption. An intact spot in the same region solves both problems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The bruise is small. The rest of the abdomen is intact.
Bruised tissue is avoided.
The edge of a bruise is still damaged tissue.
Switching regions varies absorption dose to dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: rotate within the abdomen to an intact spot.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin absorption differs by site: abdomen is fastest, then upper arm, then thigh, then buttock or hip. One anatomical site is selected and rotation occurs within that region. Avoid bruised, scarred, inflamed, or damaged areas.

questions.stem: At 1030 a 68-year-old on insulin has a fingerstick glucose of 52 mg/dL. He is alert, diaphoretic, and able to swallow. His heart rate is 112. The nurse gives 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate following the hypoglycemia protocol. Which finding shows that the treatment worked?

options.text: At 1045 his fingerstick glucose is 84 mg/dL
options.rationale: The 15-minute recheck is back above 70. That number is what shows the low has resolved.

options.text: At 1045 he says he feels less shaky and his glucose is 66 mg/dL
options.rationale: He feels better, but 66 is still under 70. The treatment is repeated.

options.text: At 1040 his heart rate is 94 and his skin is drying
options.rationale: Fewer adrenergic signs is encouraging. Without a recheck value you cannot say the glucose has recovered.

options.text: He finished the full 15 g of carbohydrate within five minutes
options.rationale: This shows the treatment was taken. It does not show what the treatment did.

questions.takeaway: Treat, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat if still under 70. The recheck number decides whether the low is resolved. How he feels does not.
questions.strategy: An evaluate question asks for evidence of the outcome. For hypoglycemia the outcome is a glucose back at 70 or above on the 15-minute recheck. Symptom relief and completing the treatment come before that evidence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A glucose of 70 or above on the 15-minute recheck.
66 is still under 70.
Symptoms improved, but there is no recheck value.
This describes the intervention, not the result.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: a recheck of 84 at 15 minutes shows the low has resolved.

questions.concept: For a blood glucose under 70 mg/dL: assess the patient, follow the hypoglycemia protocol, give fast-acting glucose if conscious, recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat treatment if still low. Never give insulin to a hypoglycemic patient.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old newly prescribed NPH insulin was taught subcutaneous injection technique yesterday. Today he gives his 0800 dose into his abdomen as a return demonstration while the nurse observes. Which observation shows that the teaching was effective?

options.text: He rolls the cloudy vial between his palms, pinches the skin, inserts at 90 degrees, and injects without aspirating
options.rationale: Every step matches the taught technique. NPH is rolled to mix the suspension. Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin.

options.text: He shakes the cloudy vial until it looks evenly mixed before drawing up the dose
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. Shaking froths the suspension and makes an accurate dose difficult to draw.

options.text: He pulls back on the plunger to check for blood before injecting
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous insulin administration.

options.text: He withdraws the needle the moment the plunger reaches the bottom
options.rationale: This needs follow-up. The needle is held in place briefly after injecting so the full dose is delivered before it is withdrawn.

questions.takeaway: Roll the cloudy vial, pinch, insert at 90 degrees, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold briefly and withdraw at the same angle.
questions.strategy: In a return demonstration the correct answer is the observation with no error in it. Each wrong option contains one step that was taught against, so read every step in each option.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A demonstration that matches every taught step.
NPH is rolled, not shaken.
Subcutaneous insulin is not aspirated.
The needle is held briefly before it is withdrawn.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: rolling, pinching, a 90 degree angle, and no aspiration show the technique was learned.

questions.concept: Subcutaneous insulin technique: pinch the skin and subcutaneous fat, insert at a 90 degree angle, do not aspirate, inject slowly, hold the needle briefly before withdrawing, withdraw at the same angle, and dispose in a sharps container immediately.
